source: The A.A. Service Manual combined with Twelve Concepts for World Service, 2026-2028 edition (BM-31), plus the 2017-2026 Final Conference Reports where cited ('YYYY Final Report, p. N'). Summaries are paraphrased; quotes are short excerpts with printed page numbers, for personal study. Content audit: 2026-10-20.

nodes.title: Alcoholics Anonymous: the general service structure (U.S./Canada)
nodes.summary: General service is the structure through which the collective conscience of the A.A. groups guides the affairs of "A.A. as a whole." When Bill W. and Dr. Bob began to wonder who would take over from them, Bill proposed that the early leadership be succeeded by the collective conscience of the groups, not by new people. The manual draws the structure as an upside-down triangle. Final authority rests with the groups, and GSRs, districts, area assemblies, the Conference, the General Service Board and the operating corporations each have a part in making the groups' conscience known. Communication runs both ways: questions and proposals travel from the groups through the structure, and information and proposals come back to the groups.
nodes.chosen_by: Not elected. Final authority rests with the A.A. groups, and their collective conscience directs the structure.
nodes.how_many: About 2 million members in 125,000 groups in about 180 countries. The U.S./Canada Conference structure has 93 areas.
duties: Carry the A.A. message (Twelfth Step work) beyond what any single group or intergroup/central office can reach
Bring the collective conscience of the groups to bear on matters affecting A.A. as a whole
Ensure the full voice of A.A. is heard and that needed services keep functioning under all conditions
Pay for A.A. services through voluntary contributions, supplemented by literature sales
facts: About 2 million members, 125,000 groups, about 180 countries (p. 2)
More than 43 million copies of the Big Book, Alcoholics Anonymous, have been distributed in over 70 languages (p. 2)
The co-founders Bill W. and Dr. Bob first met on a May day in 1935 (p. 2)
The service structure 'takes the place of government in A.A.' (p. 2)
The manual grew out of Bill W.'s 'Third Legacy Manual', first drafted in 1951. An overall revision was approved by the 2018 General Service Conference (p. 2)

Bill envisioned one Conference for the whole world. Instead, the U.S./Canada Conference came first, and others followed, such as Great Britain and India. Each is autonomous and none answers to another (p. 2, footnote)
Upside-down triangle, top to bottom: A.A. groups, GSRs, districts, area assemblies, General Service Conference, General Service Board, AAWS/AA Grapevine (p. 3)
There are 93 areas in the U.S. and Canada (Map A, p. 94; p. 4)
The Conference has about 135 members, and area delegates make up at least two-thirds of them (p. 5)
Items approved by a two-thirds majority become Conference Advisory Actions and are referred to the trustees (p. 5)
The trustees have custodial oversight of the two operating corporations, AAWS, Inc. and AA Grapevine, Inc. (p. 5)
Think of AAWS and Grapevine as 'people' and GSO as the 'place' where they work (p. 6)
According to its charter, AA Grapevine cannot accept group contributions. It is self-supporting through magazine subscriptions and content-related sales (p. 6)

quotes.text: The early leadership of A.A. would be succeeded not by new people, but by the collective conscience of the groups in A.A.
General service in A.A. flips this triangle on its head.
In this structure, the groups have final authority.

nodes.title: The A.A. Group (home group)
nodes.summary: The A.A. group, especially a member's home group, is the foundation of the whole service structure. The group meets to form a group conscience on matters that affect A.A. as a whole. The home group is where members take part in business meetings and vote, and each member has one vote. The group elects a GSR, and an alternate GSR, to carry that conscience to the district and area and to bring Conference results back. The groups also fund A.A. services through Seventh Tradition contributions.
nodes.chosen_by: Members choose a home group. The group elects its own GSR and alternate GSR.
nodes.how_many: About 125,000 groups worldwide
duties: Form a group conscience on proposed changes or actions on matters relating to A.A. as a whole
Elect a GSR and an alternate GSR
Decide its Seventh Tradition support for the General Service Board, area, district and intergroup/central office (suggestions are in pamphlet F-3; groups may vary them or not contribute)
Tell the district, area, intergroup/central office and GSO when a new GSR is elected
Hear GSR reports and give the GSR feedback when asked
Decide whether to reimburse its GSR's travel expenses, in whole or in part
facts: The home group is where members take part in business meetings and vote, and it is 'the very basis of the service structure' (p. 7)
Each member has one vote in group conscience matters (p. 7)
Concept I: the A.A. groups hold ultimate responsibility and final authority for world services (p. 7)
The groups provide both the collective conscience of A.A. and the financial support for its services (p. 2)
Two special plans for contributions: the Regular Contribution Plan and the Birthday Plan (p. 8)
When a GSR is elected, the group sends three things: (1) group name and service number, (2) the new GSR's name, address, email and phone, (3) the previous GSR's name (p. 12)
A group may set its own format and time for GSR reports, such as during announcements, at business meetings, or both. Most prefer short reports (p. 11)

If a group decides not to hear a GSR report during a meeting, the report can be shared in writing, by email or group messaging, in a shared online document, or on a noticeboard, while respecting Tradition Eleven and anonymity (p. 12)
A group can suggest a Conference theme through its district meeting or the area delegate (see Appendix U, p. 171) (p. 12)

Two group-level items in Appendix R: the pamphlet 'The A.A. Group Treasurer' (F-96 on aa.org) describes a group treasurer's role and responsibilities, and the 'Accessibilities Checklist' helps a group reduce physical barriers people may meet when attending meetings (p. 163)

quotes.text: The group meets to form a group conscience on proposed changes or actions on matters relating to A.A. as a whole.
the home group is where they participate in business meetings and cast their vote as part of the group conscience of the Fellowship as a whole.
As with all group conscience matters, each member has one vote.

nodes.title: General Service Representative
nodes.summary: The GSR links the group to A.A. as a whole and is the group's voice in general service. GSRs attend district meetings and area assemblies, where they have a voice and a vote. They vote for district and area trusted servants and the area delegate, and they help decide how Seventh Tradition money is used. The job works in both directions: the GSR carries the group's conscience to the district, the area and the delegate, and brings news, literature and Conference actions back to the group.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the group (group conscience)
nodes.term: Two years. In many areas the term coincides with the delegate's panel.
nodes.how_many: One per group (the group's elected GSR), with an alternate
qualifications: At least two years of continuous sobriety
Familiar with the group's history, priorities, traditions and procedures
Able to listen to all points of view
Has time to attend district meetings, area assemblies and the group's business meetings regularly
Working familiarity with the Twelve Traditions and A.A. recovery and service literature
Has an email address or another easy way to keep in touch with group members
Familiar with the GSO and area websites
Has the confidence of the group
duties: Attend area assemblies regularly, with a voice and a vote
Attend district meetings regularly, with a voice and a vote
Report to the group regularly, and carry the members' thoughts, concerns and wishes back to the district
Learn through district and area service meetings, and share what was learned in oral or written reports
Work with the group treasurer on Seventh Tradition support for the GSB, area and district (and intergroup/central office)
Keep the group informed about new literature, new technology applications and accessibility materials
Give the DCM or district registrar up-to-date group information, which is passed on to GSO
Serve as the group's email contact with GSO, receive Box 4-5-9, and keep the group up to date on A.A. activities worldwide
Keep the alternate GSR informed and involved
facts: The GSR votes on district and area trusted servants and on the delegate who represents the area at the Conference (p. 7)
The GSR also votes on how best to use Seventh Tradition contributions for Twelfth Step services (p. 7)
Three ways the group's voice is heard: when the GSR is present, participates, and votes (p. 7)
The weeks between election and the start of the term are a good time to study the manual (p. 9)

Suggested reading: P-19 (GSR), P-16 (The A.A. Group), F-3 (Self-Support), P-17 (A.A. Tradition: How It Developed), P-43 (Twelve Traditions Illustrated; the manual's list prints P-55), P-8 (Twelve Concepts Illustrated), and Bill W.'s 'A.A.'s Legacy of Service' (Appendix A, p. 96) (p. 9)

After GSO is notified, the new GSR receives a kit: welcome letter, Service Manual/Twelve Concepts, pamphlets and leaflets, AAWS literature order form, and Grapevine materials. All service kits can be downloaded from aa.org (p. 12)

Sources for reports: Box 4-5-9, the delegate's report, the DCM's report, 'What's New' on aa.org, the Meeting Guide app, the Conference Final Report, the GSB Quarterly Report, and intergroup lists and newsletters (p. 11)
Each group decides whether to reimburse the GSR's travel, but finances should not be a barrier to service (p. 11)
Any A.A. member may attend district meetings and assemblies, but in most areas only elected GSRs (and alternates when the GSR is absent) may vote (p. 12)
If no successor comes forward, the manual encourages rotation anyway and suggests trying another service role (p. 12)
The GSR has two jobs with the group's conscience: make sure it is heard and fully considered at the district and the area, and make it part of the delegate's thinking at the Conference (p. 4)

Books suggested for a new GSR, besides the pamphlets: Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions (the second half, on the Traditions), Twelve Concepts for World Service (second half of the Service Manual), Alcoholics Anonymous Comes of Age, Our Great Responsibility (Bill W.'s Conference talks 1951-1970) and The Language of the Heart (Bill W.'s Grapevine writings) (p. 9)

When a group elects a new GSR or alternate, it reports the change on the Group Information Change Form (F-28, Appendix I). New GSRs automatically get a digital GSR Kit (print copy on request), and GSO uses GSR information only for service communication and connection within the structure (p. 118)

Concept IX: only GSRs, meeting in assembly (or in caucus), can name committee members and finally the delegates, so groups should choose their GSR with care, and groups that have none should be encouraged to elect one (p. C-27)

quotes.text: The GSR is the link between the group and “A.A. as a whole.”
This communication is a two-way street, making the GSR responsible not only for bringing forward the group’s voice, but for taking back to the group Conference actions
When the GSR votes, the group’s voice is heard.
The GSRs of the U.S. and Canada are the very foundation of our general service structure.

nodes.title: Alternate GSR
nodes.summary: The group elects an alternate GSR to serve when the GSR isn't available. This matters most when the GSR, who has a vote, can't attend a district meeting or area assembly. The alternate may also be asked to give reports to the group. Some alternates attend district meetings, assemblies and service workshops alongside the GSR to learn, but they vote only when the GSR is absent.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the group
nodes.term: Usually the same two-year term as the GSR
nodes.how_many: One per group (the group's elected alternate)
duties: Stand in when the GSR is unavailable, especially to cast the group's vote at a district meeting or area assembly
Give reports to the group when asked
Optionally attend district meetings and area assemblies with the GSR, and volunteer at district and area workshops and service events
facts: An alternate may vote only when the GSR is not present (p. 11)
One of the GSR's listed duties is to keep the alternate informed and involved (p. 9)
Glossary: an alternate assists and supports in the service role and stands ready to step in if the office holder can no longer serve (p. 91)

quotes.text: The alternate GSR is elected by a group to serve on those occasions when the GSR is not available
although an alternate may vote only when the GSR is not present

nodes.title: Service Sponsor
nodes.summary: A service sponsor is an experienced member who helps a GSR or DCM learn the job. They answer questions about responsibilities, the structure, and how to apply the Traditions and Concepts, and they help with making reports. Like all sponsorship, it works by example. The service sponsor also helps a newer member understand the difference between serving the Fellowship's needs and meeting another group member's personal needs. The manual highly recommends a service sponsor for newly elected DCMs who don't already have one.
nodes.chosen_by: Chosen informally by the person in service. The manual suggests looking among people met or heard at area assemblies and service workshops.
nodes.how_many: Informal relationship, not an elected position
qualifications: Knowledgeable in A.A. history and the service structure
Well acquainted with the various service positions and the principles and concepts that guide general service
Familiar with the Twelve Traditions
Familiar with The A.A. Service Manual and the Twelve Concepts
duties: Answer questions about responsibilities, the structure, and the Traditions and Concepts
Share experience on managing time and expectations, and on making reports
Introduce newer members to service, such as setting up meetings, committee work and conferences
facts: More on service sponsorship is in the pamphlet 'Questions & Answers on Sponsorship' (P-15) (p. 10)
A service sponsor is 'highly recommended' for newly elected DCMs who do not already have one (p. 17)

Co-founder Dr. Bob gave four reasons for passing on what he had learned: a sense of duty; it is a pleasure; it repays his debt to the man who passed it on to him; and each time he takes out a little more insurance against a possible slip (p. 10)

quotes.text: A service sponsor can be defined as one alcoholic who has made some progress in recovery and/or performance in service and who is willing to share this experience
The basis of all sponsorship is to lead by example.
by stressing the spiritual nature of service work and by pointing out the usefulness of simple footwork and faith

nodes.title: The District
nodes.summary: A district is a division of an area, usually a cluster of groups located near one another. The district's GSRs make up the district committee and elect a DCM and an alternate DCM. The DCM carries the district's conscience to the area committee and the area assembly. The manual describes three types of district: geographic, linguistic and virtual. A district's size is set by how many groups one DCM can reasonably keep in touch with. A district that grows too large can be split, divided into subdistricts with LCMs, or organized under a DCMC.
nodes.chosen_by: Formed within the area. Boundaries can be redrawn as the number of groups changes (Appendix F, p. 113).
nodes.how_many: Varies by area. Each district belongs to one of the 93 areas.
duties: Serve the district's groups and convey their conscience to the area
Hold regular district meetings of the DCM and GSRs
Elect a DCM and an alternate DCM
Organize workshops and sharing sessions on service
Decide whether to reimburse the DCM's travel expenses
facts: Three types: geographic (the most common), linguistic and virtual (p. 14)
The district committee is typically the current GSRs, the DCM and the alternate DCM (p. 15)
Each GSR has a vote on district matters and in district elections. Whether the DCM and alternate DCM vote depends on the district (p. 15)

Many districts add a treasurer, a secretary and committee chairs. Some districts also form standing or ad hoc committees, and depending on the district, their chairs are elected by the district or appointed by the DCM (p. 15)
A current GSR who also holds one of these district positions still has only one vote (p. 15)
How often district meetings are held varies by district (p. 8)
Options when a district grows too large: split it into new districts, each with its own DCM; create subdistricts with LCMs; or use a DCMC model (p. 113)

Some districts suggest that the treasurer, secretary and committee-chair posts go to past GSRs or experienced group members from the district; depending on the district, they may or may not vote (p. 15)

quotes.text: Groups are organized into districts, generally collections of groups located near one another.
The number of groups in a district is usually determined by how many groups a district committee member, or DCM, can reasonably be expected to keep in touch with
Let the purpose of the district — to serve the district’s groups and convey their conscience to the area — be your guide.

nodes.title: District Committee Member
nodes.summary: The DCM is the voice of the district, just as the GSR is the voice of a group. The district's GSRs elect the DCM. The DCM leads district meetings, guides and informs GSRs, and visits groups, including groups that have no GSR. As a member of the area committee and a voting member of the area assembly, the DCM carries the district's conscience to the area. The manual stresses leading by example and serving with humility: GSRs should be inspired and encouraged, not told what to do.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the GSRs of the district
nodes.term: Two years. In many areas the term coincides with the delegate's panel.
nodes.how_many: One per district (in a large district using the DCMC model, one per subdistrict)
qualifications: Has served as a GSR
At least four or five years of sobriety
Familiar with both the Twelve Traditions and the Twelve Concepts
Has the time and energy to serve the district well
Able to lead a district while respecting its conscience
Has an email address or another easy way to keep in touch with GSRs and members
Familiar with the GSO and area websites
duties: Hold district meetings regularly and report area and GSO news to GSRs. May organize or deliver Conference report-backs in place of the delegate
Attend area assemblies regularly, as a voting member
Reach out to groups in the district that have no GSR
Organize workshops and sharing sessions on service
Bring problems regarding the Traditions to the delegate's attention
Help GSRs learn The A.A. Service Manual/Twelve Concepts, and introduce them to Box 4-5-9 and GSO service material
Alert GSRs to new literature, service materials and technology, and pass their questions to the area and the delegate
Help the delegate or registrar keep group contact information current in GSO's 'Fellowship Connection' database
In many areas, attend area committee meetings in addition to assemblies
facts: The DCM becomes part of the area committee, which is made up of DCMs and area officers (p. 4; glossary p. 91)
At assemblies the DCM votes on area trusted servants (including the delegate), area activities and budgets (p. 15)
Whether the DCM votes at the district level depends on the district (p. 15)
Only the elected DCM, or the alternate DCM when the DCM is absent, may vote at an area meeting. Generally only elected DCMs (and alternates whose DCMs are absent) count toward a quorum (p. 18)
Each district decides how to weigh the qualifications when it votes (p. 15)
The rotating (outgoing) DCM typically briefs the incoming DCM before the new term (p. 17)
A new DCM sets the agenda for the first district meeting as they see fit (p. 17)
The DCM should discuss a travel budget with the district at the start of the term, before spending anything (p. 17)
After the change form (F-43) is submitted, the DCM gets instructions for read-only access to Fellowship Connection (Appendix J, p. 119)
At the end of the term the DCM steps aside, even if no successor is found (p. 18)

Besides voting, the DCM can voice the district's conscience at area assemblies in two ways: by asking questions, making suggestions and proposing new ideas (such as a new way to carry the message or a revision to A.A. literature), and by conveying the district's conscience to the delegate on Conference issues so it becomes part of the delegate's thinking (p. 15)

quotes.text: While the GSR is the voice of a group, the DCM is the voice of a district.
They’ll want to be inspired and encouraged, but not told what to do.
The purpose is not to badger them into electing GSRs, but to begin to connect them to A.A. as a whole.
Here, the DCM is serving as a resource — and not as a replacement for a GSR.
The DCM is the vital link between the group’s GSR, and the area service structure, including the area’s delegate to the General Service Conference.

nodes.title: Alternate DCM
nodes.summary: The alternate DCM is elected by the district's GSRs as the DCM's backup. When the DCM can't attend, the alternate can chair the district meeting and vote on behalf of the district at an area assembly or area committee meeting. If the DCM resigns or can't serve, the alternate often steps in, but the district's GSRs decide how that is handled.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the district's GSRs
nodes.term: Two years
nodes.how_many: One per district
duties: Act as backup for the DCM
Chair the district meeting when the DCM is absent
Vote on behalf of the district at an area assembly or area committee meeting when the DCM is absent
Often step in if the DCM resigns or cannot serve, as decided by the district's GSRs
facts: Votes at area meetings only when the DCM is absent, and generally counts toward an area quorum only then (p. 18)
Depending on the district, may or may not vote at district meetings (p. 15)
Each district decides how to weigh the suggested DCM qualifications when voting for both the DCM and the alternate DCM (p. 15)

quotes.text: The alternate can chair the district meeting and vote on behalf of the district at an area assembly or area committee meeting.
Only the elected DCM or alternate DCM (when the DCM is absent) may vote in an area meeting.

nodes.title: DCM Chair (District Committee Member Chairperson)
nodes.summary: Some large city or county districts use a DCMC. Rather than one DCM serving every group, the large district is divided into as many subdistricts (also called local districts or zones) as needed, and each has its own DCM. The DCMC leads the large district's regular meetings and is the link between that district and the area. Whether the subdistrict DCMs vote at the area committee and assembly depends on the area. The manual covers this role only briefly, in the glossary, Appendix F and the Appendix J change form.
nodes.chosen_by: The manual does not say. It follows local practice. When committee members are added because of growth, the DCM's qualifications and election methods can serve as guidelines (p. 113).
nodes.term: Not specified in the manual (set locally)
nodes.how_many: One per large district organized this way (only some areas use it)
duties: Lead the regular meetings of the large district
Serve as the link between the district and the area
facts: The large district contains subdistricts, local districts or zones, each served by a DCM who may hold regular meetings of GSRs (p. 113)
In some areas those DCMs are voting members of the area committee and assembly. In others they are not (p. 113)
GSO offers a DCMC Kit, and the DCM & DCMC Information Change Form (F-43) covers both roles (Appendix J, p. 119)
The glossary entry 'DCMC: District committee member chairperson' (p. 92) was added in the 2026-2028 edition, as directed by the 76th General Service Conference (editorial updates grid, p. IX)

quotes.text: A large district in a city or county may hold regular meetings led by a DCMC, who serves as the link between the district and the area.
DCMC — District committee member chairperson.

nodes.title: Linguistic District
nodes.summary: To encourage as many groups as possible to take part, some areas include linguistic districts. These are made up of groups that hold their meetings in a particular language; the manual's examples are French, Spanish, Polish, Vietnamese and American Sign Language. A linguistic district usually has a bilingual DCM or liaison, and its boundaries may be independent of the regular geographic districts.
nodes.chosen_by: Created by an area within its own structure
nodes.how_many: Only in some areas
duties: Bring groups that meet in a particular language into the general service structure
Connect those groups to the area through a bilingual DCM or liaison
facts: Example languages: French, Spanish, Polish, Vietnamese, American Sign Language (p. 14)
Usually has a bilingual DCM or liaison (p. 14)
Its boundaries may be independent of the conventional geographic district boundaries (p. 14)
The GSO DCM/DCMC change form offers English, Spanish and French as contact-language options (p. 119)

quotes.text: These districts are made up of groups that conduct meetings in languages including French, Spanish, Polish, Vietnamese and American Sign Language.
They usually have a bilingual DCM or liaison.
Their boundaries may be independent of the conventional geographic district boundaries.

nodes.title: Geographic District
nodes.summary: The geographic district is the most common type. Its size depends on how many groups one DCM can reasonably keep in touch with, learn the problems of, and help to grow. If the number of groups rises or falls significantly, the boundaries can be redrawn.
nodes.chosen_by: Boundaries are set and redrawn within the area (Appendix F)
nodes.how_many: Most districts
facts: The most common type of district (p. 14)
Boundaries may be redrawn when the number of groups changes significantly (p. 14; Appendix F, p. 113)

quotes.text: This is the most common type of district.
District boundaries may be redrawn should the number of groups increase or decrease significantly.

nodes.title: Virtual District
nodes.summary: Some areas have added virtual districts to serve the many online groups that blossomed during the pandemic and are still active. A virtual district is made up of groups, new or previously established, that meet online and want to take part in the general service structure.
nodes.chosen_by: Created by an area within its own structure
nodes.how_many: Only in some areas
facts: Made up of new or previously established groups that meet online (p. 14)

Virtual groups are encouraged to check with their area registrar about their preferred area and district. A group that started in one place and feels rooted there may approach that local district. Some areas have recently created non-geographic districts for virtual groups, and a virtual group with no city or state of its own uses its primary contact's location (p. 117)

quotes.text: To serve the large number of online groups that blossomed in the pandemic and still remain active, some areas have incorporated virtual districts within their structure.

nodes.title: Local Committee Member (subdistricts)
nodes.summary: When a district has too many groups for one DCM, it can divide into smaller subdistricts or local districts, and each one elects a local committee member (LCM). Depending on area practice, LCMs may or may not be voting members of the area committee, and they may or may not hold regular meetings with their GSRs.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected within each subdistrict/local district
nodes.how_many: One per subdistrict, where used
facts: One of three redistricting options: new districts, LCM subdistricts, or the DCMC model (p. 113)
DCM qualifications and election methods can serve as guidelines for these added committee members (p. 113)

quotes.text: A large district could divide itself into smaller districts (often called subdistricts or local districts), each electing a local committee member.

nodes.title: Intergroup/Central Offices (outside the structure)
nodes.role_label: Not in the general service structure
nodes.summary: Intergroup and central offices serve the local groups in their own area. They keep local meeting information, provide meeting lists and literature, run local websites, and answer calls from people seeking help. Each is autonomous. The manual stresses that they are an important part of A.A. but are not part of the general service structure and are not a satellite of GSO. GSO, in New York, serves the whole Fellowship in the U.S. and Canada.
nodes.chosen_by: Each office is autonomous
duties: Maintain local meeting information and websites
Provide meeting lists and other literature
Respond to calls and inquiries from people seeking help
facts: Groups may contribute to their local intergroup/central office as part of Seventh Tradition support (p. 8)
Appendix S (p. 166) covers General Service and Intergroup/Central Offices (p. 6)
In some areas, intergroup/central office liaisons are members of the area assembly, with a voice and sometimes a vote (pp. 20, 25)

Traditionally, intergroup/central offices provide local services, while general service committees keep the groups linked to the General Service Board through the Conference. Some parts of the U.S./Canada structure have no intergroup/central office (p. 25)
A.A. groups may elect a representative to their local intergroup/central office (p. 25)

For working together, the manual points to the pamphlets 'The A.A. Group' and 'Self-Support: Where Money and Spirituality Mix', GSO's Guidelines on Intergroup or Central Offices, and Appendix S (p. 25)

From GSO's FAQ: AAWS and a local intergroup/central office are autonomous of each other. An intergroup is formed by a partnership of groups and is maintained, supervised and supported by them, and the manual calls for friendly collaboration between the two (p. 79).

Long-form Tradition Nine: the groups of a large metropolitan area elect a central or intergroup committee, which often employs a full-time secretary. A GSO listing does not put a group in local meeting lists; that is the intergroup/central office's, district's or area's job (pp. 107, 117)

Just as a group is a partnership of individuals, an intergroup/central office is a partnership of the groups in a community. It handles jobs common to all of them that are best done centrally. Experience shows these offices help most in populous areas, and there are over 800 worldwide (p. 166)

Appendix S suggests ten basic services: answering inquiries (websites, meeting lists, hotlines staffed by sober members); an office with paid workers and/or volunteers; meeting lists and literature sales; information exchange among groups; local PI/CPC with district and area committees; contact with groups in correctional and treatment facilities; local events; a bulletin or newsletter; accessibility information; a website (pp. 166-167)

A central office is often the easiest A.A. resource to find, so professionals and the public frequently contact it first. PI and CPC work is therefore often shared by general service committees and intergroups. Good communication avoids duplicated effort, and the PI and CPC Guidelines and Workbooks are on aa.org (p. 166)

Appendix S suggests meeting from time to time with the matching intergroup committees in your area to share ideas and avoid duplicated effort. What matters is not whether general service or the intergroup does the work, but that it gets done and help is there for the next alcoholic (p. 167)

GSO sends Box 4-5-9, activity updates and AAWS Highlights to every intergroup/central office listed with it. It also gives them advance notice of planned discounts or price changes, so offices should keep their contact information with GSO current (p. 167)

Experience shows that A.A. unity is best served when each group keeps its own direct contact with GSO. Listing with an intergroup/central office does not list a group at GSO, so new groups send a Group Information Form to GSO directly. Some intergroups collect New Group forms so new groups get listed with GSO right away (p. 168)

Appendix S calls intergroup/central offices A.A. service entities “directly responsible to those they serve” (Tradition Nine). Representatives of the local groups form the group conscience that guides the office (p. 168)

To form an intergroup, each group sends a representative and an alternate to a special meeting that creates the intergroup (steering) committee. The committee's outline for the groups covers: which groups take part; support is voluntary and not a condition of membership; the groups maintain the office, each naming a rep and alternate; functions and staffing; newcomer inquiries and press relations; and operating by the Twelve Traditions (p. 169)

quotes.text: While the offices are an important part of A.A., they are not part of the general service structure or a satellite of GSO.
All of A.A. benefits when intergroup/central offices and general service work together in mutual cooperation.
A central or intergroup office is an A.A. service entity that involves partnership among groups in a community
Intergroup/central offices and general service area committees are complementary, rather than competitive, A.A. operations.
Service centers usually have no authority on their own account; they derive it from the participating groups.

nodes.title: Area Assembly
nodes.summary: The area assembly is the meeting at the heart of each delegate area, where the Fellowship's democratic voice is heard. It connects the groups (through their GSRs and DCMs) to A.A.'s decision-making (through the area delegate). Its purpose is generally threefold: elect a delegate to carry the area's conscience to the annual General Service Conference, give the groups a local structure for deciding area matters together, and do Twelfth Step work that is not practical for groups, districts or intergroups to take on by themselves. Each area is autonomous in how it runs its assembly, guided by the Conference's General Warranties (Concept XII).
nodes.chosen_by: Not elected as a body; its voting members are GSRs (elected by their groups), DCMs (elected by the GSRs of their districts), and area officers (elected by the GSRs and DCMs). Area committee chairs are typically appointed by the area chair or elected by the assembly.
nodes.term: Ongoing body. It holds an election assembly once every two years plus regular (non-election) assemblies as often as the area decides.
nodes.how_many: 93 delegate areas in the U.S./Canada Conference; generally one assembly per delegate area (Charter Article 5), with additional assemblies allowed for areas with large A.A. populations or geography that causes communication problems.
duties: Elect the area delegate (and usually the area officers) every two years
Provide a local decision-making structure so groups can collectively decide area matters

Carry out area-wide Twelfth Step work such as accessibility, an area bulletin or newsletter, CPC, corrections, an informational website, language translation, literature (including Grapevine and La Viña), PI and treatment facilities
Take a good look at the agenda of every General Service Conference, and after the Conference hear full reports, question the delegate and decide what may need attention at future Conferences
Hold sharing sessions and workshops on the welfare of A.A.
Send GSO copies of area minutes, notes on sharing sessions and workshops, and letters about meetings (GSO appreciates receiving them)
facts: Typical voting members: GSRs, DCMs, area officers (including the delegate), and, in some areas, area committee chairs (pp. 20-21).
Alternate GSRs and alternate DCMs typically vote only when the GSR or DCM is not present (p. 21).
In some areas, past delegates and intergroup/central office liaisons are assembly members with a voice and sometimes a vote (p. 20).
Assemblies are generally open to all A.A. members, but each group's vote is carried by its GSR (p. 20).
A GSR is typically allowed to vote once the group has submitted the GSR's name to the area registrar or GSO's Operations department (p. 21).
Each group should preferably have its own GSR: one person gets only one vote even if they carry information for two groups (p. 21).
Proxy voting is not a common practice; normally the alternate GSR votes when the GSR is absent (p. 21).
In some areas, GSRs of prison and hospital groups have a vote (p. 21).
Most areas meet quarterly or every other month; a few monthly; where travel distances are great, semiannually or even annually (p. 21).
Assemblies run from half a day to a full weekend; they may meet at a central location, rotate among districts, or be held virtually or hybrid (p. 21).
Each area decides its own quorum; alternate DCMs typically count toward quorum only when the DCM is absent (p. 32).
Substantial unanimity typically means a two-thirds (or more) majority, in some situations three-fourths (or more); simple majority is typically one-half of votes cast plus one (p. 26).
An area may be part of a state or province, all of it, or parts of more than one, depending on the size and needs of the A.A. population (p. 26).
Charter Article 5: assemblies are composed of the elected GSRs of all participating groups, DCMs, and area committee officers (p. 125).
Charter Article 6 (footnote 5): assemblies still meet every two years to elect a delegate, but typically meet far more often for ongoing area business (p. 127).
Each area sets its own assembly schedules and agendas, based on local autonomy and group conscience. DCMs or other area trusted servants can often tell you about them (p. 4)

Most areas welcome any A.A. member to attend assemblies, in recognition of Concept IV and the right of participation; the manual also points to Bill W.'s words in A.A. Tradition, How It Developed (p. 26)

Whether a visiting member may speak at the microphone is up to each area. The member's home-group GSR already gives them a voice, and some areas have guidelines, mindful of Concept V and minority opinion, that let the request be heard while the agenda still gets done (p. 26)

GSO's Group Services assignment welcomes copies of area minutes, sharing-session and workshop notes, and letters about meetings, so it can pass on solutions that worked in one area to areas that need help (p. 21)

In the 1955 Charter each state and province 'will always be entitled to one Assembly', and one 'Assembly' meant one area structure and one delegate vote at the Conference; states or provinces with large A.A. populations could have more. The 1971 Conference allowed a state or province to be joined with another to form one assembly area, and the current text says 'delegate area' instead of 'State or Province' (pp. 121, 123, 127)

quotes.text: At the heart of each area is the assembly meeting, where the democratic voice of our Fellowship expresses itself.
Generally speaking, area assembly meetings are open to all A.A. members, but the group’s vote is carried by the GSR.
There are 93 delegate areas in the U.S./Canada General Service Conference.
“We wish to be just as inclusive as we can, never exclusive.”

nodes.title: Election Assembly
nodes.summary: A special assembly held once every two years at which the area elects its delegate, typically together with the area officers (the alternate delegate is usually elected right after the delegate). It is common for little or no other business to be done. In an election year it is usually held in the fall, giving the newly elected delegate and officers time to prepare to take office in the new panel. The delegate is usually elected by the Third Legacy Procedure, and the chair is advised to stick to it and discourage departures from it.
nodes.chosen_by: The assembly's voting members (per the area's own rules, typically GSRs, DCMs and area officers) vote by written ballot.
nodes.term: Held every two years; the delegate and other area officers are elected for two-year terms and usually take office January 1.
nodes.how_many: One every two years per area; in any one year about half of all area assemblies are electing delegates.
duties: Elect the delegate, then the alternate delegate, then the other area officers (the usual modern order)
Accept DCMs already elected by GSRs in their districts, or recess so GSRs can caucus by district to elect a DCM not elected in advance
Review and approve the election procedure, the area's guidelines on who votes, and the order of election

Send a report of the assembly, with names and addresses of the delegate, officers, committee members and GSRs attending, to the Conference secretary at GSO by December 1 (the chair directs the secretary to do this)
facts: Usually scheduled in the fall of the election year (p. 20).
It is common for little or no other business to be conducted (p. 20).

Sample order of election: early in the growth of the Conference structure the delegate was elected last; more recently the delegate is usually chosen first, followed by the alternate delegate, chairperson, secretary, treasurer, etc. (p. 110).
Those eligible for delegate in the sample format are present or past committee members; some areas ask who wishes to stand, and some allow floor nominations (p. 110).
The chair asks whether anyone is unable to serve, and that person's name is removed (p. 110).
The secretary calls the roll of voting members; two nonvoting members serve as tellers, two collect ballots, and one records and tallies votes (p. 110).
Written ballots are used; some areas use color-coded ballots to speed things up (p. 110).
Any change in the rules should be made before a vote is taken or before an election is conducted (p. 28).

Charter Article 7: whenever practicable, committee members are elected by written ballot without personal nomination, and delegates are chosen from among them by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot (p. 125).
The report to GSO is due by December 1, and those elected usually take office January 1 (p. 110).

The chair announces the procedure for electing committee members and for accepting those already elected by GSRs in their districts. If a district has not elected its DCM in advance, the chair calls a recess so that district's GSRs can caucus and elect one (p. 110)

quotes.text: At this special meeting, held once every two years, the delegate is elected, typically, along with area officers.
In an election assembly, stick to the Third Legacy Procedure and discourage departures from it.
All those elected usually take office January 1.

nodes.title: Third Legacy Procedure
nodes.summary: A.A.'s own election method, used primarily to elect delegates and regional and at-large trustees, and typically area officers too. Voters cast written ballots with one choice each; the first candidate to reach two-thirds of the total vote wins. Low-scoring candidates are withdrawn automatically after ballots 2, 3 and 4. If no one reaches two-thirds by the fourth ballot and the assembly votes against a fifth ballot, or if the fifth ballot also elects no one, the choice is made by lot ('going to the hat'). It looks like it adds chance, but in practice it eliminates the influence of factions, makes railroading a candidate difficult if not impossible, and encourages a well-qualified second-place candidate to stay in.
nodes.chosen_by: Run by the chairperson; the teller draws lots if the election goes to the hat.
nodes.term: Up to five ballots, then the hat.
nodes.how_many: Ballots 1 through 4 (unless someone is elected sooner); Ballot 5 only if a motion, second and simple majority of hands approve it.
duties: Post eligible candidates' names on a board
Each voting member casts a written ballot with one choice; post each candidate's tally
Elect the first candidate who receives two-thirds of the total vote
Withdraw low-scoring candidates automatically after ballots 2, 3 and 4
Decide by lot if no one reaches two-thirds by the final ballot
facts: Any ballot: the first candidate to get two-thirds of the total vote is elected (p. 115).
After ballot 2: anyone under one-fifth of the total vote is withdrawn, but the top two always remain; ties for second all stay in (p. 115).
After ballot 3: anyone under one-third of the total vote is withdrawn, but the top two remain; ties for second all stay in (p. 115).

After ballot 4 (no winner): the candidate with the smallest total is withdrawn, top two remain; the chair then asks for a motion, second, and simple majority of hands to hold a fifth and final ballot (p. 115).
If the fifth-ballot motion is defeated, balloting ends and the choice goes to the hat immediately (p. 115).
If the fifth ballot still elects no one, it goes to the hat with the top two (all tied first-place candidates, or the top candidate plus any tied for second) (p. 115).
The teller draws lots; the first name out of the hat is the delegate (or trustee or other officer) (p. 115).
Bill W.'s draft plan for the first Conference required a two-thirds vote to elect a delegate, with a draw from a hat if no one got it, to pull election pressure down (p. 104).
The glossary says delegates and area officers are typically elected this way by their area's assemblies (p. 93).

Charter Article 10: each area may select one trustee-at-large candidate via Third Legacy procedure, and regional delegates caucus at the Conference using it to narrow the at-large candidates (pp. 125-126).
Conference trustee elections were by paper ballot until 2020 and electronic from 2021, but the physical 'hat' is still used at the fourth or fifth ballot (2021 Final Report, p. 50).

Why the hat: Concept V says that if the majority's candidate lacks two-thirds, putting the name in a hat with the minority's choices gives the minority an equal chance, so no discontented minority trails the new delegate. Concept IX says the method reduced political friction, and the second choice can be as good a delegate, or better (pp. C-17, C-27, C-28)

quotes.text: The first candidate to receive two-thirds of the total vote is elected.
In practice, however, it has proved highly successful in eliminating the influence of factions or parties that seem to thrive on most political scenes.
Lots are then drawn by the teller, and the first one “out of the hat” is the delegate (or trustee or other officer).

nodes.title: Regular (Non-Election) Assembly
nodes.summary: Regular assemblies are typically held several times a year, with each area deciding how many and how far apart. Some areas call them workshops or general sharing sessions, appoint agenda committees, or invite speakers with general service experience. The area assembly is a vital part of the communication process from the group to the Conference: one of its most important items is a good look at the Conference agenda, and after the Conference it hears full reports, asks the delegate questions, and decides what may need attention at future Conferences.
nodes.chosen_by: Typically called by the area chair, who consults the area committee on dates and times and consults officers and committee members on the program.
nodes.term: Several times a year; most areas meet quarterly or every other month.
nodes.how_many: Varies by area: a few meet monthly, while areas with great travel distances may meet semiannually or even annually.
duties: Conduct ongoing area business
Study the Conference agenda (groups and areas inform the delegate of their group conscience through pre-Conference sessions)
Hear the delegate's post-Conference report and question the delegate
Hold sharing sessions and workshops
facts: Some areas keep business to a minimum and spend most of the time on sharing sessions or workshops (p. 20).
Agenda committees may include the officers and GSRs (p. 20).

The sample regular agenda includes the chair's report, the delegate's Conference report or GSO communications, secretary's and treasurer's reports, special committee chairs' reports, district reports, GSR time, a sharing session, intergroup/central office reports, and other business (p. 111).
Usually assemblies are not held during conventions, but occasionally they take place just before or after (p. 24).
Where travel distances are great and assemblies meet only twice a year or once a year, more emphasis is placed on district meetings, which GSRs can reach more easily (p. 21)

The sample regular agenda also includes videos from GSO, a newsletter editor's report, a brief 'information session' on GSO services led by the delegate, and local problems, ideas and suggestions (p. 111)

quotes.text: Each area decides for itself on the number — and interval between — meetings.
Most areas hold assembly meetings quarterly or every other month (a few meet monthly).
Many Conference agenda items follow a path from the A.A. group through the GSR and on through the district and area.

nodes.title: Sharing Sessions
nodes.summary: In an area sharing session everyone may contribute ideas and opinions about A.A.'s welfare, and no one is asked to defend what they say. A chair or leader, perhaps a current area officer or an experienced person from outside the body, functions more as timekeeper or referee than participant. Each person may talk for a set time (1-2 minutes is common), and usually no one speaks twice on a subject until all who wish to have spoken. Afterward, members may propose ideas as agenda items for future assemblies, DCMs may raise them at district meetings, and GSRs may take them back to their groups.
nodes.chosen_by: A chair or leader is selected, perhaps a current area officer or someone from outside the body experienced in conducting sharing sessions.
duties: Use a format that draws out even the shyest participant and keeps the more vocal from dominating
Keep the discussion going until the topic has been fully explored
Have a member take notes, typically without attributing comments to individuals by name, group or service position
facts: Speaking time of 1-2 minutes is common, but whatever the body agrees on is fine (p. 22).
Comments are typically not attributed by name, group or service position; the emphasis is on content (p. 22).
Area officers, committee chairs, GSRs and DCMs may propose ideas from a sharing session as agenda items for future assemblies (p. 23).
The glossary defines a sharing session as a meeting where everyone is invited to contribute and no actions are taken (p. 93).
Past delegates are sometimes asked to chair area sharing sessions (p. 30).

Conference-wide: a 2023 Advisory Action has all Conference members meet 'for general sharing sessions at least two times per year utilizing virtual meeting technology'; the GSB chair and the Delegate Chair set the dates and topics (2023 Final Report, p. 37).
The board also holds a General Sharing Session at each quarterly board weekend (p. 61).

Suggested topics: what to add, change or drop at assemblies; how to draw more GSRs; problems groups have faced and what worked; how districts help groups; whether A.A. literature could be more effective and inclusive; and whether groups support local, district, area and GSO services (pp. 22-23)

quotes.text: Each person offers an opinion and is not asked to defend it.
Usually no one is permitted to speak twice on the same subject until all who wish to have spoken.

nodes.title: Area Committee
nodes.summary: The area committee is focused on the health of the area, meaning growth and harmony in the Fellowship, and generally serves as the area's steering committee. It is typically made up of all the DCMs, the area officers (including the delegate and alternate delegate), and the chairs of area service committees. If GSRs are lax, a district lacks harmony, or there are difficulties in Public Information or another service, a committee member usually knows it and can turn to the full committee for help. Whether past delegates sit on it, and whether they vote, is decided by the group conscience of the area assembly.
nodes.chosen_by: DCMs are elected by the GSRs in their districts; area officers are elected by the GSRs and DCMs; service committee chairs are typically appointed by the area chair or elected by the assembly.
nodes.term: Two-year terms; the panel cycle frequently applies to area committee officers and members (Charter Article 8: concurrent two-year terms).
nodes.how_many: One per area (93 areas).
duties: Watch over growth and harmony in the area
Make sure experience is being shared among groups
Make sure the A.A. message reaches hospitals, prisons, jails and rehabilitation centers
Keep news media and professionals who deal with alcoholics informed about A.A.
See that new groups and Loners are visited and helped
Keep the area solvent and report regularly to GSRs on finances
When a new committee is elected, see that GSO gets contact information for incoming officers and committee chairs (the outgoing delegate is asked to provide it)
facts: Typical composition: all DCMs, area officers including the delegate and alternate delegate, and chairs of area service committees (p. 27).
Past delegates: some areas seat them on the committee with or without a vote; others seat only the outgoing delegate, with or without a vote (p. 27).
When a new area committee is elected, the outgoing delegate is asked to give GSO contact information for all incoming area officers and committee chairs (p. 32).
That information is stored in GSO's database, which the area registrar can also access (p. 32).
The area chair is the 'administrative leader'; the delegate could be described as the 'communications leader' (p. 32).
For terms of office of area officers, the manual points to Article 8 of the Conference Charter (p. 30).

quotes.text: The area committee is especially focused on the health of the area and thus on growth and harmony in the A.A. Fellowship.
The decision on the status of past delegates in the area is up to the group conscience of the area assembly.
The area committee generally serves as a steering committee for the area.

nodes.title: Area Officers
nodes.summary: Area officers are elected by the GSRs and DCMs to serve the area. The usual officers are the delegate, alternate delegate, chair, secretary, registrar and treasurer, along with other officers who lead special activities, usually service committee chairs. Each area's conscience decides the exact duties and qualifications, and several areas have written procedures that are passed from outgoing to incoming officers. Some areas select alternates for all committee officers, especially the chair, to provide continuity.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the GSRs and DCMs at the election assembly, typically by Third Legacy Procedure (in the usual modern order, after the delegate and alternate delegate). Committee chairs are typically appointed by the area chair or elected by the assembly.
nodes.term: Two years; the two-year panel cycle frequently applies to area committee officers too. Those elected usually take office January 1.
nodes.how_many: Typically chair, secretary, registrar and treasurer (plus delegate and alternate delegate); some areas add a Finance chair, alternates for each officer, and various service committee chairs.
qualifications: A solid period of sobriety for each office (chair: minimum three to five years)
Service experience: for chair, group, intergroup/central office, institutional and/or area affairs; for secretary, group, intergroup/central office or general service affairs
Skills that fit the office: communication and leadership (chair), office and computer skills (secretary, registrar), accounting or bookkeeping (treasurer)
Alternates generally need the same qualifications as the position they may step into
duties: Chair: preside over assemblies and run area business
Secretary: record and distribute minutes, keep mailing lists
Registrar: keep group and trusted-servant records accurate, working with GSO through Fellowship Connection
Treasurer: keep financial records and manage Seventh Tradition funds
Committee chairs: lead special activities such as PI, CPC, corrections/treatment, literature, archives
facts: Sample order of election: delegate, alternate delegate, chairperson, secretary, treasurer, etc. (p. 110).
Some areas have a Finance chair in addition to the treasurer; the area's conscience sets their respective duties and qualifications (p. 29).
Alternate officers may or may not be seated as voting members, depending on local decision (p. 30).
Several areas have written procedures for all aspects of area operations, typically passed from outgoing to incoming officers (p. 21).
The two-year panel cycle frequently applies to area committee officers and committee members too (p. 130).

quotes.text: Area officers — elected by the GSRs and DCMs to serve the area
Several areas have developed written procedures for all aspects of area operations.
Qualifications of alternates are generally the same as the qualifications for the positions they may be called upon to assume.

nodes.title: Area Chair
nodes.summary: The area chair presides over assemblies and is the area's 'administrative leader', focused on area business, while the delegate could be described as its 'communications leader'. The chair consults the area committee before setting assembly dates, makes sure members are notified, and consults officers and committee members on the agenda. The chair also keeps the delegate informed about the area and makes sure committee members know what goes on in world services. At an election assembly the chair should stick to the Third Legacy Procedure and discourage departures from it.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the assembly (GSRs and DCMs), usually after the delegate and alternate delegate in the sample order.
nodes.term: Two years (area officer term).
nodes.how_many: One per area; some areas also select an alternate chair (alternates are especially recommended for the chair).
qualifications: A solid period of sobriety (minimum three to five years)
Experience in group, intergroup/central office, institutional and/or area affairs
Sound understanding and appreciation of the Steps, Traditions and Concepts and experience applying them to local problems
Communication skills
Leadership qualities
Sensitivity to the wishes of the local area
duties: Preside over area assembly meetings
Consult the area committee before setting dates and times of assemblies
Make sure assembly members are notified of meeting dates and times
Consult officers and committee members on the program/agenda
Keep the delegate informed about what is going on in the area
Make sure committee members know what goes on in world services
facts: Chairing tips: keep motions clear and succinct, and keep attention on one subject at a time without private conversations (p. 28).
On simple matters a majority vote is enough, and a 'sense of the meeting' can sometimes replace a vote (p. 28).
Any rule changes should be made before a vote is taken or an election conducted (p. 28).
If both the area chair and alternate chair are unable to serve, the delegate may assume added responsibility (p. 34).

quotes.text: Generally speaking, the area chair runs an assembly and is the “administrative leader” of the area, focused on the business of the area.
On simple matters, a majority vote is enough — even a “sense of the meeting” can take the place of a vote at times.

nodes.title: Area Secretary
nodes.summary: The secretary records and distributes minutes of area meetings, keeps mailing lists current, sends area mailings, and, if the area conscience asks for it, prepares lively bulletins to encourage attendance at committee meetings and assemblies. The secretary can also act as a liaison between officers and committee members. In the sample election-assembly format, the secretary calls the roll of voting members and, at the chair's direction, sends the election report to GSO.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the GSRs and DCMs as an area officer, usually at the election assembly.
nodes.term: Two years (area officer term).
nodes.how_many: One per area.
qualifications: Some service in group, intergroup/central office or general service affairs
Some background in general office work
Computer knowledge and IT skills that reflect the area's needs
Ability to create a record that captures the essentials of a meeting
A solid period of sobriety
duties: Record and distribute minutes of area meetings
Keep mailing lists up to date and send out area mailings
Prepare lively bulletins encouraging attendance, if the area conscience asks for this
Act as a liaison between officers and committee members
facts: At an election assembly the secretary calls the roll of voting members (p. 110).
The chair directs the secretary to send the election report to the Conference secretary at GSO by December 1 (p. 110).

quotes.text: Records and distributes minutes of area meetings
Ability to create a record of a meeting that captures the essentials of what happened

nodes.title: Area Registrar
nodes.summary: The registrar keeps records of all groups in the area and contact details for the area's trusted servants, and works with GSO's Operations department to keep that information current. The role has evolved with Fellowship Connection, an interface that facilitates information sharing between areas and GSO, and registrars are often the first point of contact for group and trusted-servant data. Duties vary by area, but accurate information and clear communication are the foundation of the role.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the GSRs and DCMs as an area officer (the manual does not describe a separate process for this office).
nodes.term: Two years (area officer term).
nodes.how_many: One per area.
qualifications: Training on Fellowship Connection (required)
Familiarity with computer systems and spreadsheet tools, plus an understanding of data stewardship (helpful)
Familiarity with the area and district structure, and ability to communicate throughout it
Ability to organize, communicate and manage detailed information, and to relay information by email
Ability to responsibly handle and protect personal information
A solid period of sobriety
duties: Maintain records of all groups: name, meeting location, and GSR or group contact
Keep names, addresses, emails and phone numbers current for GSRs, DCMs, district and area officers, and area committee members
Work with GSO's Operations department to keep area information up to date
Enter and update data, use search filters, and download standard and custom reports
facts: A GSR is typically allowed to vote once the group has submitted the GSR's name to the area registrar or GSO Operations (p. 21).
Incoming officer and committee-chair contact information is stored in GSO's database, which the area registrar can also access (p. 32).

Groups can return the New Group Form (F-30), Group Information Change Form (F-28) and DCM & DCMC Information Change Form (F-43) locally by emailing the area registrar. A new group's 30-day pending period starts once GSO or the registrar logs its complete information (pp. 117-119)

quotes.text: Registrars often are a crucial first point of contact for A.A. groups and trusted servants’ data.
area registrars will require training on Fellowship Connection, a user-friendly interface that facilitates information sharing between areas and GSO.

nodes.title: Area Treasurer
nodes.summary: The treasurer keeps the area's financial records, reports regularly to the assembly, and receives and manages the area's Seventh Tradition funds. The treasurer also encourages contributions to area and GSO services and stays abreast of tax and legal considerations. Some areas also have a Finance chair, and the area's conscience sets the duties and qualifications of each.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the GSRs and DCMs as an area officer, usually at the election assembly.
nodes.term: Two years (area officer term).
nodes.how_many: One per area (some areas also have a Finance chair).
qualifications: A solid period of sobriety
Organizational skills for good record-keeping; accounting or bookkeeping experience
Computer skills appropriate for the position
Ability to explain financial matters to an audience without the same financial skills
duties: Keep the area's financial records
Report regularly to the assembly
Receive and manage the area's Seventh Tradition funds
Encourage contribution support for area and GSO services
Stay abreast of tax and legal considerations
facts: Most areas maintain solvent treasuries and report regularly to their GSRs on the financial picture (p. 31).

In the sample regular-assembly format, the treasurer's report is a good time to mention the leaflet 'Self-Support: Where Money and Spirituality Mix', a guide for groups planning their regular contributions (p. 111)

quotes.text: Receiving and managing the area’s Seventh Tradition funds
Ability to speak about financial matters to an audience that does not have the same financial skills

nodes.title: Area Service Committee Chairs
nodes.summary: Besides the core officers, an area committee usually has other officers who are responsible to the committee for special activities, chiefly the chairs of service committees. They are typically members of the area committee and, in some areas, vote at the assembly. The manual's list is only examples, so each area decides which committees it needs.
nodes.chosen_by: Typically appointed by the area chair or elected by the assembly.
nodes.term: The two-year cycle frequently applies to area committee members.
nodes.how_many: Varies by area.
duties: Lead the area's work in their service field
Report to the area committee and the assembly (e.g., committee chairs' reports in the sample regular agenda, p. 111)
facts: Example committees: Public Information; Cooperation with the Professional Community; Correctional and Treatment Facilities; Literature; Grapevine and La Viña; Archives; Area Convention; Accessibilities/Remote Communities; Finance; Liaison (to Intergroup/Central Offices); Translations; Technology (p. 29).
Some areas allow committee chairs to vote at the assembly (p. 21).
An intergroup/central office liaison has a vote at the assembly in some areas, and a voice but no vote in others (p. 25).
It has been found prudent for a committee, rather than one or two individuals, to run newsletters and websites (pp. 23-24).
Archives committees collect and preserve area history: written materials, photographs and audiotapes (p. 23).

quotes.text: An area committee usually has other officers who are responsible to the committee for special activities.
Area committee chairs — typically appointed by the area chair or elected by the assembly

nodes.title: Past Delegates
nodes.summary: Past delegates are a wealth of experience. Rotation keeps them from succeeding themselves or returning later as delegate, but a role can often be found for them that doesn't interfere with the current delegate or area committee. They are typically asked not to hold office as GSRs or DCMs and are encouraged to serve in other ways, such as research on service or Traditions questions, workshops, chairing sharing sessions or conventions, or Grapevine work. The assembly's group conscience decides their status on the area committee, and in some areas they are assembly members with a voice and sometimes a vote.
nodes.chosen_by: Not elected to the role; a delegate becomes a past delegate on rotating off. In some areas, special assignments come at the request of the area committee.
nodes.term: Permanent status; rotation prevents them from serving as delegate again.
nodes.how_many: Varies; since delegates serve two-year terms, an area typically gains a past delegate about every two years (inference, not stated in the manual).
duties: Lead research and develop answers on service or Traditions issues when asked
Chair area sharing sessions
Speak at special meetings that inform members about A.A. worldwide
Conduct workshops or orientations for new GSRs
Serve as Grapevine Representative
Chair an area convention committee, an area PI committee, or a state/provincial convention
Support new delegates
facts: Rotation prevents delegates from succeeding themselves or from returning later as delegates (p. 30).
Multiple Conference Advisory Actions have suggested past delegates get involved with Grapevine (p. 30).
Some areas seat past delegates on the area committee with or without a vote; others seat only the outgoing delegate (p. 27).
In some areas past delegates are assembly members with a voice and sometimes a vote (p. 20).
Several regions hold annual meetings of past and current delegates and their alternates, typically to help new delegates prepare for the Conference and strengthen communication (p. 30).
Archives committees seek local A.A. history from oldtimers, past delegates and others (p. 23).

The one-year wait after a delegate's last Conference also applies to applying as a nontrustee director of AAWS or Grapevine and as an ACM: 'A General Service Conference delegate is not eligible to apply until one year after their last Conference' (2021 Final Report, p. 49).
Example of a regional meeting of delegates: the Southwest's SWRDA, every March in Oklahoma City (see Regions).

Some regional delegate meetings now last a full weekend. They aim to prepare new delegates and strengthen communication among the Conference, GSO, the General Service Board, the Grapevine Board and A.A. as a whole, rather than to work on one area issue (p. 30)

quotes.text: the A.A. practice of rotation prevents delegates from succeeding themselves or from returning later as delegates
Past delegates are typically asked not to hold office as GSRs and DCMs, but are instead encouraged to find other ways to become involved in area service.
Past delegates often step forward, too, willing and able to support new delegates in any way they can.

nodes.title: Area Finances
nodes.summary: Supporting an area committee costs little compared with comparable activities in business firms and other organizations, but it still needs enough money or its work will be hampered. Most areas keep solvent treasuries and report regularly to their GSRs. Typical expenses include administration, literature, assembly meetings, committee travel, the delegate's travel, and a contribution toward the cost of the Conference. Methods some areas use to stay solvent include Seventh Tradition collections, group contributions under a contribution plan, and contributions from area and state convention treasuries.
nodes.chosen_by: Managed by the area treasurer (and Finance chair, where one exists) under the area's conscience.
nodes.how_many: Each area is asked to send at least $3,000 USD to the GSB to help defray the cost of the annual Conference meeting.
duties: Fund administrative costs: photocopies, postage, mass-email services, website hosting
Support public information programs and buy literature for groups in institutions
Pay assembly venue rental, and sometimes meals or transportation
Cover committee and delegate travel
Contribute toward the annual Conference
facts: Expenses vary with each area's needs and conscience and with whether events are in person, hybrid or virtual; virtual events and translation/interpretation can add costs (p. 31).
Each area is asked to send at least $3,000 USD to the GSB to help cover the annual Conference meeting; some send less and some more (p. 31).
No delegate will be denied attendance at the Conference if the area cannot afford the full amount (p. 31).
Support methods: Seventh Tradition collections at assemblies and district meetings, group contributions under a contribution plan, and contributions from area and state convention treasuries (p. 31).
Many area treasuries support the alternate delegate's expenses separately from the delegate's (p. 35).

quotes.text: each area is asked to send at least $3,000 USD to the General Service Board (GSB) to help defray the cost of the annual meeting of the Conference.
no delegate will be denied attendance at the Conference if their area cannot afford the full amount.

nodes.title: Area Delegate
nodes.summary: The delegate is elected by the area assembly to carry the area's conscience to the annual General Service Conference, a weeklong meeting generally held in April in New York, and to bring the results back to the area. Under Concept III, delegates are primarily world servants of A.A. as a whole and only secondarily area representatives, so on final decisions they may vote by their own best judgment and conscience. When they vote differently from what they know their area's conscience to be, they are asked to report this and their reasons to the area. Delegates are involved in Conference matters all year, and the manual says the delegate could be described as the area's 'communications leader'.
nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the area assembly at the election assembly, usually by Third Legacy Procedure. Under Charter Article 7, delegates are selected from among area committee members by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot.
nodes.term: One term of two consecutive years; a single term is strongly recommended. Delegates attend two Conferences.
nodes.how_many: 93, one per delegate area; about half are elected each year (odd and even panels).
qualifications: Active participation in local and area affairs as a GSR and as an area committee member for at least several years
Sufficient time to prepare for and attend the weeklong Conference (generally in April), plus the work before and after
Five or six years of continuous sobriety (the requirement varies by area)
Experience chairing business or service meetings
Knowledge of A.A. affairs, and of where to find correct information
Thorough familiarity with the Twelve Traditions and Twelve Concepts and how they apply to local problems
Ability to be open-minded and listen to different points of view
Willingness to discuss and act on vital matters with area members and other delegates
duties: Attend the annual Conference fully prepared
Communicate Conference actions to area committee members and encourage them to pass the information on to groups and intergroup/central offices
Help generate interest in serving as GSRs, DCMs and area officers, and inspire greater assembly participation
Be prepared to attend all area and regional service meetings and assemblies
Help area committees encourage Seventh Tradition support for the area, GSO and local services
Provide leadership in solving local problems involving the Traditions
Remind GSRs to inform groups and members about Grapevine, La Viña and Conference-approved literature
Pass along GSO's calls for résumés for trustee and nontrustee director positions
Cooperate with GSO in obtaining group records and periodic membership survey information
Visit groups and districts whenever possible
Assume added responsibility if the area chair and alternate chair cannot serve, or help remedy an area committee that isn't functioning effectively
Keep the alternate delegate fully informed and active
Late in year two, pass a basic knowledge of Conference proceedings to newly elected delegates
facts: The Fellowship has elected area delegates since 1951 (p. 33).
Immediately upon election, each delegate is put on GSO's mailing list for Conference materials and given a Conference dashboard password (p. 33).
Support comes from fellow delegates, past delegates, GSO staff, a service sponsor, and area pre-Conference sessions (p. 33).
The Conference week schedule runs from 9:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., sometimes later or earlier (p. 36).
Each area is asked to contribute toward the delegate's Conference expenses; the GSB General Fund pays the balance (p. 36).
Each delegate receives a cash advance on arrival in New York for basic Conference-week expenses (p. 36).
Delegates make their own travel arrangements; GSO handles all housing details (p. 36).
Areas are asked to cover the delegate's travel costs for reporting back, and many set annual travel budgets (p. 36).
Some areas rotate the delegate geographically, but no well-qualified A.A. should be passed over for geographic rotation (p. 39).
Delegates, trustees, nontrustee directors and AAWS/Grapevine staff members attend the Conference as voting members (p. 39).
Suggested preparation: read or reread A.A. Comes of Age, the Twelve Concepts and the manual, and review full Conference Reports for the past two or three years (p. 35).

Before standing for delegate, the manual suggests asking yourself: Did you enjoy and contribute to your GSR, DCM or committee service? Do you have the time? Have you talked it over with your family and employer? Do you know this manual, A.A. Comes of Age, and the Steps, Traditions and Concepts? Have you asked past delegates what the work involves? (pp. 34-35)

To prepare for a first Conference, new delegates can draw on past delegates, regional trustees and GSO staff. Second-year delegates, with more personal relationships, have an even wider circle to call on (p. 35)

GSO will ask each delegate for material before the Conference, and a prompt reply helps get it into a report, panel discussion, workshop, floor discussion or committee agenda item. Later GSO also asks for arrival time, transportation costs and hotel details (p. 36)

Delegates have three kinds of expense: attending the Conference, reporting back to groups and districts, and serving the area through each year of the term. Many areas set an annual travel budget so the delegate can accept invitations without waiting for assembly approval, and recent past delegates' expenses can help set it (p. 36)

Concept III: the groups may instruct their delegate, but a delegate who cannot vote their own conscience on a final Conference vote is 'just a messenger', not a trusted servant. Concept IV adds that delegates meet only a few days a year, so they can't know many problems firsthand (pp. C-9, C-14)

In 1990 the Conference recommended that delegates establish and maintain contact with the intergroup/central offices in their areas. The aim was to share Conference information and make sure those offices have a voice in the Fellowship through the existing service structure (p. 167)

quotes.text: A delegate serves one term of two consecutive years.
Conference Delegates are primarily the world servants of A.A. as a whole, that only in a secondary sense do they represent their respective areas.
The delegate could be described as the area’s “communications leader”
Delegates are charged with understanding the experiences, viewpoints and group conscience of their areas, while assuming responsibility for the U.S./Canada Conference as a whole.

nodes.title: Alternate Delegate
nodes.summary: Areas also elect an alternate delegate, a valuable assistant who often travels with the delegate or gives reports for them, and who in some areas has a special function on the area committee. The alternate should be prepared to step in: while standing in, they have all the rights, privileges and responsibilities of a delegate until the delegate can serve again. The delegate is expected to keep the alternate fully informed and active. An alternate who attends one Conference in the delegate's place may still be elected later to a full term.
