nodes.chosen_by: Elected by the area assembly at the election assembly by the same procedure as the delegate (usually Third Legacy), normally right after the delegate.
nodes.term: Two years, on the same cycle as the delegate.
nodes.how_many: Typically one per area.
qualifications: Generally the same as for the position they may be called on to assume (the manual's general rule for alternates, p. 30)
duties: Assist the delegate, often traveling with them or giving reports for them
Serve any special function the area committee assigns (in some areas)
Stay informed and active so they can step in for the delegate
Serve the area eagerly so they are prepared to step in
facts: The alternate delegate is typically a member of the area committee (p. 27).
In the sample election format, the alternate is elected next after the delegate by the same procedure (p. 110).
Many area treasuries support the alternate's expenses separately from the delegate's (p. 35).
An alternate who attends one Conference in place of the delegate may still be elected to a full term (p. 35).
Since the alternate may stand in the next area election for delegate, this experience is not wasted (p. 39).
Regional meetings of past and current delegates also invite their alternates (p. 30).

quotes.text: An alternate, when stepping in, acts with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities of a delegate until the delegate is again available to serve.
The alternate serves as a valuable assistant, often traveling with the delegate or giving reports for them.
An alternate delegate may, after attending one Conference in place of the delegate, be elected to serve a full term.

nodes.title: Panels (Odd / Even)
nodes.summary: A panel is the numbered group of delegates elected to begin serving at the General Service Conference in the same year; the number is that of the first Conference they attend. Because delegate terms are two years, about half the areas elect in one year and half in the next, so every Conference has a core of experienced delegates alongside first-year ones. The Conference began in 1951 with Panel 1 (37 delegates), and Panel 2 added 38 delegates in 1952. Today there are 93 areas, each listed in Appendix M as odd or even. The two-year cycle frequently applies to area committee officers and members as well, and about half the groups elect GSRs in any one year.
nodes.chosen_by: Fixed by each area's odd/even listing in Appendix M.
nodes.term: Each panel serves two consecutive Conferences.
nodes.how_many: Two panels sit at every Conference (first-year and second-year). Appendix M lists 48 odd-panel areas and 45 even-panel areas (93 total).
duties: Give the Conference continuity by rotating about half its delegates each year
facts: Each panel is numbered for the Conference where its delegates first serve; e.g., delegates first attending the 63rd Conference are Panel 63 (p. 130).
1951 (odd year) = Panel 1 with 37 delegates; 1952 (even year) = Panel 2 with 38 delegates added (p. 130).
Since Panel 1 met in 1951 and the Conference meets yearly, Panel N first serves in the year 1950 + N (e.g., Panel 76 = 2026). This is arithmetic from p. 130, not a statement in the manual.

Election assemblies are usually held in the fall (p. 20), those elected usually take office January 1 (p. 110), and the Conference is generally held in April (pp. 31, 34); so a new panel's first Conference is normally the April after its election (inference).
States with several areas may split them between odd and even; e.g., Texas Areas 65 and 67 are odd, 66 and 68 are even (pp. 131-132).
In any one year about half the groups are electing GSRs and half the area assemblies are electing delegates (p. 130).
Charter Article 8: GSR, area committee and delegate terms are concurrent two-year terms, with about half the areas electing in even years and half in odd years (p. 125).
Bill W.'s original plan: after Panels One and Two, one panel would be elected and one retired each year, so the Conference rotates while keeping continuity (p. 104).

quotes.text: A panel is a numerical designation that refers to a group of delegates elected to begin serving at the General Service Conference in a particular year.
Each panel is numbered for the Conference at which the area’s delegate will first serve.
This ensures that at any Conference, there is a core of experienced delegates alongside first-year delegates.

nodes.title: Delegate's Report-Back
nodes.summary: Reporting to groups, districts and the area after the Conference is a vital part of every delegate's job, and some call it the 'report-back'. Experience suggests delegates may want to consult the area committee before the Conference to arrange times and places for their reports. Some visit as many groups as possible in the weeks and months afterward; where distances are great, some focus on the assembly and district meetings and rely on GSRs to carry the information to groups. Reports may be printed, emailed, posted on the area website or videotaped, always protecting anonymity, while traditional methods stay important for members without computer or internet access.
nodes.chosen_by: Delivered by the delegate; the alternate may give reports for them, and where an area is too large to cover in person, officers and committee members share the load.
nodes.term: The weeks and months following each annual Conference.
duties: Consider arranging report times and places with the area committee before the Conference
Report at the area assembly, district meetings and group business meetings
Provide printed or digital versions that GSRs can pass on
Consider offering reports to intergroup/central offices
Learn from GSRs and committee members how groups and members reacted
facts: Areas are asked to cover the delegate's travel and incidental expenses for reporting back (p. 36).
With groups, delegates are unlikely to have as much time and attention as at an assembly, so 'less is likely to be more' (p. 37).
Digital options must keep anonymity at the public level: anonymity-protected website posts, emailed files, or anonymity-protected video (p. 37).
If the area is too large to cover in person, the delegate asks area officers and committee members to share the load (p. 33).

Besides asking for time on group business-meeting agendas, delegates may find that some groups offer time during regular A.A. meetings. This direct contact also stirs interest in the service structure among groups and members (p. 37)
Delegates often study report-backs given by previous delegates in their area and the area's customs, and their own style shapes the report too (p. 37)
Reporting to the Fellowship starts before the Conference: the advance information sent to delegates includes significant questions for them to take to their areas for input (p. 43)

No delegate can report everything. Over the years GSO and delegates built a reporting system together: many proceedings are written up in the Conference manual, delegates add their own notes, and the Final Conference Report later records all reports, presentations, workshops and actions (p. 43)

Bill W. on the first delegates (1951): some came home discouraged that members did not 'take fire' as they had, forgetting they had been eyewitnesses and the members had not. Yet 'they made an impression much greater than they knew' (p. 105)

quotes.text: Reporting to groups, districts, and the area back home following the annual meeting is a vital part of every delegate’s job.
Less is likely to be more.
Traditional methods of communication, such as sending printed information through the mail or making it widely available at service meetings in the areas, remain important.
Groups take note when their GSRs are inspired and passionate about what they have to report.
hence the delegate’s job of reporting is as important as the Conference program.

nodes.title: General Service Conference
nodes.summary: The General Service Conference is where the collective group conscience of U.S./Canada A.A. comes together. It operates all year round, but its annual meeting (usually in April; under the Charter it meets yearly in New York unless otherwise agreed) is the culmination of the year, when it takes actions that guide the groups in the years ahead. It comes closer to a governing body than anything else in A.A.: it can issue orders to the General Service Office, but it can never mandate or govern the Fellowship. The Conference itself is not incorporated; the General Service Board, A.A. World Services, Inc. and AA Grapevine, Inc. are, so they can handle funds and conduct A.A.'s business.
nodes.chosen_by: Not elected as a body. Under Charter Article 2 it is composed of area delegates (elected by area assemblies), the trustees of the General Service Board, directors of AAWS and AA Grapevine, and staff members of the Grapevine and General Service Office.
nodes.term: Ongoing body; the annual meeting lasts a full week, usually in April
nodes.how_many: About 135 voting members
duties: Guard A.A.'s world services and the Twelve Steps, Twelve Traditions and Twelve Concepts (Charter Art. 1)
Hear the financial and policy reports of the General Service Board and its related corporate services (Charter Art. 11)
Advise the trustees, directors and staff, engage in debate, appoint necessary committees and pass suitable resolutions, now called Advisory Actions (Charter Art. 11)
Discuss and recommend action on serious deviations from A.A. Tradition or harmful misuse of the name Alcoholics Anonymous (Charter Art. 11)
Draft a full report of its proceedings at the close of each yearly session (Charter Art. 11); today this record is the Final Conference Report
facts: The annual meeting is usually held in April and is the culmination of the year's activities (p. 40).
The Conference is not incorporated; the General Service Board, A.A. World Services, Inc. and AA Grapevine, Inc. are (pp. 40, 44).
The Conference held its first annual meeting in 1951 (p. 97).
Under the Charter it meets yearly in New York City unless otherwise agreed; special meetings may be called in a grave emergency (p. 125).

It may give advisory opinions at any time by mail or telephone poll; a 2023 Advisory Action set out a process for polling the Conference between annual meetings using virtual technology (pp. 125, 127).

Bernard S., nonalcoholic, then chair of the board of trustees and one of the architects of the Conference structure, explained why A.A. needs a Conference in his opening talk at the 1954 meeting (p. 41).
The Conference generally follows Robert's Rules of Order, with some exceptions adopted over the years (p. 173).

The General Service Conference is not the International Convention. The Convention is a Fellowship celebration held every five years and open to members worldwide; the Conference is the annual service meeting on the 'business of A.A.', where delegates, trustees, nontrustee directors and AAWS/Grapevine staff vote (p. 39)

The Conference was deliberately left unincorporated. Concept VII explains that incorporating it would have given every Conference member a legal status, in effect incorporating the whole Fellowship, an idea the Conference itself later rejected (p. 44)

GSO's Conference desk coordinates the annual Conference and keeps in touch with delegates and other Conference members all year. It produces and distributes the GSC Communications Kit and Manual, handles translation and distribution of background material, develops the Final Report (print and anonymity-protected electronic versions) and leads the Conference evaluation. It also asks areas for theme, presentation and workshop ideas (pp. 70-71).
Concept VII: in theory the Conference is an advisory body only, but in practice its traditional and financial power nearly always outweighs the trustees' legal power (p. C-21)

quotes.text: The Conference represents us, but cannot rule us.
The Conference comes closer to a governing body than anything else in A.A.
The Conference shall be a service body only, never a government for Alcoholics Anonymous.
The General Service Conference is an annual service event focused on the “business of A.A.”
We need it to ensure A.A. against government, while insulating it against anarchy
the closest thing there is to a collective group conscience for A.A. in the U.S. and Canada
Theoretically, the Conference is an advisory body only, but practically speaking it has all of the ultimate rights and powers that it may ever need.

nodes.title: What Happens During Conference Week
nodes.summary: A typical Conference lasts a full week, with sessions from morning to evening. The standing committees meet early in the week and do the principal work. Generally the last two days (or more) are spent discussing and voting on committee recommendations. On Saturday, after the last business day, a closing breakfast gives everyone a chance to say goodbye, including rotating trustees.
nodes.chosen_by: The overall format and content of the weekly schedule are reviewed and approved by the Conference Agenda Committee
nodes.term: A full week, usually in April
facts: Opening day includes roll call, a keynote address, an opening dinner and a five-speaker A.A. meeting (p. 40).
Business sessions from Sunday to Friday include committee meetings, presentations, workshops and new trustee elections (p. 40).
A delegates-only meeting is often held before opening day; it is outside the Conference itself (p. 40).
Conference committees and their corresponding trustees' committees hold an information-only joint session at the beginning of the week (p. 45).
Generally the last two days (or more) are devoted to discussion and voting on committee recommendations (p. 40).
Saturday, after the last day of business: closing breakfast with farewells from rotating trustees (p. 40).

In some years a visit to Stepping Stones, the historical home of Bill W. and Lois in Westchester County, is scheduled at the end of the Conference; in alternate years a visit to GSO is scheduled during Conference week (p. 40).

About one to two weeks before the Conference, Policy/Admissions meets by videoconference to accept admissions such as observers and temporary replacements for delegates who cannot attend (2023 Final Report, p. 37; April 9, 2024: 2024 Final Report, p. 38).
Mid-week, at the delegates-only meeting or dinner, the Delegate Chair for next year's Conference is drawn by lot (2017 Final Report, p. 4; 2025 Final Report, p. 4). See Conference Delegate Chair.
At each committee's last meeting the committee elects next year's chair and alternate (p. 45), primary committees before Archives and IC/RF (rosters).

Regional trustee and trustee-at-large elections are held during the week; trustee elections have been electronic since 2021, but the 'hat' is still used at the fourth or fifth ballot (2021 Final Report, p. 50).
Experience suggests delegates avoid planning big social events or personal business meetings during Conference week; there may be time afterward (p. 36)

Delegates may bring family to New York. A service program has matched delegates' families with local A.A. members serving as 'tour guides', and delegates can add days before or after the Conference at their own expense (p. 39)

quotes.text: A typical Conference lasts a full week, with sessions running from morning to evening.
Each delegate serves on one of the standing Conference committees, which meet early in the week and do the principal work of the Conference.

nodes.title: Conference Membership (Voting Members)
nodes.summary: Each year about 135 voting members make up the Conference, acting together as guardians of A.A. and of the Steps and Traditions. The 93 area delegates make up at least two-thirds of the body. The rest are generally 21 or 22 trustees of the General Service Board, six nontrustee directors of AAWS and Grapevine, and 15 A.A. staff members. Each member has one vote, even someone who attends in more than one capacity.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates are elected by their area assemblies. Trustees, AAWS/Grapevine directors and GSO/Grapevine staff are members by virtue of the positions they hold (Charter Art. 2).
nodes.term: Delegates serve two-year terms (Charter Art. 8); other members belong while they hold their positions
nodes.how_many: About 135: 93 delegates + 21 or 22 trustees + 6 nontrustee directors + 15 staff
duties: Act together as guardians of A.A. and of the Steps and Traditions
Vote on committee recommendations and floor actions
facts: 93 area delegates make up at least two-thirds of the Conference (p. 41).
21 or 22 trustees of the General Service Board; the board grows to 22 (15 Class B, 7 Class A) for the term of a Class B trustee selected as chair (pp. 41, 58).
6 nontrustee directors from AAWS and Grapevine (p. 41).
15 A.A. staff at the General Service Office (AAWS, Grapevine and La Viña) (p. 41).
One person, one vote: a trustee who is also a director of AAWS or Grapevine still has only one vote (p. 41).

No issue has ever divided Conference opinion with delegates opposed to the other members, but the Charter provides for that case: a two-thirds vote of members voting binds the board, provided the total vote is at least a quorum (p. 41).
The original 1955 Charter also allowed such ex-trustees or foreign delegates as the Conference might wish to invite (p. 120).

Actual voting members at recent Conferences: 133 (2017), 136 (2018), 135 (2019), 135 (2020), 132 (2021), 133 (2022), 133 (2023), 134 (2024), 137 (2025), 136 (2026); delegates were about 68-70% of the body (opening pages of each Final Report).

Why trustees, directors and staff vote (Concept IV): the Charter makes them voting members so that every group of world servants has a vote in proportion to its responsibility. Bill W. expected a few delegates to question this every year. By tradition they don't vote on reports of their own past performance (pp. C-12 to C-15)

quotes.text: Each Conference member has one vote, even if they attend in more than one capacity
93 area delegates (who make up at least two-thirds of the Conference body)

nodes.title: How an Idea Becomes an Agenda Item
nodes.summary: Agenda items can be suggested by individual A.A. members, groups, delegates, trustees, area assemblies, area committee members, and AAWS/Grapevine directors and staff. Experience suggests a GSR discuss an idea first with the group, then at district or area meetings; a district or area can then forward it to the GSO staff member serving as Conference coordinator. The staff Conference assignment studies it in light of earlier Conference actions and passes it to the trustees' Conference Committee or the appropriate Conference committee. Usually the trustees' committee decides how to program it. If a Conference committee recommendation is approved after full floor discussion, it becomes an Advisory Action. Timing: proposed agenda items (PAIs) for next year's Conference are due September 30 (2025 Final Report, p. 85); late items roll to the following year. In October the trustees' committees hear from their Conference committees, at the October/November board weekend they decide which items go forward, and committee background goes out in February.
nodes.chosen_by: Submissions go to the GSO Conference coordinator. Usually the trustees' Committee on the General Service Conference determines how each item is programmed.
duties: Step 1: An idea from an A.A. member, GSR, DCM, area committee member, delegate, trustee or GSO/GV staff may be shared or discussed at the group, district and area assembly and sent to the Conference coordinator at GSO (p. 171)
Step 2: The GSO/GV staff review it and forward it to the appropriate trustees' committee (p. 171)
Step 3: The trustees' committee may refer it to the appropriate Conference committee (p. 171)
Step 4: The Conference committee meets during Conference week and presents its recommendations in its committee report to the Conference (p. 171)
Step 5: If approved after full floor discussion, it becomes a Conference Advisory Action, which becomes binding when approved by the General Service Board (p. 171)
facts: Agenda items may come from individual A.A. members, groups, delegates, trustees, area assemblies, area committee members, and AAWS/Grapevine directors and staff (p. 43).
The staff Conference assignment provides a suggested disposition to the chair of the trustees' Conference Committee and the Director of Staff Services for consensus (p. 43).
Usually the trustees' committee programs an item as a workshop or presentation subject, a proposal, or a committee concern (p. 43).
Suggestions that do not concern overall policy are routed to the most appropriate part of the service structure (p. 43).

Items that rise to a Conference action include proposals important to A.A.'s future, policy decisions, requests to change Conference-approved literature, and items that may require the Fellowship's collective conscience (p. 44).
It has been suggested that every Conference committee hold a conference call before the January General Service Board meeting, giving delegates a further voice in agenda item selection (p. 49).

Deadline: September 30 (11:59 p.m. per aa.org for the 77th Conference). 'PAI submissions received past the deadline would be considered for the following year' (2025 Final Report, p. 85). It was September 15 from the 2022 Conference (2022 Final Report, p. 32), and a 2024 Advisory Action moved it to no earlier than September 30 (2024 Final Report, p. 38).

October feedback call: 'Prior to the November GSB weekend', the chair of the trustees' GSC Committee met Agenda (its own Conference counterpart), Policy/Admissions and Report and Charter (which have no trustees' committee, Service Manual p. 47) about related PAIs (2025 Final Report, p. 84).
From 2026 the chairs of the coming Conference's committees attend the October/November (Q4) board weekend, where trustees' committees review the PAIs (2026 Final Report, p. 49).
Since August 2025 GSO sends Conference members a quarterly PAI status grid: August 20 and November 22, 2025, and February 6, 2026 (2026 Final Report, p. 84).
Background material for all 13 committees goes out in English, French and Spanish at once in mid/late February (February 17-20, 2026) (2026 Final Report, p. 83).

Equitable Distribution of Workload (EDW): to even out committee workloads an item may go to a committee outside its usual topic. A three-year trial started with the 72nd Conference (2021 Final Report, p. 60), it was adopted in 2024 (2024 Final Report, p. 38), and it is discontinued after the 78th Conference in 2028 (2026 Final Report, p. 39).

Appendix U chart (a broad overview): an idea from a member, GSR, DCM, area committee member, delegate, trustee or GSO/GV staff, often discussed at group, district and area assembly, goes to GSO's Conference coordinator. GSO/GV staff review it and forward it to the appropriate trustees' committee, which may refer it to the appropriate Conference committee. That committee meets in Conference week and presents its recommendations in its report. A recommendation approved after full floor discussion becomes an Advisory Action, binding once the General Service Board approves it (p. 171)

quotes.text: Whatever its origin, any agenda item follows the same path to the Conference agenda
A district or an area can then forward it to the staff member at GSO who is currently serving as Conference coordinator.
The committee selected the new Proposed Agenda Item submission date deadline to be September 30.

nodes.title: Conference Advisory Actions
nodes.summary: An Advisory Action is a recommendation, from a committee or a floor action, that the full Conference approves with substantial unanimity (a two-thirds majority). After the Conference, Advisory Actions are referred to the General Service Board, which votes to affirm them; they then go to the appropriate trustees' committee, GSO or corporate board for implementation. By tradition they are binding on the board, and in practice the board rarely vetoes or overrides them. A recommendation approved by a simple majority but short of two-thirds is not forwarded to the board; it is memorialized in the Final Conference Report.
nodes.chosen_by: Voted by the full Conference (two-thirds of members voting, provided the total vote is at least a quorum), then affirmed by the General Service Board
duties: Express the informed group conscience of the Fellowship on matters of policy
Guide the General Service Board, GSO and the corporate boards, which implement them
facts: Substantial unanimity means a two-thirds majority (p. 42).
Because attendance varies during the week, two-thirds means two-thirds of members voting, as long as the total vote is a quorum (p. 173).
Any action that affects an Advisory Action, including an amendment, also needs a two-thirds majority (p. 173).
A simple majority short of two-thirds is not forwarded to the board; it is recorded in the Final Conference Report for informational and historical context (p. 43).
Concept III provides some discretion, but in practice the board rarely vetoes or overrides Advisory Actions (p. 44).
The Charter's phrase 'suitable resolutions' (Article 11) is now termed 'Conference Advisory Actions' (p. 127).
A compilation of past Conference Advisory Actions is available from GSO (p. 44).

History of the simple-majority rule: a 1986 Advisory Action made a majority-but-not-two-thirds recommendation a 'suggestion' to the board. In 2025 it was rescinded: such recommendations 'are not suggestions to the General Service Board to take action but should be memorialized in the Conference Final Report' (2025 Final Report, pp. 37-38).
GSO's compilation of Conference Advisory Actions is also available in a searchable electronic version on the Conference dashboard (p. 35)

quotes.text: When a recommendation, whether from a committee or through a floor action, is approved in full session with substantial unanimity it becomes an Advisory Action.
Advisory Actions are, by tradition, considered binding on the General Service Board.

nodes.title: Floor Actions
nodes.summary: A floor action is a recommendation made directly from the floor during the general sessions that may not have gone through a Conference committee. It lets delegates bring forward items that did not move out of committee, or items that were never on the agenda. Any matter within a committee's scope ought to go through that committee first. The maker gets two minutes to state the rationale; the chair then asks whether there is a motion to decline to consider it. If it goes forward, it is voted on like a committee recommendation and needs two-thirds to pass.
nodes.chosen_by: Proposed from the floor by a Conference member; the full body votes on whether to consider it
facts: Floor actions may be introduced at any time during the Conference except at the Sharing Sessions (p. 174).
A floor action about committee business that has not yet been concluded is out of order (p. 174).
The maker submits the floor action in writing to the Conference secretary (p. 175).
The maker gets two minutes to state the rationale; the chair then asks for a motion that the Conference decline to consider it (p. 174).
A motion to decline to consider is made without comment, needs a second, is not debatable, and needs a two-thirds vote (p. 175).
A floor action that is considered needs a second, is debatable, needs two-thirds to pass, and the minority voice is heard (p. 175).
The FAQ describes floor actions being proposed during the full session, typically the final two days of Conference week (p. 49).

The 2025 Agenda committee agreed that floor actions 'during the opening session should be allowed in cases of urgency or importance' while 'How the Conference Operates' is revised (2025 Final Report, p. 41).
Proposals to change how the Delegate Chair is chosen came as floor actions in 2023 and 2025; the Conference declined to consider both (2023 Final Report, p. 49; 2025 Final Report, p. 53).

quotes.text: members may make recommendations directly from the floor that may not have passed through a particular Conference committee. These are known as floor actions.
Floor actions may be introduced at any time during the Conference except at the Sharing Sessions.

nodes.title: How the Conference Operates (Rules of Debate)
nodes.summary: The Conference generally follows Robert's Rules of Order, proceeding as informally as possible, and has adopted some exceptions to stay closer to the spirit of A.A. Tradition. Committee recommendations reach the floor as motions already made and seconded, and members are asked to refrain from spontaneously amending a committee's work. Speakers line up at the microphones, get two minutes each, and no one speaks a second time on a topic until all who wish to have spoken once. After each policy vote, the side that did not prevail may speak.
nodes.chosen_by: The general rules of debate and voting are agreed to at the beginning of each Conference
facts: A quorum (two-thirds of all registered members) is required to conduct business (p. 173).
Committee recommendations are automatically motions that have been made and seconded (p. 173).
There are no 'friendly' amendments under Robert's Rules (p. 173).
Each speaker gets two minutes; nobody speaks twice on a topic until all who wish to have spoken once (p. 174).
Tabling postpones discussion to later in the same Conference; it needs a second, is not debatable, and passes by simple majority (pp. 174-175).
A motion to recommit returns an item to the trustees' committee or appropriate corporate board; it needs a second, is debatable, can be amended, and needs two-thirds (pp. 174-175).
Calling the question needs a second, is not debatable, and needs two-thirds (p. 175).

Only a member who voted with the prevailing side may move to reconsider; it may be seconded by either side, is not debatable, and passes by simple majority; no action may be reconsidered twice (pp. 174-175).
A motion on the floor is owned by the entire Conference body, no longer by the committee that recommended it (p. 175).

Before any vote on a recommendation, plenty of time is set aside for full discussion, including questions about its background and the committee's reasons. Concept V notes that the Conference has sometimes kept talking even when a two-thirds majority was easy to get, out of deference to minority views (p. 42)

The committee system lets the Conference deal with a large number of questions in one week. Members are encouraged to trust the process: each committee has carefully considered the items before it (p. 173)

Holding a minority view back until after the vote, when no one can rebut it, wastes time. It can force the Conference to reconsider a question that full discussion from all sides might have settled the first time (p. 173)

Floor etiquette: if someone has already stated your view, you need not repeat it at the microphone. Amending motions early in discussion or hastily calling the question can divert attention and confuse or delay business (p. 174)
The committee that made a recommendation is not asked to vote on a motion to amend it; any amendment depends on the approval of the Conference (p. 175)

In the procedures table, the minority voice is heard after votes on committee recommendations, amendments and floor actions, but not after procedural motions: tabling, recommitting, calling the question, reconsidering, or declining to consider a floor action (p. 175)

quotes.text: Recommendations of Conference committees are automatically motions that have been made and seconded.
there are no “friendly” amendments under Robert’s Rules.
Each person may speak for two (2) minutes.
Unless it has been absolutely unavoidable, the Conference has usually refused to take important decisions on anything less than a two-thirds vote.
rules exist to allow the Conference to do what it needs to do to carry out the will of the Fellowship

nodes.title: Conference Charter
nodes.summary: The Conference Charter, originally adopted in 1955, sets out what the Conference is for, who belongs to it, and how it relates to A.A. and to the General Service Board. Appendix K prints both the original 1955 text (with footnotes on later amendments) and the current U.S./Canada version. The Charter makes the Conference a service body only, never a government, and sets the key voting rules: a quorum of two-thirds of registered members, a two-thirds vote of members voting that binds the board, a three-quarters vote that can reorganize the board, and the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups to change Article 12, the Traditions or the Steps. The Conference Committee on Report and Charter reviews and recommends any necessary changes.
nodes.chosen_by: Original version adopted in 1955 and amended since by Conference action; the Report and Charter Committee reviews and recommends needed changes. Changing Article 12, the Steps or the Traditions needs the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups.
nodes.term: Original 1955; current version (U.S. and Canada)

duties: Art. 1 Purpose
Art. 2 Composition
Art. 3 Conference Relation to A.A.
Art. 4 Conference Relation to the General Service Board and its Corporate Services
Arts. 5-8 Area assemblies: composition, purpose, methods of electing, terms of office

facts: Article 1 was updated by the 1969 Conference to add 'the Twelve Steps' and by the 2021 Conference to add 'and the Twelve Concepts' (p. 122).
A quorum is two-thirds of all registered Conference members (p. 124).
A two-thirds vote of members voting binds the board and its corporate services, provided the total vote is at least a quorum (p. 124).

A three-quarters vote of all members participating in the vote may reorganize the board and the directors and staff of its corporate services; the 70th Conference added 'participating in the vote' (pp. 124, 127).
Changes to Article 12, the Twelve Traditions or the Twelve Steps need the written consent of three-quarters of A.A. groups; this applies to the original English version only (pp. 124, 127).

The original 1955 text required the written consent of two-thirds of all groups to change A.A. Tradition; the 1957 Conference raised it to three-quarters and extended it to Article 12 and the Steps (pp. 120, 123).
Delegates are free to vote as their conscience dictates and to decide which questions to take to the groups (p. 124).
The Conference may agree to hear Concept V Appeals from members of the structure below the Conference level (p. 125).
Area assemblies convene every two years to elect; in approximately half the areas elections are in even years and the rest in odd years, creating rotating panels (p. 125).
Delegates are selected from among area committee members by two-thirds written ballot or by lot (p. 125).
The General Service Board's Charter and Bylaws are subject to approval by a two-thirds vote of all Conference members; this approval is a matter of tradition, not a legal requirement (pp. 126-127).
A World Service Meeting of delegates from the various Conferences is held once every two years; the U.S./Canada delegates to it are chosen from the General Service Board (p. 124).

Where another country has its own general service structure, the U.S./Canada Conference delegates the sole right to publish its Conference-approved literature there to that structure's General Service Board. Only matters seriously affecting A.A.'s worldwide needs are for joint consideration (Charter Art. 2, p. 124)
A footnote explains that the Charter may guide other countries' GSOs, but they are autonomous and not bound by it, except where law requires (for example, copyright law) (p. 127)

The 1955 Charter pictured Conference 'Sections' in other lands, with the North American Section as the 'Senior Section'. No Section was ever to be placed in authority over another, and joint action needed a two-thirds vote of the combined Sections. The 1987 Conference (clarified in 1988) replaced this with today's wording on autonomous Conferences and the World Service Meeting (pp. 120, 122)

Art. 4: the Conference took the place of A.A.'s founders as guides and advisers to the General Service Board and its service corporations, and it is expected to give a reliable cross section of A.A. opinion. Art. 3 makes it the vehicle for A.A.'s views on vital policy and on hazardous deviations from Tradition (p. 124)
Charter Art. 11: the Conference may draft any bylaws it needs and names its own officers and committees by any method of its own choosing (p. 126)

History of the binding vote: the 1955 text made two-thirds 'of a Conference quorum' binding on the board. In 1986 this became two-thirds of members voting, as long as the total vote is at least a quorum (pp. 120, 123)

Concept V: because only a two-thirds Conference vote binds the trustees, they in effect hold a veto when the majority is narrow. They seldom use it and more often go along with a simple majority, especially when prompt action is needed (p. C-17)

Concept X: the Charter is not a legal instrument, but in practice it is the substance of a contract between the A.A. groups and their Conference. Concept XII calls it an informal agreement made between the groups and their trustees in 1955 (pp. C-34, C-48).

nodes.title: General Warranties (Charter Article 12)
nodes.summary: Article 12 of the Charter, the General Warranties of the Conference, lists the safeguards the Conference must observe in all its proceedings; it also opens Chapter 6 and is part of Concept XII. The Conference must never become the seat of perilous wealth or power, must keep sufficient operating funds plus an ample reserve, and must never place any member in unqualified authority over another. Important decisions are reached by discussion, vote and, whenever possible, substantial unanimity. No action may be personally punitive or an incitement to public controversy, the Conference may never perform acts of government, and it must always remain democratic in thought and action. Article 12 can be changed only with the written consent of three-quarters of the A.A. groups.

nodes.title: Conference Committees
nodes.summary: Most Conference agenda items are assigned to one of 13 standing committees, where they can be discussed in small groups before the full Conference considers them. Most committees work closely with a corresponding trustees' committee; the two stay in communication all year and hold an information-only joint session at the beginning of Conference week. Each committee meets twice early in the week. It can address items as they are, modify them, consider new items, take no action (generally reporting why), report Additional Committee Considerations, or refer an item back to a trustees' committee for a later Conference. Each delegate stays on the same committee for both years, and A.A. staff members serve as nonvoting secretaries.

facts: There are 13 standing committees; Archives and International Conventions/Regional Forums are the two secondary ones (pp. 45, 48).
Each committee follows a Composition, Scope and Procedure document (p. 45).

Background material on all agenda items is prepared in English, French and Spanish (p. 45); it now goes out in all three languages at once in mid/late February (February 17-20, 2026) (2026 Final Report, p. 83).
Each committee meets twice early in the week, occasionally more often if necessary (p. 45).
Joint meetings with trustees' committees share information only; no actions are taken (p. 45).
While other committees hold joint meetings, committees with no corresponding trustees' committee begin deliberating on their agendas (p. 49).
The full Conference is not obligated to accept a committee's report; the matter is decided in general session (p. 42).
Areas and districts may have corresponding committees, sometimes under different names (p. 46).

Trustees' committees with no Conference counterpart: International and the four auxiliary committees, Audit, Compensation, Compliance and Employees' Retirement (pp. 59-60). The General Sharing Session is a session, not a committee (p. 61). The Appendix C chart (p. 109) still shows an older list.
Background material is not just for committee members: it is shared throughout the Fellowship to inform and broaden the discussion of agenda items (p. 45)

nodes.title: Committee Selection by Lot
nodes.summary: Committee assignments are determined by lot. The selection is typically held each December by the Conference coordinator and the chair of the trustees' Committee on the General Service Conference, to replace outgoing delegates on each committee. Because a delegate keeps the same committee for both years, a committee is normally four or five first-year delegates plus four or five second-year delegates. Some delegates are also chosen by lot for one of the two secondary committees. Since the December 2020 draw the lot is run with a custom software app by the chair and vice-chair of the trustees' committee and the Conference coordinator, and the Final Reports describe a growing list of criteria the draw tries to respect: see the history below and the Predict page.
nodes.chosen_by: By lot (p. 45). Since December 2020 a custom software app is used, run by the chair and vice-chair of the trustees' Committee on the General Service Conference with the GSO Conference coordinator (2021 Final Report, p. 26; 2024 Final Report, p. 68).

It held at the 2019-2024 Conferences; the rebalanced draws since have broken it a few times (2 committees in 2025, 4 in 2026, rosters).

2022: the app was updated and used for the 2022 committee selection, with a Phase II project planned (2022 Final Report, p. 36).

Panel 73 (December 2022): 'five selection rounds were performed and the round with the broadest distribution was selected' (2023 Final Report, p. 64). The same report raised the tendency of some areas to get the same committees again.

Panel 75 (December 2024): assignments were rebalanced toward an even mix of first- and second-year delegates on each committee (2024 Final Report, p. 68), and 'broadest committee participation by areas' was built into the software (2025 Final Report, pp. 84-85).

2025: prioritized criteria, in order: (1) areas can be selected for any committee; (2) a more even rotation on the remaining committees; (3) wider regional representation across all committees; (4) limit adjacent areas from different regions (2025 Final Report, p. 47). They were applied to the Panel 76 draw (2026 Final Report, p. 82).

2026: a grid of every committee assignment 2017-2026 was built; using open-source AI for the draw was 'discussed but not enacted' because it does not align with AAWS's policy on AI use (2026 Final Report, p. 82).

IC/RF needs one delegate from each region, which makes its rotation hard (2026 Final Report, pp. 82-83); it had only 7 members in 2024 and 2025 (no West Central Panel 74 delegate). Since Panel 69, odd panels have filled the Northeast, East Central, Pacific and Eastern Canada seats and even panels the other four (rosters).

The Panel 77 draw is in December 2026. GSO asked that incoming-panel delegate information not be released before rotation on January 1 (2024 Final Report, p. 71), so delegates-elect come from area websites until then.
Drawing by lot is used elsewhere too: the 2024 Conference Inventory working group's Conference members were selected by lot (2024 Final Report, p. 69).

nodes.title: Electing Committee Chairs
nodes.summary: Each Conference committee elects a chair and an alternate chair by plurality at its last meeting during Conference week. The new chairs take office as soon as the Conference ends and serve through the end of the next year's Conference. Besides attending the Conference, chairs attend a General Service Board weekend in New York, which helps communication between the committee and its trustee and board counterparts. The manual says the end of January (p. 45); the board has since decided that the 77th Conference's chairs attend the October/November 2026 (Q4) weekend instead of January 2027, to give them more time on proposed agenda items (2026 Final Report, p. 49). In practice chairs and alternates are always first-year members of the committee, so they chair in their second year. At the Conference, the chair reads the committee's final report in its entirety.

facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: CPC/Treatment and Accessibilities (p. 46).

GSO's CPC desk is the office contact for professionals who have alcoholic clients. It coordinates A.A. exhibits at national professional conferences and passes local invitations to local committees. It offers CPC literature discount packages, helps produce About A.A., and serves as liaison to the NIAAA (p. 71). About A.A. is the only GSO bulletin aimed mainly at non-A.A.s (p. 77).
