It reviews and makes recommendations on new literature and revisions to existing literature, reviews new formats of existing literature (including digital and audiovisual), and recommends development of new pamphlets, books or audiovisual materials. Material for a specific area of service, such as corrections, is developed by the relevant committee.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Review and recommend on new literature and revisions to existing literature
Review new formats of existing literature, including digital and audiovisual
Recommend development of new pamphlets, books or audiovisual materials
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: Literature Committee (p. 47).
Requests for changes to Conference-approved literature are among the matters that rise to a Conference action (p. 44).

GSO's Literature desk supports local literature committees and the development and updating of Conference-approved literature, mainly recovery-focused items. It runs the calendar of event information and content ideas for Box 4-5-9 and supplies literature display packages to committees (p. 72).

Appendix R is a select list of AAWS and Grapevine items grouped by subject, such as the program of recovery, the Traditions, the group, general service and carrying the message. The full list is in GSO's combined Literature catalog, the online store is onlineliterature.aa.org, and AAWS publishes almost all its literature in English, French and Spanish (p. 161)

quotes.text: The committee’s focus is on recovery literature

nodes.title: Policy/Admissions Committee
nodes.summary: Policy/Admissions examines Conference policy. It reviews and makes a determination on requests from international boards/GSOs to be admitted as observers at the annual meeting. It reviews requests for temporary replacement of delegates unable to attend, and reviews proposals to change or expand the Conference, including requests for additional delegate areas and procedures affecting the cost of the Conference. It has no corresponding trustees' committee.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Examine Conference policy
Determine requests from international boards/GSOs to be admitted as observers
Review requests for temporary replacement of delegates unable to attend
Review proposals to change or expand the Conference, including additional delegate areas and procedures affecting Conference cost
facts: No corresponding trustees' committee (p. 47).
While other committees hold joint meetings with trustees' committees, committees without a trustee counterpart begin deliberating on their agendas (p. 49).

Its pre-Conference video meeting, set up by a 2023 Advisory Action, accepts admissions before the Conference opens (2023 Final Report, p. 37); in 2024 it met April 9 and seated an alternate for a delegate who could not attend (2024 Final Report, p. 38).
It also proposes future Conference dates: the 77th Conference is April 11-17, 2027 and the 78th April 23-29, 2028 (2025 Final Report, p. 45).

quotes.text: Review requests for temporary replacement of Conference delegates unable to attend the Conference.

nodes.title: Public Information Committee
nodes.summary: The Public Information committee works to create greater understanding, and prevent misunderstanding, of the A.A. program through public media, electronic media and PI meetings. It reviews PI pamphlets and PSAs, reaches out to young people and students, reviews membership survey data and process, and communicates with media professionals. It also evaluates digital strategies and social media efforts for carrying the message.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Create understanding of the A.A. program through public media, electronic media and PI meetings
Review PI pamphlets and PSAs
Reach out to young people and students
Review membership survey data and process
Communicate with media professionals
Evaluate digital strategies and social media efforts
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: Public Information Committee (p. 47).

GSO's Public Information desk sends the yearly Anonymity Letter to the media and forwards anonymity breaks at the level of public media to the area delegates. It also passes invitations from health fairs and schools to local committees and coordinates PSAs for TV, radio and digital platforms such as the AAWS YouTube channel (p. 72).

The March 1, 1941 Saturday Evening Post article put A.A. in the national spotlight: public confidence could swell A.A. and public ill will could stunt it. Over years of trial and error A.A. learned, among other lessons, 100% anonymity at the public level, no lending the name to other causes, no endorsements or alliances, a single purpose, no professionalism, and attraction rather than promotion (p. 101)

Concept XI: the trustees' Public Information Committee needs professional PR skill, but A.A.'s 'attraction rather than promotion' rules out ordinary sales methods, so it should always include members with long A.A. experience. One big public blunder could cost lives by turning prospects away (pp. C-39, C-65, C-66).

quotes.text: Review membership survey data and process.

nodes.title: Report and Charter Committee
nodes.summary: Report and Charter looks after the Conference's core documents. It reviews The A.A. Service Manual and the Final Conference Report and recommends changes as needed, checks annual drafts of the Conference Report for accuracy, and reviews and recommends any necessary changes in the Conference Charter. It has no corresponding trustees' committee.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Review The A.A. Service Manual and Final Conference Report and recommend changes
Review annual drafts of the Conference Report for accuracy
Review and recommend any necessary changes to the Conference Charter
facts: No corresponding trustees' committee (p. 47).
The Final Conference Report is provided through area delegates in print (English, French, Spanish) during the summer and online as an anonymity-protected digital file (p. 43).

Charter Art. 11 also calls for a condensation of the yearly report to be sent to A.A. groups throughout the world, besides the full report of proceedings supplied to all delegates and committee members (p. 126)

quotes.text: Review and recommend any necessary changes in the Conference Charter.

nodes.title: Treatment and Accessibilities Committee
nodes.summary: This committee supports members and groups who carry the message into treatment facilities and reviews efforts at bridging the gap from treatment to A.A. It also supports efforts to make sure people with accessibility concerns, including those in underserved or remote communities, have access to the message. It reviews service to meetings in treatment and other non-correctional institutional settings and to A.A.s with accessibility issues, and recommends changes and improvements.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Support members and groups who carry the message into treatment facilities
Review efforts at bridging the gap from treatment to A.A.
Support efforts to give people with accessibility concerns, including in underserved or remote communities, access to the message
Review service to meetings in treatment and other non-correctional institutions and to A.A.s with accessibility issues
Recommend changes and improvements
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: CPC/Treatment and Accessibilities Committee, the same trustees' committee that pairs with the CPC Conference committee (pp. 46-47).

GSO's Accessibilities/Treatment/Remote Communities desk supports treatment committees and corresponds with members in treatment centers. It shares experience on reaching remote communities, supports local committees working with the military, veterans and the elder community, and coordinates the confidential bimonthly LIM bulletin (p. 70).

quotes.text: Review A.A. efforts at bridging the gap from treatment to A.A.
While there are no special alcoholics, there are alcoholics who experience access barriers to receiving the A.A. message.

nodes.title: Trustees Committee
nodes.summary: The Conference Committee on Trustees reviews all résumés of nominees for the General Service Board and corporate directors. It presents the slates of nominees to the Conference for disapproval, if any. During Conference week it also participates as part of the voting body that nominates regional and at-large trustees. Its corresponding trustees' committee is the Nominating Committee.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates assigned by lot
nodes.term: Two years (both years of the delegate term)
duties: Review all résumés of nominees for the General Service Board and corporate directors
Present the slates of nominees to the Conference for disapproval, if any
Take part in the voting body that nominates regional and at-large trustees during Conference week
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: Nominating Committee (p. 48).

Regional trustee voters are the region's delegates plus an equal number of voters, half from the Conference Committee on Trustees and half from the trustees' Nominating Committee; they select by two-thirds written ballot or by lot (p. 125).
The committee's chair co-chairs the regional trustee nominating session with the trustees' Nominating Committee chair (p. 55).

quotes.text: Present the slates of nominees to the Conference for disapproval, if any.

nodes.title: Archives Committee (secondary)
nodes.summary: Archives is one of two secondary committees, formed for matters that do not need as much time as the other standing committees' agenda items. Some delegates, chosen by lot, serve on it in addition to their primary assignment. It considers practice and policy related to A.A. archives and meets during the Conference at a dinner meeting with the trustees' Archives Committee, where it may take direct action.
nodes.chosen_by: Delegates chosen by lot, in addition to their primary committee
duties: Consider matters of practice and policy related to A.A. archives
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: Archives Committee (p. 48).
Meets during the Conference at a dinner meeting with its trustees' committee (p. 48).
The Conference committee may take direct action at this meeting (p. 48).

quotes.text: Consider matters of practice and policy related to A.A. archives.

nodes.title: International Conventions/Regional Forums Committee (secondary)
nodes.summary: The second secondary committee is composed of eight delegates chosen by lot, one from each region. It considers and develops plans for forthcoming International Conventions and offers input on the implementation of Regional Forums, Special Forums and Local Forums. Like Archives, it meets at a dinner meeting with its trustees' committee during the Conference and may take direct action there.
nodes.chosen_by: Eight delegates chosen by lot, one from each region
nodes.how_many: 8 delegates (one per region; 7 in 2024 and 2025)
qualifications: Delegate; one per region
duties: Consider and develop plans for forthcoming International Conventions
Offer input on the implementation of Regional Forums, Special Forums and Local Forums
facts: Corresponding trustees' committee: International Conventions/Regional Forums Committee (p. 48).
Meets during the Conference at a dinner meeting with its trustees' committee (p. 48).
The Conference committee may take direct action at this meeting (p. 48).

In 2024 and 2025 the committee had only 7 members: no West Central delegate from Panel 74 was assigned (rosters). The trustees' committee noted 'challenges within the rotation of ICRF' because it needs all eight regions (2026 Final Report, pp. 82-83).

Since Panel 69, odd panels have supplied the Northeast, East Central, Pacific and Eastern Canada members and even panels the Southeast, Southwest, West Central and Western Canada members (rosters). So Area 65's (odd) Panel 77 delegate is unlikely to be the Southwest's IC/RF member.
Under a 2025 Advisory Action the chair and alternate are elected by written ballot from the first-year panel members (2025 Final Report, p. 37).

For each International Convention, GSO's International Convention desk handles programming, finances and facilities. It works with local A.A. committees to form a Volunteer Welcome Committee (p. 72). GSO Finance helps with the Convention's financial planning (p. 74), and Publishing produces the souvenir books (p. 76).

quotes.text: Composed of eight delegates chosen by lot, one from each region.

nodes.title: General Service Board (GSB)
nodes.summary: The General Service Board is the board of trustees of A.A. in the U.S. and Canada and the chief service arm of the General Service Conference. Its role is custodial: it protects A.A.'s vital services and looks after the Fellowship's welfare. It does not govern. It gets whatever authority it has from the Conference, and it oversees the two operating corporations, A.A. World Services, Inc. and AA Grapevine, Inc. Legally it is a New York not-for-profit membership corporation whose members are the trustees themselves.
nodes.chosen_by: Trustees are nominated by the trustees' Nominating Committee (regional trustees and trustees-at-large through Conference nominating sessions) and presented to the Conference as a slate that a majority of delegates may disapprove. They are then elected by the member trustees at the annual meeting of members, held during the 2nd quarterly board meeting on the Saturday after the Conference.
nodes.term: Depends on class: Class A serve up to two successive 3-year terms (a third is possible); Class B serve up to four successive one-year terms.
nodes.how_many: Typically 21 (7 Class A + 14 Class B). It can grow to 22 when a trustee who has reached the term limit is serving, or is newly elected, as chair. Chapter 8 gives the Class B case (15 Class B + 7 Class A); the bylaws also allow a Class A holdover (8 Class A).
qualifications: Available for quarterly board meetings in New York (3-5 days each plus travel)
Available for the week-long Conference in New York, typically held in April
Available for regular communication and for matters that come up between meetings, for Regional Forums and local events when asked, and for corporate board service as needed
duties: Act as the principal planners and administrators of overall policy and finance
Serve as custodians of AAWS and AA Grapevine and promote communication and unity among them, GSO and the board
Oversee A.A.'s public relations policy and adjust it when needed
Keep up relationships with general service structures around the world
Act as guardians of A.A.'s Steps, Traditions and Concepts
facts: The board has entire freedom of action in the routine conduct of the policy and business affairs of the A.A. service corporations, except on matters of policy, finance or Tradition that could seriously affect A.A. as a whole (Conference Charter Art. 10, pp. 50, 126)
1951: the board had 8 Class A and 7 Class B trustees, most living near New York City (p. 52)
1962: the board was enlarged to bring in A.A. trustees from away from New York (p. 52)
1966: the board was reorganized to today's 7 nonalcoholic + 14 alcoholic (p. 52)
It was originally called the Alcoholic Foundation; the bylaws were adopted April 22, 1957 (p. 134)
Trustees are not paid; the GSB covers travel and accommodation (p. 63)
An area delegate may stand for trustee one year after their last Conference (p. 63)
Mission: 'Our mission is to serve the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous.' (p. 51)

The board keeps a careful balance between trustees chosen mainly for regional and A.A. service experience and those chosen for business or professional backgrounds, and seeks a large file of qualified applicants for every vacancy that reflects A.A.'s inclusiveness and diversity (p. 51)

Long-form Tradition Nine calls the GSB trustees 'in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee'. They are custodians of A.A. Tradition, receivers of the voluntary contributions that maintain GSO, handlers of A.A.'s overall public relations, and guarantors of AA Grapevine's integrity (p. 107)
Charter Art. 10: the board is an incorporated trusteeship of alcoholics and nonalcoholics who elect their own successors, subject to approval by the Conference or one of its committees (p. 125)

Concepts VI and VIII: next to the Conference the trustees should be the most influential world servants. They are 'A.A.'s bankers', responsible for the reserve funds, and as a board they should focus on large questions of policy, finance, group relations, public relations and leadership, not the office's daily routine (pp. C-19, C-20, C-24)

The combined 2025 operating revenue of the General Service Board, A.A. World Services, Inc. and AA Grapevine, Inc. was $22,054,037 USD; in 1960 AAWS and the Grapevine together took in close to half a million dollars a year (p. C-20 and footnote)
In 2026, 90% of the trustees live 'out of town' (away from New York); Bill W.'s 1962 text said half (pp. C-25, C-26 footnote)

quotes.text: The General Service Board (the trustees) is the chief service arm of the Conference, and is essentially custodial in its character
their purpose is to safeguard the vital services provided for the Fellowship, not to govern.
The board of trustees today typically consists of 21 people
Over the years, the only changes considered necessary have been in the composition of the General Service Board, not in its duties or responsibilities.
The General Service Board is in effect a holding company, charged with the custodial oversight of its wholly-owned and separately incorporated affiliates

nodes.title: Class A (Nonalcoholic) Trustees
nodes.summary: Class A trustees are seven nonalcoholic 'friends of A.A.' chosen mainly for their professional experience and their familiarity with A.A. They do not need to stay anonymous, so they can appear in public on A.A.'s behalf. The board has included doctors, lawyers, clergy, sociologists, businesspeople and financial experts.
nodes.chosen_by: The GSB nominates them after a search. Names are collected from current and past board members, directors, delegates, and AAWS and Grapevine staff. The trustees' Nominating Committee narrows the list and invites the remaining prospects to a quarterly board meeting, then recommends one person per vacancy. After the board approves, the candidate goes on the slate presented to the Conference for disapproval, if any.
nodes.term: Two consecutive three-year terms, confirmed annually. On the chair's recommendation, the member trustees may permit a third successive three-year term.
nodes.how_many: 7 (8 if a Class A trustee who has reached the limit is serving or newly elected as chair)
qualifications: Not and never afflicted by alcoholism
Profound faith in the A.A. recovery program
Proven track record in their own field
Demonstrated interest in A.A. and experience working with A.A. and its members
Leadership skills
Time to fulfill trustee duties
duties: Bring professional wisdom and perspective to the board
Be available to appear in public on behalf of A.A. (no anonymity needed)
Carry the additional responsibilities and time commitments specific to nonalcoholic trustees
facts: Maximum service is 6 years, or 9 years with a permitted third term (p. 52)
Time served after being elected by the board to fill a vacancy between annual meetings does not count toward total service (pp. 138-139)
A vacancy-filler elected by the members serves a three-year term and is eligible for the same number of terms as any other Class A trustee (p. 138)
The board had a nonalcoholic majority of one until the 1966 reorganization (p. 52)
Besides never having had alcoholism, a Class A trustee must 'express a profound faith' in the recovery program on which A.A. is founded (p. 137)

quotes.text: since they need not maintain anonymity, they are available to appear in public on behalf of A.A.
shall be persons who are not and have not been afflicted by the disease of alcoholism

nodes.title: Class B (Alcoholic) Trustees
nodes.summary: Class B trustees are the 14 A.A. members on the board. They come in three categories that bring different viewpoints: 8 regional trustees, 4 general service trustees and 2 trustees-at-large. Under the bylaws, all trustees have the same fiduciary responsibility whatever their class or category.
nodes.chosen_by: Varies by category: regional trustees and trustees-at-large are nominated in Conference nominating sessions using the Third Legacy Procedure; general service trustees are put forward by the AAWS or Grapevine board and recommended through the trustees' Nominating Committee. All appear on the slate presented to the Conference and are elected at the annual meeting of members.
nodes.term: Up to four successive one-year (annual) terms, with no further service as a member trustee afterward (except as a holdover chair)
nodes.how_many: 14 (15 if a Class B trustee who has reached the limit is serving or newly elected as chair)
qualifications: Alcoholic A.A. member (the bylaws' term is 'ex-alcoholic')
Suggested sobriety: 10 years for regional trustees and trustees-at-large, 7 for general service trustees (none mandatory)
duties: Regional trustees give time mainly around the four quarterly meetings and the Conference, and advise the board on regional views
General service trustees serve at the same times as regional trustees and also provide continued service all year
facts: 8 regional (6 U.S., 2 Canada), 4 general service (2 AAWS, 2 Grapevine), 2 at-large (1 U.S., 1 Canada) (p. 53)
'Ex-alcoholic' means someone who has arrested their drinking and lives, as far as possible, by the Twelve Steps (p. 137)
Regional trustee and trustee-at-large nominees chosen at the Conference are then elected to the board, 'the trustees being obligated by tradition to do so' (pp. 125-126)

quotes.text: There are 14 alcoholic Class B trustees in addition to the 7 Class A trustees.
Class B member trustees shall be ineligible to serve for more than four successive annual terms

nodes.title: Regional Trustees
nodes.summary: Regional trustees are chosen for their service experience and their familiarity with A.A. principles. They bring a regional A.A. point of view to the board, but like every trustee they represent only the Fellowship as a whole. Areas in the region nominate candidates, and a nominating session at the Conference picks one using the Third Legacy Procedure. Elections follow a fixed four-year rotation set more than a decade ahead.
nodes.chosen_by: Each area may nominate a candidate (two or more areas may share one), usually picked by its assembly using the Third Legacy Procedure. The trustees' Nominating Committee checks eligibility before the Conference. At the Conference a nominating session co-chaired by the chairs of the trustees' Nominating Committee and the Conference Committee on Trustees selects one nominee, again by Third Legacy. The voters are the region's delegates plus an equal number of others, half from the Conference Trustees Committee and half from the trustees' Nominating Committee. The nominee then goes on the slate.
nodes.term: Four successive one-year terms
nodes.how_many: 8 (6 U.S., 2 Canada)
qualifications: Ten years of continuous sobriety suggested (not mandatory)
Leadership experience, good judgment, objectivity and the willingness to stand up and speak
Business or professional background helpful but not required; the board values other strengths too
duties: All general trustee duties
Serve on the AAWS or AA Grapevine board of directors for two years, normally in years 2 and 3
Bring regional views to the board and interpret board actions back home
facts: Election years: Eastern Canada and Pacific 2026/2030/2034/2038; Northeast and Southwest 2027/2031/2035/2039; Western Canada and West Central 2028/2032/2036/2040; Southeast and East Central 2029/2033/2037/2041 (p. 54)
GSO informs delegates and area officers of an upcoming opening in a May mailing; groups learn of it through Box 4-5-9 (p. 54)
The delegate sends the candidate's name and contact information to GSO's Nominating desk; the candidate then submits a signed résumé by January 1 (p. 55)
Résumés received after January 1 are returned and not considered; if a nominee withdraws after the deadline, the area may not submit another (p. 55)
The nominating session meets in a roped-off section that all Conference members can watch (p. 55)
Prior Conferences have recommended that no area submit the same person for both regional trustee and trustee-at-large at the same Conference (p. 57)

The 'equal number of voters' is partly drawn at random before the Conference: for the 2023 Northeast election, 'a random process for selecting additional voters resulted in four trustee voters and two delegate voters' (2023 Final Report, p. 65).
Elections are electronic since 2021; the 'hat' is still used at the fourth or fifth ballot (2021 Final Report, p. 50).
Southwest (Area 65's region) and Northeast elect at the 77th Conference, April 2027; résumés are due January 1, 2027 (p. 54-55).

To choose a regional trustee candidate, areas typically invite assembly members to say they are interested, and many ask for a service history. The manual suggests reviewing the GSB bylaws and the job's qualifications and responsibilities before selecting (p. 55)

Under the bylaws, regional trustees give their time mainly in four periods: the three days ending on each of the 1st, 3rd and 4th quarterly board meetings, and the week-long Conference together with the 2nd quarterly meeting on the Saturday after it. They are also expected to advise the board on regional views about policy (p. 137)

quotes.text: no trustee can be said to “represent” a geographical section — all trustees represent only the Fellowship as a whole
Resumes are submitted electronically or by mail postmarked by the January 1 deadline.

nodes.title: Trustees-at-Large (U.S. and Canada)
nodes.summary: The two trustees-at-large, one from the U.S. and one from Canada, bring a broad perspective from their ongoing contact with the international A.A. community. They represent the U.S. and Canada as delegates to the World Service Meeting and to the Meeting of the Americas (REDELA). They are also expected to attend Regional Forums in both countries.
nodes.chosen_by: All areas in the U.S. (or Canada) are notified and may submit candidates, usually chosen by assembly with the Third Legacy Procedure. The trustees' Nominating Committee checks eligibility before the Conference. During Conference week, each region's delegates caucus (usually at a regional lunch) and narrow the list to one name per U.S. region or two per Canadian region. At most 6 (U.S.) or 4 (Canada) candidates go to a Third Legacy vote by that country's area delegates plus the members of the trustees' Nominating Committee.
nodes.term: Four successive one-year terms; the two positions are staggered
nodes.how_many: 2 (1 U.S., 1 Canada)
qualifications: Ten years of continuous sobriety suggested (not mandatory)
Leadership skills and experience
Business or professional experience helpful but not required
duties: Serve on the trustees' International Committee and other committees
Serve as delegates to the World Service Meeting (every two years) and the Meeting of the Americas (in the other years)
Attend Regional Forums in the U.S. and Canada; schedules permitting, one in each of the eight regions over four years
Be available for other service activities requested by areas, regions or the board
May be appointed directors of a corporate board and may fill in for regional trustees
facts: Staggered terms ensure there is a trustee-at-large with experience in the position (p. 57)
Maximum of 6 U.S. or 4 Canadian candidates go forward to the vote (p. 57)
For trustees-at-large the board may set certain business or professional qualifications. The 1979 Conference changed the Charter's 'will' to 'may' (pp. 123, 125)

quotes.text: They bring to the board’s discussions a broad perspective informed by their ongoing contact with the international A.A. community.
There are two trustees-at-large on the board — one from the U.S. and one from Canada.

nodes.title: General Service Trustees
nodes.summary: General service trustees are A.A. members who serve on the AAWS or Grapevine boards and are available at any time to help GSO or Grapevine staff solve problems. They have traditionally been chosen for business or professional backgrounds, and many have worked in publishing, technology, public relations, finance or administration. They are drawn from current or past nontrustee directors, so the corporate boards already know their qualifications.
nodes.chosen_by: The résumé of one qualified candidate who has served at least a year on the AAWS or Grapevine board is submitted to the trustees' Nominating Committee (the bylaws-section duties call them 'nominated by the two corporate boards'). If the committee accepts the candidate, it recommends them to the full GSB for the slate; if not, the committee may pick another qualified candidate or ask the corporate board for another.
nodes.term: Up to four successive one-year terms
nodes.how_many: 4 (2 from AAWS, 2 from Grapevine)
qualifications: Seven years of continuous sobriety suggested (not mandatory)
Business or professional experience considered essential
Leadership skills and experience
At least one year of service on the AAWS or Grapevine board
duties: Attend all meetings of their corporate board (eight or more a year)
Be available to consult with GSO or Grapevine staff at any time
Provide continued service to the board throughout the year
facts: Chosen from current or past nontrustee directors (p. 56)
On top of the regional trustees' schedule (board weekends and Conference week), the bylaws expect general service trustees to give continued service to the board all year round (pp. 137-138)

quotes.text: General service trustees are chosen from among current or past nontrustee directors of the two corporate boards
must be available for all meetings of their respective boards (eight or more each year)

nodes.title: Chair of the General Service Board
nodes.summary: The chair presides over board meetings, co-chairs the General Service Conference and acts for the board between meetings. The chair may be a Class A or a Class B trustee and serves a four-year term on top of any service already completed as a trustee. A chair who has reached the trustee term limit keeps a trustee seat for the chair's term, so the board can grow to 22; Chapter 8 describes this for a Class B chair (15 Class B + 7 Class A). Legally the chair is the corporation's president, but the title is used only when the law requires it.
nodes.chosen_by: The trustees' Nominating Committee recommends an officer slate, which the board settles before the Conference and presents to the Conference like the trustee slate. The Board of Trustees then elects the chair at its 2nd quarterly meeting (the Saturday after the Conference).
nodes.term: Four years, or not more than four successive annual terms under the bylaws
qualifications: A Class A or Class B trustee; someone who has served the maximum trustee period may also be elected and keeps a trustee seat during the chair term
May not be an employee of the GSB
duties: Preside over trustees' meetings
Co-chair the General Service Conference
Act on behalf of the GSB between board meetings
Appoint members of trustees' committees, subject to GSB approval
Serve as an ex-officio member of all trustees' committees
Take part in board meetings and the annual Conference
Take part in all Regional Forums
Appoint the assistant treasurer, assistant secretary and any other non-elected officers, subject to board approval
Designate the nominating committee; set each meeting's place and time of day and the agenda order
facts: A Class A chair past the term limit keeps a seat, so Class A can reach 8 (p. 137)
A Class B chair past the term limit keeps a seat, so Class B can reach 15 and the board 22 (pp. 58, 137)
A chair who is past the trustee term limit stops being a trustee on the day the chair term ends (p. 137)
Board chairs who rotate off are usually designated trustees emeriti (p. 58)
The bylaws' limit of four successive annual terms for the chair did not apply to the chair who was serving at the end of 1966 (p. 139)

quotes.text: That four-year term is over and above the term they may have served as a Class A trustee (up to six years) or as a Class B trustee (up to four years).
No employee of the General Service Board may serve as the chair.
will expand the number of member trustees then serving on the Board to twenty-two (22)

nodes.title: Trustees Emeriti
nodes.summary: The board usually names former board chairs as trustees emeriti after they rotate off. They are invited to quarterly board meetings and to the Conference as a resource of 'corporate memory', and are sometimes asked to share how earlier boards worked and reached a group conscience. They have no vote.
nodes.chosen_by: Designated by the General Service Board, typically from board chairs who have rotated off
nodes.term: Not stated
nodes.how_many: Not stated
qualifications: Typically a past chair of the General Service Board
duties: Attend quarterly board meetings and the annual Conference when invited
Share experience with past board decisions and processes when asked
facts: They do not vote on any matter before the GSB or the Conference (p. 58)

quotes.text: Trustees emeriti do not vote on any matter before the General Service Board or the Conference.
They are a resource of corporate memory

nodes.title: Trustees' Committees (GSB committees)
nodes.summary: The board has 14 committees: 10 standing and 4 auxiliary. For the most part they mirror the Conference committees, and the auxiliary ones handle compliance and oversight. They meet quarterly during board weekends, with virtual meetings in between as needed. Each committee has a trustee as chair and usually a GSO staff member as secretary. Members are trustees and AAWS/Grapevine directors, and some committees add appointed committee members (ACMs).
nodes.chosen_by: The GSB chair appoints committee members, subject to board approval at the 3rd quarterly board meeting. Committees of the Board are created by resolution of a majority of the entire Board.
nodes.term: Not stated
nodes.how_many: 14 committees (10 standing + 4 auxiliary), generally 6-9 members each
qualifications: Members are trustees and AAWS/Grapevine directors, plus ACMs on some committees
duties: Standing: Archives; CPC/Treatment and Accessibilities; Corrections; Finance and Budgetary; General Service Conference; International; International Conventions/Regional Forums; Literature; Nominating; Public Information
Auxiliary: Audit; Compensation; Compliance; Employees' Retirement
May form subcommittees for specific projects, including materials for Conference approval
Trustees' committee chairs contact their Conference committee chairs after each board weekend and hold calls on proposed agenda items
facts: Matching pairs: General Service Conference committee goes with the Conference Agenda Committee; Nominating with the Conference Trustees Committee; Finance and Budgetary with the Conference Finance Committee (pp. 58-60)
CPC/Treatment and Accessibilities corresponds to two Conference committees (p. 58)
International and the four auxiliary committees have no corresponding Conference committee (pp. 59-60)
The board treasurer chairs Finance and Budgetary (p. 59)
Audit meets at least yearly with the independent auditor and recommends one each year (p. 60)
Compensation meets yearly with consultants; the affiliate boards make the actual pay decisions (p. 60)
Compliance has five randomly selected returning trustees, including an alternate, supported by the GSO Staff Coordinator (p. 60)
Most Conference committees meet jointly with their trustees' committee on the first day of the Conference (p. 63)
By law, no committee may fill board or committee vacancies, amend or repeal the bylaws, or fix directors' compensation for board or committee service (pp. 141-142)
Finance and Budgetary oversees all AAWS and Grapevine financial matters plus three funds: the General Fund, the Reserve Fund and the Postretirement Medical Fund (p. 59)

The trustees' General Service Conference Committee (Agenda's counterpart) works on the Conference's procedures, agenda and theme, considers how workloads are spread among Conference committees, and looks for better ways for Conference members to communicate (p. 59)

The trustees' Literature Committee develops new and revised Conference-approved literature, reviews items for revision or discontinuance, and oversees the updates to The A.A. Service Manual that the Conference recommends (p. 59)
The Compliance Committee reviews and upholds the processes in the GSB Code of Conduct and Confidentiality Policy (p. 60)

The trustees' Public Information Committee carries out pending Conference Advisory Actions on public information, one example of how Advisory Actions reach the trustees' committees for implementation (p. 60)

Bill W.'s 'senior' trustees' committee, the General Policy Committee, met town-meeting style for four to six hours on the Sunday before each quarterly board meeting. It became the General Sharing Session in October 1977 (pp. C-40, C-75).

The Concepts footnote, repeated in the revised Concept XI essay, says the General Sharing Session meets three times a year for about two hours on the Saturday before the board meeting, on the long-range plans of board committees and other topics of special interest. Its members are all trustees, AAWS and Grapevine directors and staffs, and the appointed members of board committees; p. 61 says it is held each quarterly board weekend (pp. C-36, C-67).

quotes.text: There are currently 10 standing and four auxiliary committees of the General Service Board.
The chair of a committee is a trustee, and the secretary is usually a GSO staff member.

nodes.title: Trustees' Nominating Committee
nodes.summary: This standing committee reviews trustee selection procedures. It recommends Class A trustees, general service trustees, nontrustee directors and the officer slate. It checks the eligibility of regional trustee and trustee-at-large nominees and takes part in the Conference sessions that select them. Its counterpart is the Conference Committee on Trustees.
nodes.chosen_by: Designated by the GSB chair (bylaws); members are appointed by the chair, subject to board approval
nodes.term: Not stated
nodes.how_many: 1 committee
duties: Review procedures for selecting candidates
Review and approve nontrustee director candidates and general service trustees nominated by the corporate boards
Recommend Class A trustee candidates
Recommend the slate of GSB officers
Review regional trustee and trustee-at-large nominees for eligibility before the Conference
Its chair co-chairs the regional trustee nominating session; its members vote in the regional trustee and trustee-at-large sessions
Consult with the AAWS and Grapevine boards on potential directors and trustees
Approve ACM candidates
facts: The area delegate sends a regional trustee candidate's name and contact information to the committee's secretary, who sends the candidate a link to submit a signed résumé (p. 55)

GSO's Nominating desk supports this committee. It announces board vacancies widely to attract a diverse, talented and accomplished pool of applicants, and it coordinates the selection process, supplying the information, forms, guidelines and procedures (p. 72).

Concept XI: the Nominating Committee's 'first and last duty' is to fill every vacancy with the best person obtainable. It must work carefully and well ahead of time, refuse casual recommendations, and guard against the natural habit of recommending people a little less able than oneself (pp. C-37, C-38).

quotes.text: Proposed new member trustees to the General Service Board shall be nominated by a nominating committee designated by the chair.

nodes.title: Appointed Committee Members (ACMs)
nodes.summary: ACMs are A.A. members with strong service or professional experience who serve on certain trustees' committees in areas such as Corrections, Accessibilities, CPC, Public Information and Literature. They are not trustees. They serve without pay, with travel and accommodation covered by the board.
nodes.chosen_by: Suggestions come from trustees, delegates, staff, directors and past and present committee members. The committee chair and staff secretary evaluate résumés, the chair or a designee interviews eligible candidates, and the trustees' Nominating Committee approves. The GSB chair then makes the appointment.
nodes.term: One year, which may be extended depending on committee projects (maximum four years)
nodes.how_many: Not stated
qualifications: Special qualifications, service experience and dedication
A past Conference delegate is not eligible until one year after rotation
duties: Bring expertise to the trustees' committee's work
facts: Maximum of four years of service (p. 61)

quotes.text: Appointed committee members serve for one year, but the term may be extended depending on committee projects (maximum four years).
(Candidates who are past Conference delegates are not eligible until one year after rotation.)

nodes.title: GSB Officers
nodes.summary: The Board of Trustees elects five officers: a chair, a first vice-chair, a second vice-chair, a secretary and a treasurer. The chair appoints the assistant treasurer, the assistant secretary and any other officers, subject to board approval. The vice-chairs step in, in order, if the chair is absent or disabled. Under New York law the chair and vice-chairs are the president and vice-presidents, but they use those titles only when legally required.
nodes.chosen_by: The Nominating Committee recommends a slate of trustees as officers, which the board settles before the Conference and presents to the Conference like the trustee slate. The Board elects the officers at its 2nd quarterly meeting, or at any meeting to fill a vacancy. In practice the board now elects the first vice-chair, second vice-chair and secretary by the Third Legacy Procedure (2024 Final Report, p. 100; 2026 Final Report, p. 108).
nodes.term: Chair: up to four successive annual terms; other terms not stated
nodes.how_many: 5 elected officers plus the appointed assistant treasurer and assistant secretary
qualifications: Elected officers come from a slate of trustees; no GSB employee may serve as chair
duties: Chair: duties of a president under New York law
Vice-chairs: perform the chair's duties in order when needed
Secretary and treasurer: customary duties; the treasurer chairs the Finance and Budgetary Committee
Chair and secretary (or a vice-chair and assistant secretary) analyze mail votes of Conference delegates; the secretary or assistant secretary mails the result
facts: Elected at the 2nd quarterly meeting, the Saturday after the Conference
The chair's appointees are approved at the 2nd quarterly meeting; committee appointments at the 3rd
'the GSB used the Third Legacy Procedure to elect the first vice-chairperson, second vice-chairperson and secretary board officers for 2026' (2026 Final Report, p. 108).
The treasurer must be a Class A trustee; a 2026 proposal to remove that requirement got no action (2026 Final Report, p. 109).

The officers printed at the front of a Final Report are the slate elected after the previous Conference. Annual meeting dates: April 30, 2022; April 29, 2023; April 20, 2024; May 3, 2025; May 2, 2026 (Final Reports; see Trustees & Boards for the current slate).

quotes.text: elect a chair, a first vice-chair, a second vice-chair, a secretary, and a treasurer
they shall at no time employ such titles, except as may be required for the execution of legal documents

nodes.title: GSB Bylaws (Appendix O)
nodes.summary: The GSB bylaws are the legal rules for the board. They contain the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions and the short form of the Twelve Concepts. They set the board's size and classes, term limits, removal and vacancies, officers, meetings, quorum, committees and how amendments are made. They also bring in Conference delegates on key matters: new trustees, bylaw amendments, new affiliate corporations, and decisions of principle the board sends to a mail vote. If a majority of delegates disapproves, the board is barred or expected to refrain.
nodes.chosen_by: Adopted by the GSB on April 22, 1957, after Conference consideration. Amendments need 75% of all trustees, or only a majority of trustees present if the amendment has gone to Conference delegates and they did not disapprove.
nodes.term: Not applicable
nodes.how_many: Not applicable
duties: Assert the board's negative right to prevent changes to the Twelve Steps and make it custodian of the Twelve Traditions; neither may be changed except as the Charter provides
Give the Board of Trustees the powers of a Board of Directors under New York law
facts: Written by Bernard S. ('Bern'), an international lawyer, long a nonalcoholic trustee, and board chair from 1951 to 1956
Trustees are 'members' only to comply with New York membership-corporation law
Each trustee signs an agreement to be bound by the bylaws
'Entire membership' means 21 voting member trustees when there are no vacancies
Quorum is two-fifths of member trustees
The fiscal year is the calendar year
If dissolved, assets go to 501(c)(3) institutions with court approval, never to any member, trustee, officer or private individual

The bylaws say the board claims no ownership of the recovery program, because the Steps, like all spiritual truths, are open to everyone. It claims only a 'negative right' to block, as far as it can, any change, alteration or extension of the Twelve Steps unless the Fellowship itself asks for it under the Conference Charter (pp. 134-135)

The Fellowship regards the board as the custodian of the Twelve Traditions: the bylaws require it to do its best to keep them intact, and neither to change, alter or add to them itself nor, as far as it can, let others do so, except as the Conference Charter provides (p. 135). Compare the Conference's role as 'guardian' of the Traditions (p. 128)

The bylaws describe the board as 'an agency created and now designated by the Fellowship' to keep services available to people who seek, through A.A., a way to arrest alcoholism by applying the Twelve Steps (p. 134)

The trustees have every power New York law gives a board of directors, but the bylaws expect them to use those powers in keeping with the Fellowship's faith, guided by the Twelve Steps, the Twelve Traditions and the Conference Charter (p. 139)

The 75% amendment rule also covers the board's Certificate of Incorporation. If Conference delegates are consulted and do not disapprove, a Certificate amendment needs only a majority of members present, provided the yes votes at least equal a quorum (p. 143)

The GSB bylaws let the board indemnify present or former trustees and officers against judgments, fines, settlements and legal expenses from civil or criminal proceedings arising from their service, but never when a final judgment finds bad faith, active and deliberate dishonesty, or a personal gain they were not entitled to (p. 142). The AAWS bylaws make this mandatory ('shall', p. 150); Grapevine's, like the GSB's, make it optional ('may', p. 159)

quotes.text: now has but one purpose, that of serving the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous.
any modification, alteration, or extension of these Twelve Steps, except at the instance of the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous
it is regarded by the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous as the custodian of these Traditions

nodes.title: Trustee Participation at Forums and World Meetings
nodes.summary: Trustees take part in Regional, Local and Special Forums. These are sharing sessions that keep the board and staff in touch with members, and no formal actions come out of them. The two trustees-at-large usually serve as U.S./Canada delegates to the World Service Meeting and the Meeting of the Americas (REDELA), which alternate years.
nodes.chosen_by: Regional Forums rotate at each region's request. Board participation in Regional and Local Forums needs approval from the trustees' International Conventions/Regional Forums Committee.
nodes.term: Not applicable
nodes.how_many: Not applicable
duties: Regional Forums: no registration fee; the GSB pays for meeting rooms
Local Forums: 1.5 or 2 days; the Local Forum Committee pays expenses; the GSB sends one board member and one person from GSO or the Grapevine office, and displays literature at board expense
Special Forums: for members who could not normally attend a Regional or Local Forum, and where there is an expressed need based on culture, language or geography
facts: Forum Final Reports go to all attendees and are available on GSO's website (p. 62)
The World Service Meeting is every two years, alternating between New York and another member country (p. 62)
REDELA is held in the years without a WSM, rotating among member countries (p. 62)

Regional Forums alternate by year: Western Canada, Eastern Canada, Southeast and Pacific in even years; Northeast, East Central, West Central and Southwest in odd years (2026-2027 schedule, 2026 Final Report, p. 98).

2027 forums: Northeast May 20-23 (Niagara Falls), East Central June 25-27 (Green Bay), West Central September 10-12 (Duluth), Southwest September 30-October 3 (Kansas City, Missouri) (2026 Final Report, p. 98).
The 29th World Service Meeting: Lisbon, Portugal, October 4-8, 2026 (2026 Final Report, p. 94). Next International Convention: St. Louis, Missouri, July 4-7, 2030 (2026 Final Report, p. 98).

The World Service Meeting is a forum where delegates from around the world share experience, strength and hope and look for ways to carry the message in any nation and language. It can also express a worldwide group conscience, and it encourages sound service structures (p. 62)
REDELA, the Meeting of the Americas, offers help to A.A.s where no service structure has been set up and gives countries a forum to share experience of sponsorship across borders (p. 62)

At Regional Forums, members can meet board members and GSO staff and receive complimentary service literature. GSO's Regional Forums desk arranges translation where needed, works with each host committee and helps Local and Special Forum committees on request (p. 73).

quotes.text: As all Forums are intended to be sharing sessions, no formal actions result.
Regional Forums carry A.A.’s message of love and service by improving communication at all levels of our Fellowship.

nodes.title: The Board's Operating Corporations (Concept VIII)
nodes.summary: The General Service Board does its administrative work through two affiliate corporations, A.A. World Services, Inc. (AAWS) and AA Grapevine, Inc. The board does not interfere with their daily operations. It keeps 'custodial oversight' by electing their directors, approving their budgets and holding authority over their bylaws. Each corporate board mixes trustees, nontrustee directors and paid A.A. executives, an example of the Concept IV 'right of participation'.
nodes.chosen_by: Both are membership corporations whose members are the GSB trustees. The trustees elect each corporation's directors at an annual members' meeting held the day after the Conference closes.
nodes.term: Directors are elected for one-year terms (bylaws).
nodes.how_many: 2 corporations, each currently with a 9-director board
duties: AAWS oversees GSO service and publishing, Archives, Finance and communications with A.A. service entities and offices around the world; publishes A.A. books and pamphlets
AA Grapevine, Inc. oversees the Grapevine office; publishes Grapevine, La Viña, Grapevine books and other content-related items
Both submit budgets that the trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee reviews and recommends to the GSB
facts: Three corporate mechanisms for custodial oversight: electing directors, approving budgets, and authority to change corporate bylaws (p. 64)
The trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee reviews both corporations' financial results and recommends their budgets to the GSB (p. 64)
The Conference itself is not incorporated, but the GSB, AAWS and AA Grapevine are (p. 40)
AAWS was incorporated as a not-for-profit in 1962 and AA Grapevine in 1971; both are now membership corporations whose members are the trustees (p. C-47, footnote 3)
Each corporation's fiscal year runs January 1 to December 31 (pp. 151, 160)

In the manual's overview, AAWS employs GSO personnel, directs GSO services and is responsible for aa.org and A.A.'s broad publishing; AA Grapevine, Inc. employs editorial and business personnel and publishes Grapevine and La Viña across its digital platforms (aagrapevine.org and aalavina.org) (p. 5)

Long-form Tradition Six: property of real use to A.A. should be incorporated and managed separately, keeping the material apart from the spiritual, and an A.A. group as such should never go into business (p. 107)

A Charter footnote says AAWS and AA Grapevine are affiliates of the General Service Board, not 'subsidiaries', although the Charter text speaks of 'subsidiary services'. They are separate not-for-profit corporations: each corporate board handles its own routine policy and business and creates its own committees, while the trustees, acting as members of each corporation, elect the directors (pp. 50 footnote 1, 126-127)

Concept VIII: the board's role toward AAWS and Grapevine is custodial oversight, not management. Each corporation should have its own charter, working capital, executive, employees, offices and equipment, and reserve funds stay with the trustees, so that money and authority are never concentrated in one entity (pp. C-24 to C-26)

Concept VIII rejects two consolidations: making the board an operating company (a large business needs a full-time single executive, and a trustee chair can't give the time or be paid) and merging everything into one big service corporation (too much executive authority in one place). Bill W. warns that consolidation for accounting simplicity or tax savings will be tried again and again (pp. C-25, C-26)

Concept X: the trustees' authority over AAWS and Grapevine is not only ultimate but 'absolute' the moment they choose: they can elect new boards of directors at any time, control the budgets and withhold operating funds. While things go well, they should not interfere with or usurp the corporations' operating authority (p. C-35).

quotes.text: The General Service Board has custodial oversight over both of these corporations, which it exercises by electing the directors of each.
No class is set in absolute authority over another.
This is the corporate or “participating” method of doing business
There is always a powerful connection between money and authority.

nodes.title: General Service Board Reserve Fund
nodes.summary: The board of trustees set up the Reserve Fund in 1954. Its main purpose is to keep AAWS and Grapevine services running in an emergency or disaster and to pay costs beyond their means, such as major leasehold improvements or technical upgrades. It also gives the GSB and its two affiliates time to adjust to changed economic or other conditions. By Conference action, the fund may hold no more than one year of combined operating expenses of AAWS, Grapevine and the GSB General Fund. The manual's FAQ compares it to a group's prudent reserve.
nodes.chosen_by: Withdrawals are authorized by the GSB on the recommendation of the trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee.
duties: Fund essential AAWS and Grapevine services during emergencies or disasters
Fund costs beyond AAWS/Grapevine means, such as major leasehold improvements or technical upgrades
Give the GSB and its two affiliates time to plan for changed economic or other conditions
facts: Established by the board of trustees in 1954 (p. 65)
Capped at one year's combined operating expenses of AAWS, AA Grapevine and the GSB General Fund (p. 65)
If the fund exceeds the 12-month limit, one year is allowed to review the level, then a second year to formulate actions to bring it below 12 months (p. 65)
The office and the Finance and Budgetary Committee continuously monitor the balance and the number of months of expenses it covers (p. 65)
The manual's FAQ says the fund covers anywhere from nine months to a year of combined AAWS and Grapevine expenses (p. 69); the year-end 2025 figure in the Concept XII footnote was lower (p. C-59)
When possible, AA Grapevine's excess income after operations moves to the Reserve Fund each year (p. 87)

On December 31, 2025, the Reserve Fund held $11,562,418 in assets. After a $540,000 liability for Grapevine subscriptions, the balance was $11,022,418, enough for 6.12 months of the $21,617,181 combined operating expenses of AAWS, the GSB and Grapevine (p. C-59).

Concept XI asks the trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee to keep setting money aside for the Reserve Fund in good times, and to invest it so that at least two-thirds is available at any moment without loss (pp. C-38, C-65).

In 1960 the Reserve Fund was a little over $200,000, about one year of World Office expenses, saved mostly from book income. In about half of the previous twenty years it covered deficits when group contributions fell short (p. C-51).

Bill W. argued that the income from A.A. book sales is not really profit. It is the sum of many small contributions from book buyers, and the Reserve Fund built from it belongs wholly to A.A. (p. C-52).

quotes.text: the fund is limited to no more than one year’s combined operating expenses of A.A. World Services, Inc., AA Grapevine, Inc. and the General Fund of the General Service Board.

nodes.title: Licensing, Copyrights & Trademarks
nodes.summary: A.A. owns and controls its own literature and its name, so that A.A. principles stay intact and the message is not garbled. AAWS and Grapevine have registered trademarks and logos, and substantially all their publications are protected by registered copyrights. Both corporations monitor reprinting and copying closely so the copyrights are not eroded or lost. AAWS refuses permission for novelty items, and anyone wanting to use A.A. logos or photographs should ask GSO first.
duties: Monitor reprinting and copying of AAWS and Grapevine material
Grant or refuse permission to reprint copyrighted material
facts: In 1993 AAWS announced it was discontinuing official use of all the circle/triangle trademarks and service marks (p. 65)
AAWS does not grant permission to reprint A.A. material on novelty items such as bumper stickers, t-shirts, mugs or greeting cards (p. 69)
The Big Book's First and Second Editions are public domain in the U.S. only; the Third and Fourth Editions are copyrighted worldwide; all Internet postings of any edition need AAWS permission (p. 69)
GSO's Legal, Licensing and IP department handles permission requests in more than 111 languages across more than 100 countries (p. 75)
AA Grapevine does not grant permission to reproduce its logo, registered trademarks, artwork or cartoons on other websites or publications (p. 85)
Members wanting to use logos or photographs from aa.org or the literature should first contact GSO and the AAWS intellectual properties administrator (p. 79)

Local A.A. publications may reprint the Steps, Traditions and Concepts and quote a phrase, sentence or brief paragraph from A.A. literature (such as the Big Book, the Twelve and Twelve, this manual and Conference-approved pamphlets) without a prior written request; the proper credit line should be included. Websites may post brief excerpts under the same guidelines (pp. 23-24)

The A.A. Preamble is copyrighted by AA Grapevine. Beneath it, and beneath any Grapevine or La Viña article reprinted locally, the line 'Copyright © (Month, Year) AA Grapevine, Inc./La Viña. Reprinted with permission.' should appear (p. 24)

Although AAWS no longer uses the circle and triangle as official marks, any group or district may put the symbol on newsletters, meeting schedules or other A.A. material, and no AAWS permission is needed (p. 24)

Using A.A.'s marks on goods or services that do not come from A.A. and were not approved by A.A. infringes and dilutes them; over time the marks would come to stand for things that are not A.A. and lose their meaning (p. 65). When you ask permission, GSO usually asks for a copy of what you plan to use and answers within a few days. The aim is to protect the marks, not to discourage event flyers or websites, and photographs often carry their own restrictions (p. 79).

The principle goes back to 1938. The founders turned down Harper's offer of a $1,500 royalty advance for the Big Book: it would have left them in debt, and A.A. ought to own and publish its own literature. They sold Works Publishing stock instead (p. 98)

Appendix N gives the complete list of registered trademarks and service marks that symbolize A.A.: A.A., Alcoholics Anonymous, The Big Book, the 'Blue People' graphic, Grapevine, La Viña, The Grapevine, AA Grapevine, GV, AA Grapevine Digital Archive and Audio Grapevine (p. 133)
The 'Blue People' graphic is a copyrighted AAWS design and trademark. Only the AAWS board, the AA Grapevine board, the General Service Board and GSO may use it (AAWS, June 17, 2016) (p. 133)

Concept XII: A.A. will share its principles with anyone but asks other agencies not to use the A.A. name publicly. Early Conferences decided against incorporating the name, even by act of Congress, because a lawsuit is a public controversy and the whole Fellowship would have had to be incorporated. The name Alcoholics Anonymous and the abbreviation A.A. were legally registered in 1972 (pp. C-58, C-59).

quotes.text: A society like ours ought to control and publish its own literature.
AAWS holds the copyrights of A.A. material in trust for A.A. as a whole.
Reprinted from (name of publication, page number), with permission of Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc.
A.A. is prepared to give away all the knowledge and all the experience it has — all excepting the A.A. name itself.

nodes.title: Corporate Bylaws (Appendices P & Q)
nodes.summary: The AAWS and AA Grapevine bylaws set the legal rules for both boards. The trustees are the corporations' members. They elect the directors each year and alone can amend the bylaws. Both sets of bylaws share the same core rules: one-year director terms; a limit of four consecutive full terms for directors who are not trustees (the AAWS President and the Grapevine Publisher are exempt); removal by three-quarters votes; and a board meeting in the week before each quarterly GSB meeting.
nodes.chosen_by: Members of each corporation (the GSB trustees) elect directors by majority ballot at the Annual Meeting (Grapevine Members may also vote by proxy).
nodes.term: One-year director terms
nodes.how_many: AAWS: 9 directors; Grapevine: 7 to 10 (currently 9)
qualifications: At least four directors must be Members of the Corporation (trustees), at least two of them Class B trustees
facts: AAWS members are the GSB trustees; Grapevine members are the members and trustees of the GSB (pp. 144, 153)
Annual Meeting of Members: the day immediately after the scheduled close of the General Service Conference (pp. 144, 153)

Order of business at Members' meetings: minutes, officers' reports, election of directors (at the Annual Meeting), consideration of budget (if required), communications, unfinished and new business (pp. 146, 155)
AAWS board is fixed at nine directors; Grapevine's may be 7 to 10, set by resolution of the Members (pp. 146, 155)
Directors who are not trustees (other than the AAWS President or the Grapevine Publisher) may not be elected to more than four consecutive full terms (pp. 146, 155)
The board may remove a director for cause by 3/4 of the entire board; the Members may remove one with or without cause by 3/4 of the entire Membership (pp. 146, 155)
Quorum is a majority of the entire board, with at least one director present who is a Member (trustee) (pp. 147, 156)
Special board meetings must be called by the Chair on the written demand of at least one-fifth of the entire board (pp. 147, 156)
Directors' meetings need at least 10 days' notice, which a director can waive (pp. 147, 156)

Mid-year vacancies are filled (AAWS) or may be filled (Grapevine) for the unexpired term by majority vote of the remaining directors; new seats created by enlarging the board are filled by the Members (pp. 147-148, 156)
The Chair and President are elected annually by the board from among its own number; no employee may serve as Chair (pp. 148, 157)
Committees of the Board must have at least three directors (pp. 150, 159)
Budget is submitted for approval at the first GSB trustees' meeting after January 1 (pp. 151, 160)
Bylaws are amended only by a 2/3 vote of the Members; the board of directors cannot amend them (pp. 152, 160)
Grapevine bylaws allow Members to vote by proxy and add an Assistant Secretary officer (pp. 154, 157-158)

At each Annual Meeting of Members, the AAWS and Grapevine boards present an annual report for the last fiscal year, certified by the corporation's independent public accountants (or otherwise verified under section 519 of New York's Not-for-Profit Corporation Law) (pp. 144, 153)

At AAWS, committees of the corporation (as opposed to Committees of the Board) may include people who are not directors but cannot bind the corporation. The AAWS bylaws also list nine matters no committee may decide, four more than the GSB and Grapevine lists: electing or removing officers and directors, approving a merger or dissolution, recommending the sale of substantially all assets, and approving changes to the certificate of incorporation (p. 150)

The AA Grapevine bylaws printed in Appendix Q were last revised in September 2020 (p. 160). The Members set Grapevine's board size within the 7-10 range by resolution, but may not reduce it in a way that cuts short a sitting director's term; with no resolution, the size is the number elected at the most recent election (p. 155)
Each corporation must also set procedures for approving any spending that goes beyond its approved budget (pp. 151, 160)

quotes.text: The Membership of the Corporation shall consist of the trustees of The General Service Board of Alcoholics Anonymous, Inc.
No employee of the Corporation may serve as the Chair.
The Board of Directors shall not have the authority to alter, amend or repeal the Bylaws.

nodes.title: A.A. World Services, Inc. (AAWS)
nodes.summary: AAWS is one of the GSB's two operating corporations and employs most of the General Service Office staff. Its four main functions are Services, Publishing, Finance and Archives. It publishes Conference-approved literature, protects A.A.'s copyrights and runs the GSO staff desks. Its nine-member board combines trustees, nontrustee directors and two paid GSO staff (the general manager and the staff coordinator), and the GSO general manager serves as president.
nodes.chosen_by: Directors are elected annually by the corporation's members (the GSB trustees) at the Annual Meeting after the Conference. Nontrustee director nominees go through the AAWS and trustees' Nominating Committees and the GSB.
nodes.term: Directors: one-year terms; nontrustee directors up to four successive terms
nodes.how_many: 9 directors: 2 general service trustees, 2 regional trustees, 3 nontrustee directors, 1 GSO staff coordinator, 1 GSO general manager
qualifications: At least four directors must be GSB trustees, at least two of them Class B (bylaws)
duties: Budget preparation for service and publishing operations
Pricing of new and revised publications
GSO service activities
Carrying out Conference and GSB recommendations
Reprint permissions, copyright concerns and other legal matters
facts: Nine directors in total (pp. 66, 146)
The GSO general manager is CEO and president of AAWS (pp. 66, 70)
The board meets at least four times a year (p. 66)
Six board committees: Communication and Language Services; Services and Technology; Finance; Publishing; Nominating; Internal Audit (pp. 66-67)
The AAWS chair appoints the members of board committees (p. 66)
GSO has had a full-time general manager since 1960 (pp. C-47, C-70)
The AAWS board grew from seven to nine members in April 1975 (p. C-75)
About 88 of GSO's roughly 100 employees work for AAWS (p. 87)

Publishing, Inc.; the Traditions' copyright line names 'Alcoholics Anonymous Publishing (now known as Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc.)'. Today A.A. nodes.title: How Conference-approved Literature Is Made
nodes.summary: New A.A. literature is added only after careful study. Conference and trustees' committees usually research the need first. Committee and staff members review drafts, which can take months or years. The finished manuscript then goes to the appropriate Conference committee, and if that committee recommends approval it goes to the whole Conference. If two-thirds of Conference members approve it, the piece may carry the 'Conference-approved' designation. GSO Publishing hires writers and handles printing and distribution.

nodes.title: AA Grapevine, Inc.
nodes.summary: AA Grapevine, Inc. is the GSB's second operating corporation. It is a multimedia publisher of Grapevine, the international journal of A.A., and La Viña, its Spanish-language magazine, along with books, apps, podcasts and a story archive. It aims to support itself through subscriptions and content-related sales and accepts no contributions or advertising; any La Viña shortfall is covered by the GSB General Fund. The publisher serves as its president and is a Conference member.
nodes.chosen_by: Directors are elected annually by the corporation's members (the GSB trustees). Nontrustee director nominees go through the Grapevine and trustees' Nominating Committees and the GSB.

The first issue (June 1944) went to every A.A. member serving in the World War II armed forces, who came to call the magazine their 'meeting in print', and to the secretaries of all known groups in North America (p. 80).

The Grapevine Story Archive keeps almost every Grapevine article and letter published since June 1944 online, including every Grapevine article by co-founder Bill W., and readers can browse it by department, topic or date (p. 84). The Conference has long urged members and groups to buy bulk or monthly subscriptions as a way of reaching institutions such as prisons and hospitals, professionals, and newcomers (p. 68).

La Viña exists because the 1996 Conference asked AA Grapevine, Inc. to publish it. The Conference saw that Grapevine could not be expected to carry the whole cost alone and asked the General Service Board to help; that is the origin of the General Fund transfer noted above (p. 68).

It started as a local newsletter for New York City-area members, but Bill W. and the editors soon saw a wider use: drawing scattered groups together and telling the public about the new program (p. 170)

About a year and a half after the first issue, Bill W. asked the groups whether they wanted Grapevine as their national publication, and they adopted it at once. He wanted it independent of any one person, group or office, even the Central Office and the Alcoholic Foundation, though loosely tied to the Foundation for continuity and soundness (p. 170)

Between 1944 and 1971 Bill W. wrote roughly 150 Grapevine pieces, among them two essay series that introduced the Twelve Traditions; in later years he used the magazine to work out his thinking on A.A.'s basic spiritual principles (p. 170)

Bill W. treated the magazine as one of his main channels to the groups. He floated his plan to rebalance alcoholic and nonalcoholic trustees there, and used it to present the new General Service Conference to the Fellowship (p. 170)
A Grapevine editor wrote the A.A. Preamble, drawing on the foreword to the Big Book's first edition. It first appeared in the June 1947 issue, and AA Grapevine still holds the copyright (pp. 24, 170)
Some Grapevine articles were later reprinted as personal stories in the Big Book's second, third and fourth editions, and others in Conference-approved books and pamphlets (p. 170)

All Editorial department members who make content decisions are sober A.A. members.

nodes.title: The General Service Office (GSO)
nodes.summary: GSO, in New York City, is made up of the employees of AAWS and AA Grapevine. The two corporations are independent but coordinate human resources, finance and shipping, and keep archival records covering both. GSO serves A.A. groups in the U.S. and Canada and supports A.A. internationally, especially where there is no service structure. As the earliest GSO, it is generally regarded as the 'senior' office. It acts as a clearinghouse for A.A. experience and oversees publication of Conference-approved literature.
nodes.chosen_by: Employees of AAWS and Grapevine, led by the AAWS General Manager and the Grapevine Publisher (both A.A. members)

GSO gives local A.A. office information to anyone looking for meetings. Where no local office exists, it gives group contact information for Twelfth Step purposes. Its services are regularly reviewed against the Fellowship's needs, technology and available resources (p. 77).

Office history: the Big Book was written in Newark, N.J. In 1940 the office moved to a two-room office on Vesey Street (mail to Box 658), with Ruth H. (nonalcoholic) as A.A.'s first national secretary and book sales as its only support. In 1941-45 it moved to Lexington Avenue opposite Grand Central, and later to 44th Street (pp. 100-103)

GSO's employees are employed by A.A. World Services, Inc. (Grapevine's staff by AA Grapevine, Inc.), not by the General Service Board. Any Conference-ordered reorganization of staff would have to follow employment law (pp. 87, 127)

Paid workers per member have fallen as A.A. grew: one per 1,000 members at first, one per 3,000 ten years later, one per 7,000 in 1960, and about one per 17,000 in the U.S. and Canada in 2020. World services cost about $200,000 a year in 1960 (pp. C-50, C-51; the 2020 figure is footnote 1, printed on p. C-59).

nodes.title: Contributions & Self-Support
nodes.summary: Contributions sent to 'GSO' actually go to the General Service Board, which is responsible for all Seventh Tradition money. Following the Seventh Tradition, it accepts money only from A.A. members, groups and other A.A. entities. The Conference caps individual gifts and bequests but sets no limit for groups. Contributions from groups and members cover some, but not all, of AAWS service expenses; net publishing income covers the rest.
qualifications: Contributors must be A.A. members, A.A. groups, or other A.A. entities (areas, districts, conventions, roundups, intergroup/central offices)
facts: Individual member limit: $7,500 USD per year, which cannot be earmarked (p. 88)
Bequest limit: a one-time bequest of up to $12,500 USD, only from an A.A. member (pp. 88, 89)
No limit on contributions from an A.A. group (p. 88)
In recent years, fewer than 50% of groups listed with the GSB contributed to it (p. 88)

Self-support practices many groups use: the Regular Contribution Plan, the Birthday Plan, and Grapevine/La Viña subscriptions (subscriptions support Grapevine, which cannot accept contributions) (p. 88)
AAWS expenses are split into service and publishing (p. 88)
GSO does not pass contributions on to areas, districts or intergroups; requests to do so are returned (p. 89)

When a member asks what GSO does with the group's money, the manual points the GSR to Chapter 10, the DCM, the delegate and the service sponsor, and to two pieces of service material: 'Services Provided by GSO/AAWS' (F-176; aa.org now numbers it SMF-176) and 'Seventh Tradition Fact Sheet — Your Seventh Tradition Contributions' (F-203) (p. 12)

The limits are recent: a 2024 Advisory Action raised the individual yearly limit from $5,000 to $7,500, and a 2025 Advisory Action raised the one-time bequest limit from $10,000 to $12,500 (Advisory Actions page, M-39). The 2026-2028 manual's editorial grid records updating the bequest and memorial-gift amounts on pp. 88-89 to $12,500 and $7,500 (p. IX).

Gifts made in memory of a deceased member follow the same rules as any other contribution: they are accepted only from A.A. members and groups, and a gift from an individual member is subject to the $7,500 limit (p. 88).

Each group decides by group conscience how much to give and to which service entities. Many areas suggest a formula for splitting contributions, and the pamphlet 'Self-Support: Where Money and Spirituality Mix' covers this in more detail (p. 89). On request, GSO's Finance function supplies self-support packets, group contribution envelopes and birthday envelopes (p. 75), and the GSB supplies Birthday Plan envelopes at no charge (p. 88).

Warranty One: because the board refuses outside contributions and keeps each person's gift to a modest amount, the Conference cannot become dangerously wealthy. The delegates, who control the ultimate supply of service funds, also check anyone seeking too much personal authority (p. C-49).

Concept XII notes that delegates, committee members and GSRs have found pressure appeals for money unwanted and unneeded in A.A. They simply show what the giver's service dollar does to steer alcoholics to A.A. and keep A.A. united, and the contributions follow (p. C-50).

quotes.text: There is no limit on the amount of contributions that may be made to GSB by an A.A. group.
contributions are actually made to the General Service Board, which is responsible for all Seventh Tradition contributions.
Group participation in A.A. is part of our spiritual heritage, and is more important than the dollar amount of the contributions.

nodes.title: GSO Staff Members & Assignment Rotation
nodes.summary: Thirteen GSO Staff Member Assignments ('desks'), Self-Support and Finance included (the manual's p. 70 sentence still says twelve), are filled by a rotating group of professionals who are also A.A. members. Each covers one area of service, such as Conference, Corrections, Public Information or International. Staff answer the Fellowship's emails and calls, support local committee chairs, and serve as secretaries to the trustees' and Conference committees tied to their desk. Most staff members rotate to a new desk every two years. Each staff member is expected to be able to do, or learn to do, any job in the office; Bill W. gave the security and continuity of the office as the main reason for rotation and equal pay.

Staff rotation and equal pay began after the office nearly collapsed. One highly paid staff member had kept tight control and hired assistants who would not compete with her. When she and an assistant broke down, the office lost an estimated $50,000 in group contributions over three years (p. C-45).
