nodes.title: Guiding Principles
nodes.summary: A.A.'s service structure is held together by shared spiritual principles, not by rules or government. Bill W. named three legacies: Recovery, Unity and Service. He called the sum of every A.A. service, from a Twelfth Step call to the General Service Office, the Third Legacy. The Twelve Traditions, the Twelve Concepts for World Service and the principle of rotation explain why the structure works the way it does. Appendix F shows how districts, areas and regions can be redrawn as A.A. grows.
nodes.chosen_by: No one elects these. The Fellowship adopted them: the Traditions were declared A.A.'s platform at the 1950 Cleveland Convention, and the Concepts were adopted by the 12th General Service Conference in 1962.
nodes.how_many: Three Legacies; Twelve Traditions; Twelve Concepts (Concept XII holds six General Warranties)
facts: Bill W. called Recovery, Unity and Service the Fellowship's chief inheritances from A.A.'s first 20 years (p. 93).
Anything that helps reach a fellow sufferer is an A.A. service, and the sum of all services is the Third Legacy of Service (p. 96).
Rotation flows from Tradition Two ('Our leaders are but trusted servants; they do not govern') and is referenced in Concepts IX and XI (p. 112).
The groups took final responsibility for world services at the 1955 St. Louis International Convention (C-3).
On July 3, 1955, the Conference became guardian of the Traditions and sole successor to co-founders Dr. Bob and Bill (p. 128).

Changing the Twelve Traditions or the Article 12 Warranties needs written consent from at least three-quarters of the registered groups that respond, with no less than six months to consider (p. 128).
The Traditions were first published in long form in the Grapevine in May 1946 (p. 102).
Several thousand members at the 1950 Cleveland Convention declared the Traditions the platform for A.A. unity (p. 102).
Tradition Nine (long form) says rotating leadership is best and that each group needs the least possible organization (p. 107).
Each area runs its assembly by its own conscience, and Concept XII's General Warranties are its guide to staying democratic (p. 19).

The manual's copyright page carries the A.A. Preamble (reprinted with AA Grapevine's permission), the Declaration of Unity and the 'I Am Responsible' declaration; page X is captioned 'A.A. International Convention, St. Louis, Missouri, 1955', the Convention where the groups took over responsibility for world services (pp. II, X; C-3)

In discussing Warranty Six, Bill W. lists the liberties the Traditions give members and groups: no penalties for nonconformity; no fees or dues, only voluntary contributions; no member expelled, since membership is the individual's choice; each group runs its own affairs, asked only to avoid harming A.A. as a whole; and any alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group if, as a group, they have no other purpose or affiliation (p. C-58).

quotes.text: an A.A. service is anything whatever that helps us to reach a fellow sufferer
Three Legacies — Recovery, Unity and Service.
These Concepts therefore aim to record the “why” of our service structure
When anyone, anywhere, reaches out for help, I want the hand of A.A. always to be there. And for that: I am responsible.

nodes.title: Principle of Rotation
nodes.summary: Rotation means regularly passing service jobs on to new people, so that responsibility for A.A. is shared through changing leadership. It comes from Tradition Two (leaders are trusted servants who do not govern) and is referenced in Concepts IX and XI. Trusted servants step aside when their terms end, even if no successor is in sight, and look for a different way to serve. Outgoing servants often share their experience with the person who follows. The manual calls stepping out of a position you love a step into humility, which for some is the spiritual essence of anonymity, since there is no A.A. 'status' to compete for.
nodes.chosen_by: Rotation is a practice, not an office. Groups, districts and areas elect replacements when terms end. Delegates rotate by panel: in approximately half the areas assembly elections are held in even years and in the rest in odd years.
nodes.term: GSRs, DCMs, area officers and delegates usually serve two-year terms, and a delegate serves only once. Class B trustees serve up to 4 years and Class A trustees up to 6, plus a 4-year term for a board chair. Most GSO staff change assignments every two years.
duties: Step aside when your term ends, even if the position may go unfilled; offer to serve somewhere else (pp. 12, 18)
Share your experience with and brief your successor (pp. 17, 112)
If you can no longer carry out the position's responsibilities, experience suggests you be asked to resign so a new trusted servant can be elected (p. 112)
Where the position has an alternate, the alternate may help and can step in if needed (p. 112)
facts: Glossary: rotation is the spiritual principle of sharing responsibility for A.A. through changing leadership (p. 93).
Rotation flows from Tradition Two and is referenced in Concepts IX and XI (p. 112).
Each service entity decides what makes a GSR, DCM or other trusted servant 'inactive'. Experience suggests asking that person to resign (p. 112).
GSRs and DCMs are encouraged not to serve another two-year term just because no one else has volunteered (pp. 12, 18).
Rotation keeps delegates from succeeding themselves or returning later as delegates. Past delegates are usually asked not to serve as GSRs or DCMs (p. 30).
A past delegate may stand for trustee one year after their last Conference (p. 63).
Past delegates can't become appointed committee members until one year after rotation (p. 61).

Under the current Conference Charter, approximately half the areas hold assembly elections in even years and the rest in odd years, creating rotating panels (p. 125). The original 1955 Charter called these rotating Panels One and Two (p. 121).
Bill W.'s plan seated odd-numbered Panel One in 1951 and Panel Two in 1952. After that, one panel is elected and one retires each year (p. 104).
Some areas rotate delegate selection between parts of the area, such as rural and urban, but a well-qualified member should not be passed over for this (p. 39).
Concept XI: a group secretary can change every six months and an intergroup committeeman every year. A delegate must serve two years and a trustee four (C-46).
Concept IV: paid staff cannot become trustees, because that would interfere with the trustees' four-year rotation (C-13).
GSO staff assignments used to change every year. Since an AAWS Board discussion in March 1965, most staff rotate every two years (C-71, C-77).
Board chairs who rotate off are usually designated trustees emeriti (p. 58).
Rotating trustees say their farewells at the closing breakfast on the Saturday after Conference business ends (p. 40).

quotes.text: Rotation — The spiritual principle of sharing the responsibility for A.A. through changing leadership.
Traditionally, rotation ensures that group tasks, like nearly everything else in A.A., are passed around for all to share.
Rotation helps to bring us spiritual rewards far more enduring than any fame.

nodes.title: Twelve Concepts for World Service
nodes.summary: Bill W. wrote the Twelve Concepts, and they were adopted in 1962. They record the 'why' of A.A.'s world service structure. Ultimate authority rests with the collective conscience of the whole Fellowship (I), and the Conference is its active voice (II). Each part of the structure has rights of Decision (III), Participation (IV) and Appeal and Petition (V). Concepts VI to XI describe how the trustees, the board's corporations and their staffs are organized and led. Concept XII, Article 12 of the Conference Charter, sets the General Warranties that keep the Conference prudent and democratic.
nodes.chosen_by: Written by Bill W. and adopted by the 12th General Service Conference on April 26, 1962. The short form was approved by the 1971 Conference.
nodes.how_many: 12 Concepts, in a short form and a long form, each with an essay
facts: Adopted by the 12th Annual General Service Conference on April 26, 1962 (C-I).
The short form was approved by the 1971 Conference and approved for inclusion in the Service Manual in 1974. It also appears in the General Service Board Bylaws (C-III; p. 135).
The 1985 Conference recommended printing the original 1962 essays, with factual updates as numbered footnotes (C-III).

The 71st Conference called for an 'Amendments' section and the 76th approved it (C-2, C-61). It holds an updated Concept XI essay, with incorporated endnotes marked (E), and preserves the original 1962 wording of passages changed by Advisory Action; those passages are marked (A) in the main essays.
Concept I: final responsibility and ultimate authority for world services rest with the collective conscience of the whole Fellowship (C-IV).
Concept II: the Conference is the active voice and effective conscience of A.A. in its world affairs (C-IV).
Concept III: each element (Conference, board, corporations, staffs, committees, executives) has a traditional 'Right of Decision' (C-IV).
Concept IV: a 'Right of Participation', meaning voting representation in reasonable proportion to responsibility (C-IV).
Concept V: a 'Right of Appeal', so minority opinion is heard and personal grievances get careful consideration (C-IV).
Concept VI: the trustees, acting as the General Service Board, take the chief initiative and active responsibility in most world service matters (C-IV).
Concept VII: the board's Charter and Bylaws are legal instruments. The Conference Charter is not; it relies on tradition and the A.A. purse (C-IV).
Concept VIII: trustees plan and administer overall policy and finance. They hold custodial oversight of the service corporations by electing all of their directors (C-IV).
Concept IX: good leadership is needed at every level, and the trustees must take on the world service leadership the founders once held (C-IV).
Concept X: every service responsibility should be matched by an equal service authority whose scope is well defined (C-IV).
Concept XI: the trustees need the best possible committees, corporate directors, executives, staffs and consultants (C-IV).
Concept XII: the General Warranties. The Conference follows the spirit of the Traditions, never becomes a seat of perilous wealth or power, and stays democratic (C-IV).
Concept III makes delegates world servants of A.A. as a whole first and area representatives second, so on final decisions they may vote their own judgment and conscience (p. 39).
In line with Concepts IV and V, the Conference may hear Concept V appeals from members of the structure below Conference level (p. 125).
Concept IX calls the Third Legacy method (two-thirds vote or lot) highly satisfactory for choosing delegates (C-27).
Custodial oversight, the relationship between the GSB and AAWS and AA Grapevine, is described in Concept VIII (p. 92).

How to read the Concept essays: numbered footnotes are later factual updates, but footnotes marked with an asterisk were written by Bill W. himself in the years after the first printing; (A) marks wording changed by Advisory Action (pp. C-III, C-2)

Bill W. built the Concepts on 'checks and balances' rather than an authoritarian setup. Ideas that run through them: no one in unqualified authority over another; large, dissimilar operations separately incorporated; no undue concentration of money or influence; authority equal to responsibility at each level; no double-headed executive direction (p. C-2)

Bill W.'s Introduction: change does not necessarily mean progress. Anyone proposing a structural change need only make a strong case to both the trustees and the Conference, and a far-reaching change should first be labeled 'experimental', then recorded in an Amendments section so the original text stays on record (p. C-1)

quotes.text: Final responsibility and ultimate authority for A.A. world services should always reside in the collective conscience of our whole Fellowship.
Every service responsibility should be matched by an equal service authority, with the scope of such authority well defined.
The group of twelve related principles of service that have emerged from A.A.’s service accomplishments and mistakes since its beginning
Yet we should always realize that change does not necessarily spell progress.

nodes.title: General Warranties of the Conference (Concept XII)
nodes.summary: Concept XII is Article 12 of the Conference Charter. It opens with a pledge that the Conference will observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition, followed by six Warranties. The Conference will never become a seat of perilous wealth or power, and will keep enough operating funds plus an ample reserve. No member will hold unqualified authority over others. Important decisions will be reached by discussion, vote and, where possible, substantial unanimity, and no action will be personally punitive or stir public controversy. The Conference will never perform acts of government and will stay democratic. The Conference can amend the first eleven Articles of the Charter itself, but changing a Warranty needs the written consent of three-quarters of the directory-listed groups that vote.
nodes.how_many: Six Warranties
facts: Warranty One: never become the seat of perilous wealth or power (C-49).
Warranty Two: sufficient operating funds plus an ample reserve (C-50).
Warranty Three: no Conference member placed in unqualified authority over others (C-52).
Warranty Four: important decisions by discussion, vote and, whenever possible, substantial unanimity (C-53).
Warranty Five: no action personally punitive or an incitement to public controversy (C-54).
Warranty Six: never perform acts of government, and stay democratic in action and spirit (C-58).
The Conference can amend the first eleven Articles of the Charter at any time. Article 12 stands in a class by itself (C-48).
Changing a Warranty needs written consent from three-quarters of the directory-listed groups that vote, and six months are allowed to deliberate (C-48).
Bill W. describes all the Warranties as counsels of prudence (C-48).
The Conference is called 'the guardian of the Traditions of Alcoholics Anonymous' (C-49).

Bill W. ranked the Warranties with the Twelve Traditions. He saw prudence as a middle ground between fear and recklessness, and said the Warranties should change only on positive evidence that they are defective, and then only by common consent of the groups (pp. C-48, C-49).

Warranty Three protects the Right of Participation, so Conference action alone can never overturn it. Bill W. read it more broadly: A.A. will not tolerate absolute human authority in any form, a safeguard reinforced by Appeal and Petition (p. C-53).

Warranty Four: if an urgent decision cannot wait, a majority (even a bare one) may decide to end debate and act, and a majority must override a small minority that obstinately misuses substantial unanimity to block clearly needed action (p. C-53). This is Bill W.'s 1962 principle; under today's rules of debate, calling the question needs two-thirds (p. 175).

Warranty Five: when A.A. is attacked publicly without justification, the best defense is usually complete public silence. A misinformed critic may be answered privately and temperately, often through friends. Justified criticism may be acknowledged privately, with thanks (p. C-55).

As 'guardian' of the Traditions, the Conference does not sue or publicly punish violators. It tells them privately that they are out of order, keeps up persuasion, offers mediation in internal disputes, and relies on A.A. opinion, public opinion and ongoing education about the Traditions (pp. C-55, C-56).

quotes.text: would require the written consent of three-quarters of all the directory-listed A.A. groups who would actually vote on any such proposals
that it never becomes the seat of perilous wealth or power
Many AA’s have already begun to call Article 12 of the Conference Charter “The A.A. Service Bill of Rights.”
abstain completely from any and all acts of authoritative government which could in any wise curtail A.A.’s freedom under God.

nodes.title: Changing Boundaries: Districts, Areas, Regions
nodes.summary: As A.A. grows, the service map can be redrawn. A district with more groups than one DCM can serve may split into new districts, create subdistricts with local committee members, or become a large district led by a DCMC. If an area's delegate and other trusted servants can no longer serve their groups well, the area committee(s) may ask GSO for an application for an additional delegate area. An area may also ask to move to a different region. Both kinds of change go to the General Service Conference.
nodes.chosen_by: District changes are worked out among the groups, districts and area. New delegate areas and changes of region go through GSO and the General Service Conference; the Conference Policy/Admissions Committee reviews requests for additional delegate areas.
nodes.how_many: 93 delegate areas; 8 regions (6 U.S., 2 Canada)
facts: There are 93 delegate areas in the U.S./Canada Conference (p. 26).
There are six regions in the U.S. and two in Canada. Each region sends a regional trustee to the board (p. 93).
District boundaries may be redrawn when the number of groups rises or falls significantly (p. 14).
Linguistic districts may have boundaries independent of the geographic districts (p. 14).

A proposal to redraw area boundaries or add an area may come from a member, GSR, district, area, or several areas together. Proposals accepted for the Conference agenda go to the appropriate Conference committee(s) before the full Conference (p. 26).
The Conference Policy/Admissions Committee reviews requests to create additional delegate areas (p. 47).
In a 1961 memo, Bill W. said the Conference is not a political body that needs a rigid formula of representation (p. 114).

quotes.text: There are many variations, but the goal is the same: to take care of expansion at the district level.
It should be reemphasized that the Conference is not a political body, demanding a completely rigid formula of representation.

nodes.title: Redistricting (Growing Districts)
nodes.summary: When a district has more groups than its DCM can keep in touch with, it can reorganize in one of three ways. It can divide into two or more new districts, each with its own DCM. It can split into smaller subdistricts, each electing a local committee member (LCM). Or it can stay one large district whose meetings are led by a DCMC, with as many subdivisions as needed, each served by a DCM. Good communication and cooperation among groups, districts and the area matters during any of these changes.
nodes.chosen_by: New DCMs and LCMs are elected locally. A DCM's qualifications and election methods serve as guidelines.
facts: Option 1: new districts, each with its own DCM (p. 113).

Option 2: subdistricts (also called local districts), each electing a local committee member. Depending on area practice, LCMs may or may not vote on the area committee or hold regular meetings with their GSRs (p. 113).

Option 3: a large city or county district holds regular meetings led by a DCMC, who links the district to the area. Its subdivisions (subdistricts, local districts or zones) are each served by a DCM (p. 113).
In some areas these DCMs vote on the area committee and assembly; in others they do not (p. 113).

quotes.text: New Districts: Divide the district into two or more districts, each with its own DCM.
If it were not for adding committee members to take care of new groups as A.A. grows, the General Service Conference might well become unwieldy.

nodes.title: Forming a New Delegate Area
nodes.summary: If the A.A. population has grown so much that the current delegate and other trusted servants can no longer give adequate service and communication, members may want to form a new area. The area committee or committees write to GSO and ask for an application for an additional delegate area. The four-page form asks about geography, A.A. population and how well developed the existing area structure is. Requests go to the Conference, where the Policy/Admissions Committee reviews them.
nodes.chosen_by: The area committee(s) start the request through GSO. The Conference Policy/Admissions Committee reviews it, and it comes before the full Conference.
facts: The application is four pages (p. 113).
It asks how often assemblies are held and whether there is an alternate delegate (p. 113).
It asks how often district meetings are held, how many DCMs are active, and whether they assist the delegate and alternate (p. 113).
It asks the number of active GSRs (p. 113).
It asks for five years of geographic and A.A. population growth, broken down by year (p. 113).
The form checks whether the problem is geography and population, or whether the current area structure could be developed further to support the delegate (p. 114).
The Conference Policy/Admissions Committee reviews requests to create additional delegate areas (p. 47).

quotes.text: the area committee or Committees involved may write to GSO and request an application for an additional delegate area.
What we shall need will always be enough delegates at the Conference to afford a reliable cross section of A.A. plus enough more to make sure of good local communication.

nodes.title: Changing an Area's Region
nodes.summary: An area may decide it belongs in a different region. The area committee first informs GSRs of the advantages and disadvantages. A simple majority of GSRs must be present or answer a mail poll, and two-thirds of them must agree before the area petitions. The delegate then works through GSO and the trustees' Nominating Committee to poll the delegates of both regions. Two-thirds of the delegates from each region must approve before the Conference acts, and the change takes effect at the end of the Conference that approves it.
nodes.chosen_by: Area GSRs vote first, then two-thirds of the delegates from each region involved approve, and the General Service Conference makes the final decision.
duties: Area committee: inform GSRs in advance of the advantages and disadvantages (p. 114)
Delegate: notify GSO, which supplies a form for the delegate to confirm the conditions were met (p. 114)
Delegate: on behalf of the assembly, write to the secretary of the trustees' Nominating Committee with the completed form, and copy the trustees in both regions (p. 114)
Delegate: ask GSO to write to every area delegate in both regions, asking them to get their areas' group conscience and return an approval/disapproval card (p. 114)
facts: A simple majority (one-half plus one) of the area's GSRs must be present or answer a mail poll (p. 114).
Two-thirds of those present or responding must agree before the area petitions (p. 114).
Two-thirds of the delegates from each region involved must approve before the proposal goes to the Conference (p. 114).
The change takes effect at the end of the Conference that approves it (p. 114).

quotes.text: Approval by two-thirds of the delegates from each region involved is required before the proposal is presented to the General Service Conference for action.
A change of region will become effective at the end of the Conference, at which it may be approved.

nodes.title: From the Founders to the Groups (1935–1962)
nodes.summary: How the authority for A.A.'s world services passed from its two co-founders to the groups. In 1937 the first groups asked Dr. Bob and Bill W. to create services for A.A. as a whole. The founders handed the work, step by step, to the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation (1938). Final authority could not pass to a self-appointing board that few members knew, so the first Conference met in 1951, and at St. Louis in 1955 the groups took final responsibility. The Twelve Concepts (1962) record why.
facts: Bill W. tells the hand-over in stages: Dr. Bob passed nearly all his part to Bill, and Bill gave the trustees money matters, then the office, public relations and the Grapevine, staying on as an adviser (pp. C-6, C-7).
Bill W. separates ultimate authority, which the founders kept until St. Louis in 1955, from the active, immediate authority they delegated to the trustees (C-7).
For a long time most trustees opposed calling a conference of delegates, fearing politics, confusion, expense and strife, and many members said 'Let's keep it simple' (pp. C-3, C-4).
In the dozen years after the Foundation was created, membership grew from 50 to 100,000 (C-3).
It took about five more years after the first Conference for everyone to be convinced that Tradition Two applied to everybody, founders and trustees included (pp. C-4, C-5).
Works Publishing, Inc. was later renamed A.A. Publishing, Inc.; it is now a division of A.A. World Services, Inc. (C-7, footnote).
The founders hoped to avoid a common trap: originators who fail, in their own lifetimes, to delegate their authority, responsibility and leadership (C-8).

quotes.text: The early leadership of A.A. would be succeeded not by new people, but by the collective conscience of the groups in A.A.
At St. Louis it went from Dr. Bob and me to the A.A. groups themselves.
But could we stand heart failure at our world center?

nodes.title: A.A.'s Legacy of Service (Bill W., 1951)
nodes.summary: Appendix A reprints Bill W.'s 1951 essay 'A.A.'s Legacy of Service'. It defines an A.A. service as anything that helps reach a fellow sufferer and calls the sum of all services the Third Legacy. The essay traces how the early trustees (the Alcoholic Foundation), the Big Book, the New York office and the Traditions grew between 1937 and 1950. It explains why the founders decided the trustees needed a direct link to the groups. The result was the General Service Conference, first held in April 1951, with delegates elected in rotating panels by a two-thirds vote or by lot.
facts: In 1937, at Dr. Bob's Akron home, the co-founders first saw that wholesale recovery of alcoholics was possible (p. 97).
John D. R., Jr., the philanthropist, declined to give a large sum for fear of professionalizing A.A., but donated $5,000 (p. 97).
To finance the book, Bill and Hank P. sold shares in a new company, Works Publishing (par value $25). 'Alcoholics Anonymous' came out in April 1939 (pp. 98–99).
Liberty Magazine's 'Alcoholics and God' (September 1939) brought about 800 letters (p. 99).
The Saturday Evening Post article by Jack A. (March 1, 1941) brought 6,000 appeals for help. Membership grew from 2,000 to 8,000 that year (p. 101).
The suggested group contribution was then $1.00 per member per year, earmarked for office work only (p. 101).
In 1945 there was one paid worker for every 98 groups; by 1955, one for every 230 (p. 103).
In 1950 the trustees authorized Dr. Bob and Bill to devise the Conference plan (p. 104).

The plan: one delegate per state or province (more where many members live), odd Panel One seated in 1951 and even Panel Two in 1952, and election by a two-thirds vote or, if close, by drawing from a hat (p. 104).
Under the charter as first drawn, a two-thirds Conference vote could give the trustees flat directions, and a simple majority was a strong suggestion (p. 104).
The first Conference was in April 1951. The Conference has met each year since, in April or May in New York (pp. 97, 104).
The Conference agreed to rename the Alcoholic Foundation the General Service Board of Alcoholics Anonymous (p. 105). Concept I dates the renaming to 1954 (C-3).
Bill W.'s Foreword: carrying the message (the Twelfth Step) is the basic service A.A. gives, its principal aim and the main reason it exists (p. 1)

For years objectors said a Conference would be expensive and might plunge A.A. into disruptive politics when delegates were elected. Dr. Bob's mortal illness and 'the relentless logic of the situation' moved the trustees to act in 1950 (p. 104)
The Alcoholic Foundation was renamed the General Service Board because the word 'Foundation' suggested charity, paternalism and maybe big money. From then on A.A. would pay its own way (p. 105)

quotes.text: The sum total of all these services is our Third Legacy of Service.
This would cause the Conference to rotate, while maintaining some continuity.
As I watched all this grow, I became entirely sure that Alcoholics Anonymous was at last safe — even from me.
The most vital, yet least understood, group of services that A.A. has are those that enable us to function as a whole
Concerning any given service, we therefore pose but one question: “Is this service really needed?”
The group conscience could safely act as the sole authority and sure guide for Alcoholics Anonymous.

nodes.title: Conference Delegate Chair
nodes.summary: Each Conference has a Delegate Chair (also printed 'delegate chairperson'): a second-year delegate who gives the welcome address at the opening session and, in one Delegate Chair's words, reminds the Conference 'of its spiritual nature' (2025 Final Report, p. 5). The Delegate Chair for next year's Conference is chosen by lot during Conference week at the delegates-only meeting or dinner, from first-year delegates; since about 2022 only from those not already elected chair or alternate chair of a committee (2024 Final Report, p. 46). The Service Manual does not describe the role; it comes from the Final Reports and from guidelines added to the Conference Manual in 2025. Not to be confused with 'delegate chairs' (plural), which in trustees' reports means the delegates who chair Conference committees.
nodes.chosen_by: By lot ('from the hat') during Conference week at the delegates-only gathering, among willing first-year delegates. Since about 2022 the draw follows the committee elections and uses the delegates not already chosen as a committee chair or alternate (2024 Final Report, p. 46). In 2017-2018 it was drawn at the Tuesday delegates-only meeting, before the committees voted, so the Delegate Chair could also be a committee alternate (2017 Final Report, p. 4).
nodes.term: One year: chosen at one Conference, serves through the next (the delegate's second year)
nodes.how_many: One per Conference. An alternate Delegate Chair is printed for some years (2010, 2018, 2019), none since.
qualifications: A first-year delegate at the Conference where the choice is made
Willing to serve; since about 2022, not already elected a committee chair or alternate
duties: Gives the welcome address at the opening session (e.g. 2024 Final Report, p. 3; 2026 Final Report, p. 3)
Helps keep the Conference mindful of its spiritual purpose (2025 Final Report, p. 5)
Sets the dates and topics of the virtual all-Conference sharing sessions, at least twice a year, with the GSB chair (2023 Final Report, p. 37)
Attends the board weekend with the Conference committee chairs, as the board has invited since 1991 (2019 Final Report, p. 21)
Passes the gavel to the incoming Delegate Chair at the close of the Conference (2024 Final Report, p. 4)
facts: 2017: 'At the Delegates Only meeting Tuesday evening, Ben B., Oklahoma, was selected as the delegate chair for the 68th Conference', with an alternate chosen the same night (2017 Final Report, p. 4); likewise in 2018 (2018 Final Report, p. 4).

2025: 'then again from another hat to be the Delegate Chair' (2025 Final Report, p. 4); the guidelines for electing the Delegate Chairperson were included in the 2025 General Service Conference Manual (2025 Final Report, p. 85).

Floor actions in 2023 (one nominee per region, then by lot) and 2025 (each committee nominates one, then a Third Legacy vote) would have changed the process; the Conference declined to consider both, so they are not Advisory Actions (2023 Final Report, p. 49; 2025 Final Report, p. 53).
The Delegate Chair for the 78th Conference (2028) will be chosen at the 2027 Conference from Panel 77 delegates, including Area 65's.
Since 2021 the Delegate Chair has alternated between the U.S. and Canada every year (2021 Canada ... 2027 Canada). No document requires it: treat it as a pattern, not a rule.

'Delegate chairs' (plural) means committee chairs: e.g. 'delegate chairpersons be invited to attend the October board weekend' (2026 Final Report, p. 85) and the 'Delegate Committee Chair Orientation' (2023 Final Report, p. 64).

The Service Manual uses the term only once: GSO's Conference desk 'coordinates Delegate Chair Orientation' (p. 71). Like the plural 'delegate chairs' above, this most likely means the orientation for Conference committee chairs, not the single Delegate Chair.

quotes.text: electing the General Service Conference Delegate chair from the remaining delegates (not yet selected for Committee or alt chair) remains a viable procedure
The role of the Delegate Chair is to remind the Conference of its spiritual nature

nodes.title: Regions (8)
nodes.summary: Areas are grouped into eight regions, six in the U.S. and two in Canada. A region is not a level of authority: it is the grouping from which a regional trustee comes to the General Service Board (p. 93) and the unit for Regional Forums. Regions also shape committee assignments: the lot spreads each committee across regions, and since July 2020 the four smaller regions (Southwest, West Central, Eastern Canada, Western Canada) are meant to have no more than one delegate on a committee. Many regions hold their own delegate meetings; the Southwest's are SWRDA (every March) and SWRAASA (even years, in October).
nodes.chosen_by: Region boundaries change only through Appendix F: two-thirds of the area's GSRs agree, then two-thirds of the delegates of each region involved, then the Conference (p. 114).
nodes.how_many: 8 regions: Northeast, Southeast, East Central, West Central, Southwest and Pacific (U.S.); Eastern Canada and Western Canada. The Southwest has 11 areas in 7 states, including Area 65 (Northeast Texas).
facts: Regional trustees are elected two regions at a time on a fixed calendar; Northeast and Southwest next elect in 2027 and 2031 (p. 54).

Regional Forums are held in each region every two years (pp. 73, 93): Western Canada, Eastern Canada, Southeast and Pacific in even years; Northeast, East Central, West Central and Southwest in odd years (2026 Final Report, p. 98).

Next Southwest Regional Forum: September 30-October 3, 2027, Kansas City, Missouri, hosted by Area 39 (2026 Final Report, p. 98). The last one was November 14-16, 2025 in Albuquerque (2026 Final Report, p. 18).
Several regions hold annual meetings of past and current delegates and their alternates, to help new delegates prepare for the Conference (p. 30).

SWRDA, the Southwest Region Delegates Assembly: every March in Oklahoma City (March 12-14, 2027) for past delegates, past regional trustees, the current regional trustee and the serving delegates and alternates. It works like a mock Conference (Area 66 and 68 service calendars; NETA Handbook p. 12).

SWRAASA, the Southwest Regional A.A. Service Assembly: every two years in October, hosted in turn by the region's 11 areas: 2024 Area 65, 2026 Area 67 (October 9-11), 2028 Area 66 (October 13-15) (area websites and flyers). So the Southwest has a regional gathering every fall: SWRAASA in even years, the Regional Forum in odd years.

Small-region rule (July 2020): 'the Southwest, West Central, Eastern Canada and Western Canada regions should have no more than one delegate represented on a committee' (2021 Final Report, p. 26). It held at the 2019-2024 Conferences and has been broken a few times since the Panel 75 rebalancing (rosters).
IC/RF has one delegate per region. Since Panel 69 the odd panels have filled the Northeast, East Central, Pacific and Eastern Canada seats and the even panels the other four (rosters).
No area changed region and no area was added between 2017 and 2026: 93 areas in every roster.

quotes.text: A grouping of several areas from which a regional trustee comes to the board of trustees.

nodes.title: Recent Changes (timeline 1998-2026)
nodes.summary: The structure changes slowly, by Advisory Action or board decision. This timeline lists changes in the 2017-2026 Final Reports that matter when you follow the Conference: committee names, the committee draw, the agenda process and the board's officers. No area was added and no regional boundary changed in those years (93 areas in every roster).
nodes.chosen_by: Changes come from Conference Advisory Actions, General Service Board decisions and trustees' committee decisions recorded in each Final Report.
facts: 1998-2015: the trustees' CPC and Treatment committees were combined (April 1998); 'Special Needs-Accessibilities' was added in 2009 and 'Special Needs' dropped from the name in November 2015 (2017 Final Report, p. 43).
2016: the last 'Additional' Regional Forum was held, for the Southwest Region in Denver (2017 Final Report, p. 56).
2019: the committee printed as 'Conference Agenda' through 2018 appears as 'Agenda' from 2019 (rosters).

2020: the Conference Committee on Grapevine became 'Grapevine and La Viña' (2021 Final Report, p. 37). The committee draw moved to a custom app for December 2020, and the small-region rule was added to the assignment process (2021 Final Report, p. 26). The trustees' GSC committee proposed an EDW process with a September 15 PAI deadline, and the Conference Policy/Admissions committee asked for a more developed plan for 2021 (2020 Final Report, pp. 22, 57).

2021: a three-year Equitable Distribution of Workload (EDW) trial was approved, starting with the 72nd Conference, and the PAI deadline moved up to September 15, first for the 2022 Conference (2021 Final Report, p. 60; 2022 Final Report, p. 32). Trustee elections became electronic, with the hat kept for the fourth or fifth ballot (2021 Final Report, p. 50).
2022: Area 48 (Hudson/Mohawk/Berkshire) was renamed Northeast New York (2024 Final Report, p. 145).

2023: the GSB chair resigned in January 2023 (2023 Final Report, p. 4). Advisory Actions set up at least two virtual all-Conference sharing sessions a year and a pre-Conference Policy/Admissions video meeting (2023 Final Report, p. 37). The Panel 73 draw kept the best of five rounds (2023 Final Report, p. 64).

2024: EDW adopted; the PAI deadline moved to no earlier than September 30 (2024 Final Report, p. 38). The board used the Third Legacy Procedure to select its officers and elected a past Class B trustee as chair (2024 Final Report, p. 100). Draws rebalanced toward an even mix of first- and second-year delegates from Panel 75 (2024 Final Report, p. 68).

2025: prioritized committee-selection criteria (2025 Final Report, p. 47); PAI deadline fixed at September 30 (p. 85); workshops replaced by Conference Inventory sessions (p. 4); the 1986 simple-majority 'suggestion' rule rescinded (pp. 37-38); Delegate Chair guidelines added to the Conference Manual (p. 85).

2026: a proposed Conference digital committee got no action, so there are still 13 committees (2026 Final Report, p. 49); the 77th Conference's committee chairs attend the October/November 2026 board weekend instead of January 2027 (p. 49); EDW ends after the 78th Conference (p. 39); a 13th GSO staff assignment, Self Support/Finance, was added in September 2025 (p. 66).

2016 and 2025: an Advisory Action of the 66th Conference (2016) removed two paragraphs about women workers from the published Concept XI essay, and the 75th Conference (2025) removed the word 'woman' from a Concept IV sentence. The Amendments section preserves the original wording of both; the paragraphs are also available from GSO's Archives (p. C-74).

quotes.text: Following the 78th General Service Conference the Equitable Distribution Workload (EDW) process be discontinued.

see_also.note: how authority passed from the founders to the groups

nodes.title: Area Activities: Newsletters, Websites, Archives, Conventions
nodes.summary: Besides electing a delegate and studying the Conference agenda, many areas take on service work that is hard for one group or district to do alone. The manual describes area archives (collecting and preserving local A.A. history), area newsletters or bulletins, area, state, provincial and regional conventions, and area websites, and it urges good relations with local intergroup/central offices. For newsletters and websites it advises that a committee, not one or two people, be in charge. It also explains how local publications may reprint A.A. literature and how to protect anonymity online.
nodes.chosen_by: Each area decides which activities to take on. Conventions are often set up by the area committee or by a special committee the area chair appoints; newsletters and websites are best run by a committee.
nodes.how_many: Varies by area
duties: Archives: collect and preserve area history (written materials, photographs, audiotapes), seeking material from oldtimers, past delegates and committee members
Newsletter or bulletin: local A.A. news, group and committee information, and reprinted A.A. material with the proper credit line
Conventions: usually weekend events with speakers, panels, presentations and workshops
Website: share meeting and service information, practice anonymity at all times, and link to intergroup meeting lists rather than duplicate them
Intergroup liaison: keep good relations and communication with local intergroup/central offices
facts: Newsletter ideas from local experience: theme issues using excerpts from A.A. literature, readers' letters (with permission and anonymity protected), committee minutes, an events calendar, and a subscription drive to build paid readership (p. 23)

Area, state, provincial and regional conventions are usually weekend events; area committees or special committees appointed by the area chair often set them up, and GSO has guidelines on conferences and conventions (p. 24)
An A.A. website is a public medium, so it needs the same anonymity safeguards as press, radio and film. Some areas add password-protected, members-only sections where full names may be used (p. 24)
Where an active intergroup/central office already publishes meeting information, area websites may simply link to it (p. 24)
Websites may post brief excerpts of A.A. literature under the newsletter rules, link to items on the GSO or Grapevine sites, and use a thumbnail of a pamphlet, book or video as that link (p. 24)
Areas may post A.A. public service announcements (PSAs) directly on their websites; PSAs can also be viewed on aa.org (p. 24)
For more help, GSO offers the 'FAQ on A.A. Websites', the A.A. Guidelines on the Internet and guidelines on archives (pp. 23-24)

quotes.text: An A.A. website is a public medium, which has the potential for reaching the broadest possible audience
A.A. intends PSAs to be widely shared.

nodes.title: Authority and Responsibility (Concept X)
nodes.summary: Concept X says every service responsibility needs an equal authority whose limits are clearly defined. Bill W. traces a chain of ultimate authority: the groups over the Conference, the delegates over the trustees, the trustees over AAWS and Grapevine, their directors over officers, and officers over staff. Ultimate authority is held in reserve and used in full only in an emergency; day to day, each trusted servant needs enough delegated authority to do the job. Authority is defined by legal means (such as the corporations' charters), by tradition (such as the Right of Decision; the Conference Charter itself is not a legal instrument) and by principles for settling conflicts: when two bodies share a matter, one has senior jurisdiction and there is always a clear point of final decision. Tradition Two sums it up: the group conscience is the ultimate authority and the trusted servant the delegated authority.
facts: The groups hold final authority for world services; the delegates are in ultimate authority over the trustees, the trustees over AAWS and Grapevine, those directors over their officers, and officers over staff (p. C-33).
Ultimate authority should almost never be used in full, only in an emergency, when delegated authority has failed or keeps exceeding its scope (p. C-34).

Proper uses: groups can elect better delegates or withhold funds; delegates can censure or reorganize the trustees; trustees can do the same with the corporations; a corporation can replace executives or staff (p. C-34).
Authority is defined by legal means, by traditional means, and by principles for interpreting doubtful or conflicting situations (p. C-34).
The trustees have a legal right of veto over the Conference, to be used only in rare cases (p. C-34).

When two bodies share a matter, one holds senior jurisdiction, the junior one must be heard, and there must be a clear point of final settlement; lesser conflicts are not loaded onto the trustees (p. C-36).
The Rights of Appeal and Petition guard against a bare majority acting as a pseudo-ultimate authority and executives over-bossing their assistants (p. C-36).

quotes.text: Indeed ultimate authority should practically never be used in full, except in an emergency.
Authority can never be divided into equal halves.
Here we see the “group conscience” as the ultimate authority and the “trusted servant” as the delegated authority.

nodes.title: The Board's Helpers: Committees, Directors, Executives and Staff (Concept XI)
nodes.summary: Concept XI says the trustees need the best possible standing committees, corporate directors, executives, staff and consultants, because these people do most of the daily work and are what most A.A.s see of world service. Bill W.'s 1962 essay describes five trustees' committees and the two service corporations, then sets out principles for paid workers: executive direction rests in one person with clear authority; pay is in reasonable relation to the commercial world; staff rotate among assignments on equal pay; and paid workers take part as full team members. The 76th Conference approved an Amendments section with a revised essay that works the old endnotes into the text: ten standing committees today, the General Policy Committee now the General Sharing Session, nine-member corporate boards, a full-time general manager and two-year staff rotation.
nodes.how_many: 10 standing trustees' committees (5 in 1962) and 2 service corporations
facts: In 1962 the board had five standing committees: Nominating, Finance and Budgetary, Public Information, Literature and General Policy (p. C-37).

Today there are ten: Archives, CPC/Treatment and Accessibilities, Corrections, General Service Conference, International, International Conventions/Regional Forums, Nominating, Finance and Budgetary, Public Information and Literature (p. C-63).
None of the board's committees is executive: they do not run the service corporations, but may recommend anything to the corporations or to the trustees (pp. C-41, C-67).
AAWS and Grapevine carry about nine-tenths of the direct Headquarters effort (p. C-41).
Bill W. opposed merging AAWS and Grapevine: the operations are too different, and too much money and executive authority should not sit in one entity (p. C-41).
Having AAWS run the Grapevine's business side would create double-headed management and leave the Grapevine board virtually powerless (pp. C-42, C-43).
Bill W. warned against structural tinkering just to save money (p. C-43).

quotes.text: A board or a committee can never actively manage anything, in the continuous executive sense.
We are helping others in order to help ourselves.

nodes.title: Ultimate Authority and Delegation (Concepts I-II)
nodes.summary: Concepts I and II explain where final authority for world services lives and why it had to be handed on. Bill W. and Dr. Bob first held it and passed money, the Big Book, public relations and the Grapevine to the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation piece by piece. But a self-appointing board that few members knew could not hold the ultimate responsibility, and in 1948 news of Dr. Bob's fatal illness showed the founders were almost the only link between the trustees and the groups. So the groups took ultimate authority at St. Louis in 1955 (Concept I). Because thousands of groups cannot run services themselves, they delegated active authority to their Conference, which became the Fellowship's voice and conscience, except for changes to the Traditions or Article 12 (Concept II).
facts: 1937: the Akron and New York groups authorized Dr. Bob and Bill W. to create over-all services to spread the message world-wide (p. C-6)
1938: the Alcoholic Foundation was formed as a small trusteeship of A.A. members and nonalcoholic friends; at first its trustees handled money matters only (p. C-6)

The trusteeship was meant to provide what single groups could not: uniform literature, a public relations policy, answers to pleas for help, help for new groups, a monthly magazine and translations (p. C-3)
1940: the stock of Works Publishing, Inc. was turned over to the trustees so the Big Book was held in trust for the Fellowship (p. C-7)
1941: groups began sending contributions to the Foundation for the service office, completing the trustees' control of world service money (p. C-7)
In the dozen years after the Foundation was created, A.A. membership grew from 50 to 100,000 (p. C-3)

As early as 1945 it began to be clear that the founders' ultimate responsibility should never go wholly to a self-appointing board little known to members; Bill W. calls this the difference between ultimate and immediate authority (p. C-7)
1948: news that Dr. Bob was fatally ill showed only a representative conference could replace the founders; most trustees had long opposed calling one (p. C-4)
Tradition Two was written in 1945; the experimental Conference of 1951 tested whether it could apply to A.A. as a whole, and by St. Louis in 1955 it was settled (pp. C-4, C-5)
Concept II (long form) excepts any change in the Twelve Traditions or in Article 12 of the Charter from the Conference's authority (p. C-V)

quotes.text: The groups assumed that responsibility at the St. Louis International Convention of 1955.
For the first time it was seen that only a representative conference could take the place of Dr. Bob and me.
the groups must delegate the actual operational authority to chosen service representatives who are fully empowered to speak and to act for them.
In the course of these developments the great difference between ultimate and immediate service authority became apparent.

nodes.title: Conference and Trustees: Tradition and Law (Concepts VI-VIII)
nodes.summary: Concepts VI to VIII describe the balance between the Conference and the board. The Conference has the final say on large questions of policy and finance. But it meets only once a year, so it gives the trustees wide administrative authority: they act like the directors of a large corporation and are A.A.'s bankers. Legally the board holds full power under its own charter and bylaws, while the Conference Charter is not a legal document. In practice the Conference nearly always prevails, through the force of tradition, its large majority of delegates and, in an extremity, the groups' purse. The board keeps a seldom-used veto for clear charter violations or reckless actions, budget cuts, and plans that become unworkable. Concept VIII then splits the trustees' job in two: on the larger questions of overall policy and finance they plan and manage directly through their own committees, while toward AAWS and Grapevine their role is custodial oversight, which they exercise by electing all of those boards' directors.
facts: Concept VI: the Conference traditionally has the final decision on large matters of general policy and finance, but leaves the chief initiative and active responsibility to the trustees (pp. C-V, C-19)

Bill W.'s corporate analogy: the groups are the stockholders, the delegates their proxies at the 'annual meeting', and the trustees the directors of a 'holding company' that owns the operating services (p. C-20)
Footnote: AAWS and AA Grapevine are legally affiliates, not subsidiaries; the trustees, acting as their Members, elect their directors (p. C-20)

Besides AAWS and the Grapevine, the trustees handle world-wide public relations, lead in forming A.A. policy and guard the Traditions; as 'A.A.'s bankers' they invest and use the reserve funds (p. C-20)

The Conference's practical power rests on the Charter's tradition, its large majority of group-chosen delegates and, in an extremity, the delegates' ability to deny the board the groups' contributions (p. C-21)

Rejected in 1950 when the Charter was drawn: incorporating the Conference, nationwide elections for trustees (a 'political shambles'), and having the Conference nominate and elect trustees itself (pp. C-21, C-22)
So the Conference got the right to reject, but not elect, new trustee candidates; a footnote adds that regional and at-large trustees are now elected during Conference week (pp. C-22, C-23)
Like a U.S. president who seldom vetoes, the trustees can accept Conference direction without giving up their legal rights; each side should avoid overusing its power (p. C-22)

Veto cases: (1) an action clearly violating the Conference's or the board's charter, or reckless enough to seriously harm A.A., after a refused request to reconsider; (2) reducing the budget in a fiscal year; (3) cancelling a plan made unworkable by unforeseen conditions (p. C-23)

quotes.text: The A.A. groups are the stockholders; the Delegates are their representatives or proxies at the “annual meeting”
the practical power of the Conference will nearly always be superior to the legal power of the Trustees.
the Conference was given the right to reject, but not to elect, new Trustee candidates.
because the one is protected by tradition and the other by law.

nodes.title: Rights of Appeal and Petition (Concept V)
nodes.summary: Concept V protects minorities in two ways. The Right of Appeal encourages any minority (in a staff, committee, corporate board or among the trustees) to file a minority report when it thinks the majority is badly wrong, and makes it a duty to bring one to the Conference when a mistake could seriously hurt A.A. as a whole. The Right of Petition lets any worker, paid or unpaid, take a personal grievance straight to the General Service Board without fear of reprisal. Bill W. points to protections already built in: the Third Legacy hat, the Conference's habit of not deciding important matters on less than two-thirds, and the Charter rule that only a two-thirds vote binds the trustees.
facts: A minority that is wrong still serves when it forces thorough debate on an important issue (p. C-16)
The Right of Petition will seldom be used, but its existence restrains those in authority from unjust uses of power (p. C-16)

The groups cannot be informed enough to act directly on many service matters, so A.A. trusts a qualified minority, the hundred-odd Conference members, to act as its group conscience in most service affairs (pp. C-16, C-17)
In the Third Legacy method, if the majority's candidate lacks two-thirds, the name goes into the hat with the minority's choices, giving them an equal chance (p. C-17)
The Conference has usually refused to take important decisions on less than a two-thirds vote, and often keeps debating even when two-thirds is easily reached (p. C-17)

Because a Conference vote binds the trustees only when it reaches two-thirds (Bill W.: 'two-thirds of a Conference quorum'), the trustees in effect hold a veto over narrow majorities; in practice they seldom use it (p. C-17)
Bill W. cites De Tocqueville's warning about the 'tyranny' of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities (p. C-18)

Bill W. hoped the Rights of Appeal and Petition would one day be written into the Conference Charter; the current Charter now names them and lets the Conference agree to hear Concept V appeals from members below Conference level (p. C-18; p. 125)

quotes.text: The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority.
it should then charge itself with the actual duty of presenting a minority report to the Conference.
He or she should be able to do this without prejudice or fear of reprisal.
This gives the Trustees a power of veto in cases where the majority is not great.

nodes.title: Right of Decision (Concept III)
nodes.summary: Concept III gives every part of world service (the Conference, the trustees, the corporate boards, committees, staff and executives) a traditional discretion. Within its defined job, each decides which problems it settles itself and which it reports on, consults about or sends up for direction. Bill W. argues that charters alone cannot settle questions like how far groups should instruct their delegates. Dropping all rules would bring anarchy, and writing rules for everything would bring too much red tape. The A.A. answer is Tradition Two's trusted servants: trust leaders to apply their authority case by case, keep ample power to correct real failures, and never let the right excuse missing reports, overreach or failure to consult.
nodes.how_many: Four applications (A-D): the Conference; the delegates; the trustees; the headquarters corporations, committees, staff and executives
facts: The groups have the right to instruct their delegates, but carried to extremes this assumes group opinion beats a Conference that has the full facts and debate (p. C-9)
A delegate who cannot vote their own conscience on a final Conference vote is, in Bill W.'s words, just a messenger and not a trusted servant (p. C-9)
Remedies remain: the groups can send better delegates, the Conference can censure or reorganize the trustees, and the trustees can elect better directors and hire better help (p. C-10)
A: the Conference decides which matters it settles itself and which it refers to the groups, or more usually to committee members or GSRs (p. C-11)
C: the trustees decide when to act on their own and when to ask the Conference for guidance, approval or direction (p. C-11)
D: headquarters corporations, committees, staff and executives decide when to act alone and when to refer a problem to the next higher authority (p. C-11)
The right never excuses skipping reports on significant actions, constantly exceeding defined authority, or failing to consult those entitled to be consulted (p. C-11)

quotes.text: it should be the traditional right of all world service boards, committees, and executives to decide which problems they will dispose of themselves
the “instructed” Delegate who cannot act on his own conscience in a final Conference vote is not a “trusted servant” at all
If the Conference does not function well, the groups can send in better Delegates.
We trust God, we trust A.A., and we trust each other.

nodes.title: Right of Participation (Concept IV)
nodes.summary: Concept IV says each kind of world servant should have a vote in proportion to its responsibility. The Charter makes the trustees, the AAWS and Grapevine directors and their executive staffs voting Conference members. The board likewise puts nontrustee volunteers and paid staff on the corporate boards and its committees, where everyone votes as an equal. Bill W. learned this the hard way: when the early trustees held all the authority and the office staff all the responsibility, conflicting orders from two trustee committees and a check-signing trustee's absolute say over the payroll caused real trouble. Participation has limits. Paid staff cannot become trustees, and by tradition trustees and service workers do not vote on reports of their own past work.
facts: The Charter makes the trustees, the AAWS and Grapevine directors and their executive staffs voting members of the Conference (p. C-12)
The board could legally fill the corporate boards with its own trustees only, but a strong tradition says it never should (p. C-12)
In 1962 AAWS had seven directors, two of them trustees; today it has nine, four of them trustees (p. C-12; footnote, p. C-15)
For linkage, a Grapevine editor or staff member is invited to AAWS meetings, and a world service nominee should attend all Grapevine meetings, corporate and editorial (p. C-12)
Paid executives, staff and accountants are invited to each quarterly board meeting; they may join the debate but do not vote (p. C-13)

Early on, two trustee committees (policy and administrative) with no office members ran the office and sometimes gave conflicting orders; a trustee-treasurer once tore up the staff's paychecks for being issued early (pp. C-13, C-14)

By tradition trustees and service workers do not vote on reports of their own past activities; job qualifications, pay and a sweeping board reorganization caused by board misfunction are the other special cases, but none of this bars the trustees from voting on structural changes (pp. C-14, C-15)
Delegates meet only a few days once a year, one more reason to let better-informed trustees and staff vote where no self-interest is involved (footnote, p. C-14)
Bill W. noted in 1962 that trustees and headquarters people had never yet voted as a bloc; they disagree among themselves as sharply as the delegates do (p. C-15)
The 75th Conference (2025) removed the word 'woman' from a Concept IV sentence about paid staff directors; it is marked (A) and the original is kept on p. C-74 (pp. C-13, C-74)

quotes.text: When the time comes to ballot, there are no “superiors,” no “inferiors,” and no “advisers.”
Although they do not vote, these workers may freely participate in debate.
Trustees and service workers alike should refrain from voting on reports on their own past activities.
Just as there are no second-class AA’s, neither should there be any second-class world service workers, either.

nodes.title: Service Leadership (Concept IX and Bill W.'s 1959 essay)
nodes.summary: Concept IX says a well-designed structure works only as well as the people serving in it, and finding good leaders is a problem that is never solved for good. The base of the structure is the GSRs, committee members and delegates chosen by the groups, so groups should choose GSRs with care. Bill W. backs the two-thirds-or-lot method for delegates and says the board of trustees must take over the leadership the founders once gave. He reprints his April 1959 Grapevine essay 'Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need', which the delegate chapter also excerpts (p. 38). A leader turns principles, plans and policies into action so well that others want to help. Good leadership leads by example rather than power-driving, consults widely, credits better ideas, never passes the buck, gives its reasons, compromises cheerfully but stands firm when it must, takes criticism well, and has vision, the ability to make good estimates of the future.
nodes.chosen_by: Not an office. Bill W. describes the qualities of any leader in A.A. service (pp. 38, C-27 to C-31).
qualifications: Puts principles, plans and policies into dedicated, effective action
Consults widely before deciding new and important matters
Will drop their own plan for a better one and give credit to its source
Give-and-take: compromises cheerfully, but stands firm when truly necessary
Hears constructive criticism and keeps the critic's friendship
Tolerance, responsibility, flexibility and vision, needed in service leaders at every level (p. C-31)
facts: In 1962 the base was several thousand GSRs, several hundred area committee members and nearly a hundred delegates, the groups' direct agents (p. C-27)

Only GSRs, in their assembly meetings (or in caucus), can name committee members and finally the delegates, so groups should choose GSRs carefully and groups without one should be encouraged to elect one (p. C-27)

The two-thirds-or-lot method reduced political friction and makes a delegate feel like a world servant, not the winner of a contest; the second choice can be as good a delegate, or better (pp. C-27, C-28)
The board ran from 1938 to 1951 without a Conference; linking it to the Fellowship made the trustees accountable (p. C-28)
The April 1959 Grapevine essay 'Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need' is reprinted in the Concept IX essay and excerpted in the delegate chapter (pp. 38, C-29)
A politico always tries to give people what they want; a statesman knows when and when not to, and may stand against a misinformed majority when something vital is at stake (p. C-29)
Opposition for opposition's sake is fatal to leadership; when asked, a leader must give good reasons (p. C-30)
Vision means making good estimates of the near and distant future; 'One day at a time' is about our emotional lives, not a reason to skip planning (pp. C-30, C-31)
Self-support (no outside gifts) and anonymity each grew from a tentative idea to an experimental policy, a firm policy and finally a deep conviction (p. C-31)
Bill W. names two failures: the leader who power-drives and provokes rebellion, and the one who meekly takes orders and uses no judgment (p. 38)
Once it has, or can get, enough general backing, good leadership decides and acts promptly, but only within its defined authority and responsibility (p. 38)
Bill calls heavy, long-continued criticism the 'acid test' of leadership (p. 38)

quotes.text: the operating results of our structure can be no better than the personal performance of those who must man it and make it work.
“Our leaders do not drive by mandate, they lead by example.” In effect, we are saying to them, “Act for us, but don’t boss us.”
When called upon, leadership must always give its reasons, and good ones.
Good leadership never passes the buck.
progress is nearly always characterized by a series of improving compromises.

nodes.title: AAWS & Grapevine Officers
nodes.summary: Each operating corporation has its own officers, elected every year by its board of directors. The Chair runs the board: it presides at board meetings, approves their agendas and may not be an employee. The President runs the business, and at AAWS this is the GSO general manager, at Grapevine the publisher. A Vice-Chair and a Vice-President stand in for them. The Secretary keeps minutes, notices and the register of Members, and the Treasurer holds the funds and reports in writing at every regular board meeting. The board can remove any officer at any time.
nodes.chosen_by: The board of directors, every year, at its first meeting after the Annual Meeting of Members (the newly elected board meets at once to organize and elect officers). The Chair and President must be chosen from among the directors. The directors also fill any officer vacancy.
nodes.term: One year (elected annually); the board may remove any officer, with or without cause, at any time
nodes.how_many: AAWS: 7 (Chair, Vice-Chair, President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer, Assistant Treasurer). Grapevine: 8 (adds an Assistant Secretary). The board may add other officers.
qualifications: Chair and President must be directors
No employee of the corporation may serve as Chair
duties: Chair: presides at board meetings and approves their agendas

President: general charge and supervision of the corporation's business; signs authorized contracts and checks with another officer, but no bond, mortgage or contract without the board's specific authority
Vice-Chair / Vice-President: act for the Chair / President when absent or disabled
Secretary: minutes of board and Members' meetings, notices, the corporate seal and an alphabetical register of Members
Treasurer: custody of funds and securities, books open to any director, and a written report of receipts, disbursements and financial condition at each regular board meeting
Assistant Treasurer (and, at Grapevine, Assistant Secretary): act when the Treasurer (Secretary) is absent or disabled

nodes.title: Listing a Group with GSO (forms F-30, F-28)
nodes.summary: GSO lists groups, not meetings. A new group fills out the New Group Form (F-30, Appendix H) so communication can flow between the group and the U.S./Canada structure: its district, its area and GSO. The form asks the group to choose a preferred district and area, and gives a primary contact, often the GSR. Many groups meet for a month or two before applying. Once the information is logged, a 30-day pending period (1990 Advisory Action) lets the delegate and DCM welcome the group, and then GSO emails the digital Group Handbook. A listing is not an endorsement: GSO neither monitors nor oversees any group. Later changes, such as a new GSR, go on the Group Information Change Form (F-28, Appendix I).

nodes.title: GSO Archives
nodes.summary: The GSO Archives keeps A.A.'s permanent record and is one of AAWS's four main functions. It collects copies of everything AAWS and AA Grapevine print or produce, plus board minutes, committee reports and other lasting records. It preserves them by digitizing and other archival methods and catalogs them so they can be searched. It answers history questions from members, staff, trustees, directors and outside researchers, and it maintains the Archives portal on aa.org. It also helps local archives committees and area and district archivists. Visitors to GSO can tour its exhibits and library.

nodes.title: The A.A. Service Manual and how it changes
nodes.summary: The A.A. Service Manual, bound with Bill W.'s Twelve Concepts for World Service, explains the U.S./Canada general service structure and the roles of the trusted servants who make it work. It grew out of Bill W.'s 'Third Legacy Manual' and calls itself a permanent work in progress. A new edition comes out every two years: GSO's Group Services desk coordinates the updates, and the Conference Report and Charter Committee reviews the manual. The 2026-2028 edition ('Revised: September 2026') now opens with an Editorial Updates Grid, added at the 76th Conference's direction, that lists each change, its page and its source: a Conference action or an editorial update by GSO's Publishing Department, GSO staff, AA Grapevine, the AAWS Board or the General Service Board.

duties: Explain each service role, from GSR to trustee

nodes.title: The 1955 Resolution (Appendix L)
nodes.summary: At A.A.'s Twentieth Anniversary Convention in St. Louis in July 1955, Bill W. offered a resolution declaring that the Fellowship had come of age and was ready to take full possession of its Three Legacies. The co-founders had created the General Service Conference in 1951 with the authority of the Alcoholic Foundation's trustees. The Resolution made it their permanent successor: guardian of the Traditions, keeper of the world services and voice of the whole Fellowship's group conscience. Bill presented this as a way to prevent future strivings for prestige or personal power and to let A.A. function permanently. The Resolution also set the safeguard: the Traditions and the Article 12 Warranties cannot change unless the registered groups are notified, given at least six months, and three-quarters of those responding consent in writing.

nodes.title: The Twelve Traditions (short and long forms)
nodes.summary: Appendix B prints the Twelve Traditions twice: the familiar short form and the original long form. Several Traditions underpin the service structure. Tradition Two names one ultimate authority, a loving God as expressed in the group conscience, and calls leaders trusted servants who do not govern. Tradition Four (long form) asks any group, regional committee or individual planning action that could greatly affect A.A. as a whole to confer with the General Service Board trustees first. Tradition Eight lets service centers employ special workers while A.A. stays nonprofessional. Tradition Nine allows service boards and committees directly responsible to those they serve, and its long form calls the trustees, in effect, A.A.'s General Service Committee. Bill W. says the Traditions grew mainly out of the headquarters' correspondence and public relations experience. They were first published, in long form, in the Grapevine in May 1946.
nodes.chosen_by: Drafted by Bill W. with helpers at headquarters from the office's experience; declared A.A.'s platform for unity at the 1950 Cleveland Convention (p. 102).
nodes.term: Not applicable
nodes.how_many: 12, in a short form and a long form (Appendix B)
facts: In late 1945 a friend suggested codifying the office's experience into simply stated principles. The ideas came chiefly from correspondence and public relations work (p. 102)

At first only groups in serious trouble took the Traditions seriously, and others reacted violently or with indifference. Five years later the 1950 Cleveland Convention declared them A.A.'s platform for unity (p. 102)
Bill W. said such a code could never become rule or law, but could guide trustees, headquarters and groups with growing pains (p. 102)
Long form, Tradition Three: 'Any two or three alcoholics gathered together for sobriety may call themselves an A.A. group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation.' (p. 106)

Long form, Tradition Four: a group answers only to its own conscience in its own affairs, should consult neighboring groups its plans affect, and should confer with the GSB trustees before any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole (p. 106)

Long form, Tradition Six: considerable property of real use to A.A. should be incorporated and managed separately, a group should never go into business, and clubs or hospitals should not use the A.A. name (p. 107)

Long form, Tradition Seven: large gifts, or gifts carrying any obligation, are unwise, and treasuries that keep piling up funds beyond prudent reserves for no stated A.A. purpose are a concern (p. 107)

Long form, Tradition Eight: professionalism means counseling alcoholics for fees or hire. A.A. may pay alcoholics for special services it would otherwise hire nonalcoholics to do, but Twelfth Step work is never paid (p. 107)

Long form, Tradition Nine: the small group elects a secretary, the large group a rotating committee, and a metropolitan area's groups a central or intergroup committee. The GSB trustees are in effect A.A.'s General Service Committee: custodians of the Tradition, receivers of the contributions that maintain GSO, handlers of overall public relations and guarantors of the Grapevine's integrity (p. 107)

quotes.text: A.A., as such, ought never be organized; but we may create service boards or committees directly responsible to those they serve.
The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee.
no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees
Such a traditional code could not, of course, ever become rule or law.

nodes.title: Trustees' International Committee
nodes.summary: The International Committee is a standing committee of the General Service Board with no matching Conference committee. It looks for ways to carry the message to alcoholics in other countries, especially where no service structure exists yet. It shares experience, supports translations of A.A. literature and encourages regional and zonal meetings, and it is the main link between the worldwide A.A. community and the U.S./Canada board. The two trustees-at-large sit on it and serve as delegates to the World Service Meeting and the Meeting of the Americas (REDELA).
nodes.chosen_by: Members are appointed by the GSB chair, subject to board approval (p. 58); the trustees-at-large are members (p. 57)
nodes.term: Not stated
nodes.how_many: 1 committee; no corresponding Conference committee
duties: Suggest ways to carry the message internationally, particularly in countries with no established service structure
Share experience, support translations of A.A. literature in other languages, and encourage regional or zonal meetings
Serve as the primary link between the international A.A. community and the U.S./Canada General Service Board
facts: It is one of the board's 10 standing committees and has no corresponding Conference committee (pp. 58-59)
