nodes.title: Stimulating Interest in General Service (Appendix V)
nodes.summary: Most members care first about their group, their own sobriety and helping other drunks one-on-one, and that is as it should be. General service has exactly the same aim, carrying the message to the alcoholic who still suffers, but the link is not always direct or obvious, and communication about service tends to break down. So some 'stimulators' are usually needed: visits by the delegate and area committee, workshops, shared district events and direct outreach to inactive districts. Once members are well informed about service, they often want to take part.
facts: Many areas offer visits by the delegate or area committee members, who come to group or district meetings to talk about general service (p. 172)
Workshops on the Traditions, Concepts or other aspects of service are often effective, and two or more districts sometimes sponsor a service event together (p. 172)

One area put committee members in charge of sharing sessions in their own districts, with a report back at the monthly assembly. It gave GSRs and committee members as many jobs as it could and invited visitors to its assemblies to see the work (p. 172)
Another area showed service and informational videos at group meetings 239 times and answered hundreds of questions about general service (p. 172)
To reactivate inactive or unrepresented districts and groups, district and area officers contact groups directly about service events and chances to carry the message beyond the group level (p. 172)
In district-to-district sponsorship, an active district shares its experience and suggestions to 'jump start' activity in an inactive neighboring district (p. 172)

quotes.text: service can add a rich dimension to their sober lives and Twelfth Step work
Once A.A. members are well informed about service, they often want to become involved and to take on their own service responsibilities.

glossary.definition: GSO's monthly in-house Steps, Traditions and Concepts meeting, facilitated by the Staff Coordinator.

One of the General Service Board's two operating corporations. It oversees the General Service Office and publishes Conference-approved and service literature (p. 91). Think of AAWS and Grapevine as the people and GSO as the place where they work (p. 6).
GSO's newsletter for professionals who work with alcoholics, such as those in healthcare, law, corrections and the clergy.
A temporary committee set up for a specific task that the regular committee system can't easily handle. It is dismissed once it delivers its result to the body that created it.

The manual's shorthand for the split of roles: the area chair runs assemblies and area business (administrative leader), while the delegate could be described as the link between the area, the Conference and A.A. as a whole (communications leader).

A recommendation from a Conference committee or a floor action that the full Conference approves with substantial unanimity (two-thirds of members voting, provided a quorum votes). It is referred to the General Service Board, which votes to affirm it; by tradition it is binding on the board.

An item for the Conference agenda. Individual members, groups, delegates, trustees, area assemblies, area committee members, and AAWS/Grapevine directors or staff may suggest one. Staff first review it against past Conference actions. The trustees' Conference Committee or the right Conference committee then decides when, where and whether it goes on the agenda.
The original name of A.A.'s board of trustees, created in 1938. It was later renamed the General Service Board of Alcoholics Anonymous; Concept I dates the renaming to 1954.
A service worker at the group, district or area level who assists in the role and stands ready to step in if the office holder can no longer serve.
The area's elected assistant to the delegate who stands ready to step in. When stepping in, they have all of a delegate's rights, privileges and responsibilities.

A section starting at C-61, called for by the 71st Conference and approved by the 76th. It holds an updated Concept XI essay and preserves the original 1962 wording of passages changed by Advisory Action; those passages are marked (A) in the main essays.
An A.A. member who serves on a specific trustees' committee, such as Public Information or Corrections, because of their knowledge and experience in that field.

One of 93 geographic areas of the U.S. and Canada, each of which sends a Conference delegate. A state or province usually has one area, but places with many A.A. members may have two or more. Some areas cover parts of more than one state or province.

A meeting of GSRs and committee members (DCMs and area officers) to discuss area affairs and, every other year, to elect a delegate and committee officers. The manual calls it the place where the democratic voice of the Fellowship expresses itself.
The area's steering committee, typically made up of all DCMs, area officers (including the delegate and alternate delegate) and area service committee chairs.
Trusted servants elected by the GSRs and DCMs to serve the area. They typically include the delegate, alternate delegate, chair, secretary, registrar and treasurer.
A self-support method in which members contribute on their A.A. birthday each year, in an amount they choose for each year of sobriety. They give directly to the GSB or through their group.
GSO's quarterly newsletter (News and Notes from GSO), in English, French and Spanish. Free digital subscriptions are available through aa.org.
Brings debate to a halt while members decide whether to proceed directly to a vote. It needs a second, is not debatable, and needs two-thirds.
A nonalcoholic 'friend of A.A.' on the board, chosen for professional expertise; there are 7.
An alcoholic A.A. member on the board; there are 14, in three categories (regional, general service, at-large).

An item a Conference committee discussed without making a recommendation to the Conference as a whole. It is not actionable or debated; it is included in the committee's final report and serves as a suggestion to the matching trustees' committee.
An A.A. staff member who serves as nonvoting secretary of a Conference committee, helping prepare its report and serving as a resource.
Handling important Conference matters through committees, so that a large number of questions can be dealt with during Conference week.
The document each Conference committee follows.
An appeal from a member of the structure below Conference level that the Conference may agree to hear, in keeping with Concepts IV and V.
Twelve related principles of service drawn from A.A.'s service successes and mistakes, set out by Bill W. in The A.A. Service Manual/Twelve Concepts for World Service.
The General Service Conference. The word can mean the whole structure of committee members, GSRs and delegates in an area, or the annual spring meeting of delegates in New York.

The founding document, originally adopted in 1955, that defines the Conference's purpose, composition and relationship to A.A. and the General Service Board. Appendix K prints both the original and current versions.

The GSO staff member currently serving on the Conference assignment. Receives proposed agenda items (p. 43), coordinates Conference communication (p. 71) and, with the chair and vice-chair of the trustees' GSC Committee, runs the December committee draw (p. 45; 2024 Final Report, p. 68).
A site maintained by GSO where Conference materials, background and communications are posted for Conference members. Delegates receive a password immediately upon election.

Books, pamphlets, videos and other material reviewed and recommended by the appropriate Conference committee and approved by two-thirds of Conference members; it may then carry the line 'This is A.A. General Service Conference-approved literature.'
A GSO service that lets incarcerated alcoholics write to A.A. members on the outside.
District, area, trustee and Conference committees that carry the message to professionals who work with problem drinkers.
The trustees' role is to safeguard A.A.'s vital services and the Fellowship's welfare, not to govern.

The relationship between the General Service Board and its two operating corporations, AAWS and AA Grapevine (described in Concept VIII). The board exercises it by electing their directors, approving their budgets and having authority to change their bylaws.
An experienced GSR elected by the district's GSRs. The DCM represents the district's groups at area committee meetings and coordinates service in the district.
Leads the regular meetings of a large district and links it to the area. Subdivisions within the district are each served by a DCM. The 76th Conference added this term to the glossary.
The A.A. member elected every other year to represent the area at the annual Conference meeting in New York and to bring back to the area the results of that meeting.
A member of the corporate board of AAWS or Grapevine. The boards include nontrustee directors (A.A. members chosen for business or professional experience), trustees and A.A. staff.
A division within an area, represented by one or more committee members. It is usually a cluster of nearby groups, but it may also be linguistic or virtual (pp. 4, 14).
Typically the current GSRs in the district plus the DCM and alternate DCM. Many districts add a treasurer, a secretary and committee chairs.
Meetings of the DCM and the GSRs of the groups in a district.
One of two nonvoting volunteer boards (Grapevine and La Viña) that advise the editorial staffs. Members serve one four-year term.
A special assembly held once every two years, usually in the fall of an election year, to elect the delegate and typically the area officers, with little or no other business.
In the corporate bylaws, the total number of voting directors the corporation would have if there were no vacancies.
The bylaws' word for a Class B trustee: someone who has arrested their drinking and lives, as far as possible, by the Twelve Steps.
A user-friendly interface that facilitates information sharing between areas and GSO. Area registrars require training on it to keep group and trusted-servant records current.

The complete record of reports, presentations, workshops and all actions taken by a Conference. It is provided through area delegates in print (English, French, Spanish) during the summer and online as an anonymity-protected digital file.
A recommendation made directly from the floor during the general sessions that may not have passed through a Conference committee.
CEO and president of AAWS. The GM is an A.A. member who, with the Grapevine Publisher, leads the daily operations of GSO.
Movement-wide services, performed by anyone in the general service structure (GSR, DCM, delegate and so on). The structure lets the groups' collective conscience guide A.A. as a whole (p. 2).

The board of 14 alcoholic (Class B) and 7 nonalcoholic (Class A) trustees that safeguards A.A.'s Traditions and funds. It oversees GSO, AAWS and AA Grapevine, Inc. When a Class B trustee is chosen as chair, the board grows to 22 (15 Class B and 7 Class A) for that term.

A reserve set up by the trustees in 1954 to keep AAWS and Grapevine services running in an emergency. It is capped by Conference action at one year's combined operating expenses of AAWS, Grapevine and the GSB General Fund.

The body that links the groups to GSO and the General Service Board, acting as the group conscience of A.A. as a whole. It meets six days a year, but its members work on Conference affairs all year. Members are elected from the 93 area assemblies, whose members are in turn elected by the GSRs.
The office in New York City, staffed by AAWS and Grapevine employees. It serves groups in the U.S. and Canada and publishes A.A. literature.
A Class B trustee drawn from current or past nontrustee directors; two come from the AAWS board and two from the Grapevine board.

Sharing on topics affecting A.A. as a whole among trustees, directors, committee members and staff, held at General Service Board weekends (p. 61); the Concepts footnote says three times a year, for about two hours on the Saturday before the board meeting (C-36, C-67).

Article 12 of the Conference Charter, also Concept XII: a pledge to observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition plus six Warranties, such as never becoming the seat of perilous wealth or power and never performing acts of government. Changing them needs the written consent of three-quarters of the directory-listed groups that vote, with six months to deliberate.
The most common type of district. Its size is set by how many groups one DCM can reasonably keep in touch with.
Some areas' policy of choosing delegates from different parts of the area in turn (for example rural and urban). The manual says no well-qualified member should be passed over for it.

glossary.term: Going to the hat (choice by lot)
glossary.definition: The final step of the Third Legacy Procedure when no candidate reaches two-thirds: after the fourth ballot if a fifth ballot is voted down, or after a fifth ballot with no election. The teller draws, and the first name out of the hat is elected.
A.A.'s international journal, online and in print. AA Grapevine, Inc. is one of the board's two operating corporations and runs Grapevine's operations and finances.
What the group forms when it meets on proposed changes or actions on matters relating to A.A. as a whole. Each member has one vote.
The group's link to A.A. as a whole and its contact with GSO. A voting member of the area assembly, and also of district meetings (p. 8).
The group's or district's contact with the Grapevine office.
The group where a member takes part in business meetings and casts their vote as part of the Fellowship's group conscience. The manual calls it the very basis of the service structure.

A GSR, DCM or other servant who can no longer carry out the position. Each service entity decides what 'inactive' means. Experience suggests asking the person to resign so a new servant can be elected.

An autonomous local service office that serves the groups in its area. It is important to A.A., but it is not part of the general service structure or a satellite of GSO (p. 6). Many areas have an intergroup/central office liaison who links these offices with the area committee; in some areas the liaison votes at the assembly, in others they have a voice but no vote (p. 25).
A fund through which GSO provides A.A. literature where no local office exists and resources are limited.
An information-only session at the beginning of Conference week between a Conference committee and its corresponding trustees' committee. No actions are taken.
The bimonthly Spanish-language magazine published by AA Grapevine, first issued in June 1996.
The member elected by each subdistrict (local district) when a large district divides. Depending on the area, LCMs may or may not vote on the area committee or meet regularly with their GSRs.

A district of groups that meet in a particular language (for example French, Spanish, Polish, Vietnamese or ASL). It usually has a bilingual DCM or liaison, and its boundaries may be independent of the geographic districts.
A 1.5- or 2-day forum for remote, sparsely populated, urban or underserved A.A. communities; the Local Forum Committee pays expenses.

A confidential bimonthly bulletin sent to Loners (lone members), Homers (housebound members), Internationalists (seagoing A.A.s), Port Contacts and Loner Sponsors. It shares excerpts of their correspondence and lists LIM members who wish to write to each other.

A poll of all Conference members (the bylaws' “Conference delegates”, p. 135) with at least two weeks' notice. It is used when trustees judge a pending decision to involve principle or basic policy and a delay will not harm the Fellowship. If a majority votes against, the board is expected to refrain.
A zonal meeting of the general service structures of North, Central and South America, held in the years without a WSM.
Trustees are the legal members of the GSB corporation under New York law; 'entire membership' means the full 21 voting trustees with no vacancies.
The legal members of AAWS and AA Grapevine, Inc. These are the GSB trustees, who elect the directors and alone can amend the bylaws.
Meetings, Events and Travel Services: the GSO team that coordinates travel and plans events such as the Conference, Regional Forums and the World Service Meeting.

After each vote on policy, the side that did not prevail is given a chance to speak. Occasionally this leads to another vote that reverses the first. If the motion passes with two-thirds, the minority speaks. If it gets a majority but fails for lack of two-thirds, the majority speaks (p. 173).

The trustees' self-guidance statement. Mission: to serve the Fellowship of A.A. Vision: clear and effective leadership, directly responsible and responsive to the Fellowship through the General Service Conference. Action: guided by the Steps, Traditions and Concepts, the board plans overall policy and finance, acts as custodian of AAWS and AA Grapevine, oversees public relations policy, keeps up ties with service structures worldwide, and guards the Steps, Traditions and Concepts.
Returns a motion or proposal to the respective trustees' committee or appropriate corporate board for further consideration. It must be seconded, is debatable, can be amended, and needs two-thirds.

An A.A. member, chosen for business or professional experience related to the corporation's work, who serves as a director of AAWS or Grapevine without being a trustee. There are three per board, and they serve on most GSB standing committees.
Each area's designation in Appendix M showing which alternating cycle its delegate belongs to. About half the areas elect in one year and half the next.

A numbered group of delegates elected to begin serving at the Conference in a particular year. The number is that of the first Conference they attend (e.g., Panel 63 delegates first attend the 63rd Conference).
The original rotating halves of the Conference. Panel One (odd) was seated in 1951 and Panel Two (even) in 1952. Since then one panel is elected and one retires each year.
A delegate who has completed their term. Rotation prevents them from serving as delegate again, and they are typically asked not to hold office as GSR or DCM.
District, area, trustee and Conference committees that carry the message by working with the media.
CEO and president of AA Grapevine, Inc. The publisher reports to the Grapevine board and is a Conference member.
A report on the activities of the General Service Board, AAWS and AA Grapevine, in English, French and Spanish.

The minimum number of members who must be present for proceedings to be valid. Each area sets its own, and alternate DCMs typically count only when their DCM is absent (p. 32). Conference: two-thirds of all registered Conference members (p. 124). General Service Board: two-fifths of the member trustees (p. 141).
A motion to reconsider a vote, made only by a member who voted with the prevailing side; it may be seconded by anyone and passes by simple majority. No action may be reconsidered twice.
Changing district structure as groups grow so each committee member can stay in touch with their groups. Options are new districts, subdistricts with LCMs, or a large district led by a DCMC.
A group of areas that together supply a regional trustee to the board. There are six regions in the U.S. and two in Canada.

A weekend sharing and information gathering where members meet board members and GSO staff. Each region holds one every two years, and generally four take place each year. Even years: Western Canada, Eastern Canada, Southeast, Pacific; odd years: Northeast, East Central, West Central, Southwest (2026 Final Report, p. 98).

Annual meetings held by several regions for past and current delegates and their alternates, typically to help new delegates prepare for the Conference and strengthen lines of communication. The Southwest's is SWRDA.
A Class B trustee nominated from one of the eight regions who brings a regional A.A. viewpoint; 6 U.S., 2 Canada.

An assembly typically held several times a year for ongoing area business, a look at the Conference agenda, post-Conference reports, workshops and sharing. Some areas call it a 'workshop' or 'general sharing session'.
A self-support method in which groups send a set amount or percentage every month or quarter. It and the Birthday Plan are two special plans many groups use to support A.A. service entities (p. 8).
What some call the delegate's report to groups, districts and the area after the annual Conference meeting.

glossary.term: Right of Appeal / Right of Petition
glossary.definition: Concept V. Appeal makes sure minority opinion is heard. Petition makes sure personal grievances are heard and properly acted on.
Concept III. Each part of world service (Conference, board, corporations, staffs, committees, executives) has traditional discretion to act within its role.
Concept IV. Each group of world servants gets voting representation in reasonable proportion to its responsibility.
The group's or district's contact with the Grapevine office for La Viña.
The spiritual principle of sharing responsibility for A.A. through changing leadership.

Archives and International Conventions/Regional Forums. Some delegates, chosen by lot, serve on one of them in addition to their primary assignment; each meets at a dinner meeting with its trustees' committee.
An informal alternative to a vote on simple matters. The chair asks, 'Is it the sense of the meeting that…?', and if there are no 'nays', there is accord.
The A.A. Service Manual/Twelve Concepts for World Service. It explains the general service structure and includes the Conference Charter, the General Service Board Bylaws and the Twelve Concepts.
An alcoholic who has made some progress in recovery and/or service and shares that experience with someone just starting out in service.
A newsletter published three times a year with excerpts from letters by people in custody. Local corrections committees distribute it to groups behind the walls.

A group, district, area or Conference meeting where everyone is invited to contribute ideas and comments on A.A. matters and no actions are taken. Floor actions cannot be introduced at Conference Sharing Sessions. Since 2023 all Conference members also meet virtually for general sharing sessions at least twice a year (2023 Final Report, p. 37).
Usually one-half of the votes cast plus one. It is used for simple or routine matters.
The list of proposed trustees presented to the Conference (the officer slate is presented the same way); it becomes final unless a majority of Conference members disapproves.
A senior GSO staff member who coordinates GSB correspondence, serves as assistant secretary to the GSB and sits as a voting director on the AAWS board.

One of the rotating GSO staff jobs, each covering one area of service such as Corrections, PI or Conference. The manual's list (pp. 70-73) has thirteen, including Self-Support and Finance, added in this edition (p. IX), although p. 70 still says twelve. GSO created that assignment in September 2025 (2026 Final Report, p. 66).
The 13 Conference committees (11 primary, 2 secondary) to which most agenda items are assigned.

The board has 10 standing and 4 auxiliary committees, and for the most part they mirror Conference committees. The auxiliary ones (Audit, Compensation, Compliance, Employees' Retirement) handle compliance and oversight and have no Conference counterpart.

A smaller part of a large district. A subdistrict may elect its own LCM; in a large district led by a DCMC, each subdistrict, local district or zone is served by a DCM, who may hold regular GSR meetings.

Typically a two-thirds (or more) majority, in some situations three-fourths (or more). Used for controversial or complex issues and for some elections, to promote unity. At the Conference, every matter of policy (Advisory Action), and any action or amendment affecting one, needs it. There it means two-thirds of the members voting, provided the total vote is at least a quorum (p. 173).
The Conference Charter's original wording (Article 11) for what are now termed Conference Advisory Actions.
Postpones discussion to a later time during the same Conference. It needs a second, is not debatable, and passes by simple majority.
A nonvoting member selected to count ballots at an election assembly. In the Third Legacy Procedure, the teller draws the lot from the hat.
Bill W.'s service manual, first drafted in 1951. The current A.A. Service Manual grew out of it.
Bill W.'s name for the sum of all A.A. services, meaning anything that helps reach a fellow sufferer, from the Twelfth Step itself to GSO's national and international work.

A.A.'s electoral method, used primarily for delegates and regional and at-large trustees, and typically for area officers. Written ballots are cast, two-thirds of the total vote elects, low candidates are withdrawn after ballots 2, 3 and 4, and if no one is elected by the final ballot the choice is made by lot.
Recovery, Unity and Service, which Bill W. called the Fellowship's chief inheritances from A.A.'s first 20 years.
A member of the General Service Board: 14 are A.A. members (Class B) and 7 are nonalcoholic (Class A).
One of two alcoholic trustees, one from the U.S. and one from Canada. They represent the U.S. and Canada at the World Service Meeting and the Zonal Meeting of the Americas (REDELA).
Former board chairs, typically, whom the board invites to its meetings and to the Conference as a nonvoting source of corporate memory.

The image the manual uses for general service. Unlike a typical organization, final authority rests with the groups, shown at the broad top, and each section below them has a part in making the groups' conscience known.
A district of online groups (new or established) that want to take part in general service. Some areas added them to serve the many online groups that blossomed in the pandemic and are still active.

The book company created to publish 'Alcoholics Anonymous', funded by selling stock at a par value of $25. It was later audited and incorporated; Bill W. and Hank P. donated their shares to the Alcoholic Foundation, and the other 49 subscribers' shares were bought back with a loan, so the book would belong to A.A. as a whole. In 1940 its stock passed to the trustees. It was later renamed A.A. Publishing, Inc., today a division of AAWS.

A worldwide meeting of delegates from the various General Service Conferences, held every two years and alternating between New York and another member country (p. 62). The U.S./Canada delegates are usually the two trustees-at-large (p. 57). REDELA is held in the other years. The 29th WSM was in Lisbon, October 4-8, 2026 (2026 Final Report, p. 94).

The second-year delegate who serves as the Conference's delegate chairperson for one Conference: gives the welcome address and, with the GSB chair, sets the virtual sharing sessions. Chosen by lot at the previous Conference from first-year delegates not elected a committee chair or alternate. Not the same as 'delegate chairs' (plural), which in trustees' reports means the delegates who chair Conference committees.

A suggestion submitted for a future Conference agenda. PAIs for next year's Conference are due September 30; later ones go to the following year (2025 Final Report, p. 85). GSO reports their status in a quarterly PAI status grid (2026 Final Report, p. 84).

Before the November board weekend, the chair of the trustees' GSC Committee meets the Agenda, Policy/Admissions and Report and Charter committees to hear whether related PAIs should go to their Conference committee (2025 Final Report, p. 84).

A process that spreads agenda items across Conference committees, sometimes outside a committee's usual topic. Trial from the 72nd Conference (2021 Final Report, p. 60), adopted in 2024, discontinued after the 78th Conference in 2028 (2026 Final Report, p. 39).

Chosen at random, by drawing. Conference committee assignments are determined by lot (p. 45); the Third Legacy Procedure can end by lot ('going to the hat', p. 115); the Delegate Chair and some working groups are also chosen by lot (2024 Final Report, pp. 46, 69).

Southwest Region Delegates Assembly: a yearly March meeting in Oklahoma City for past delegates, past regional trustees, the current Southwest regional trustee and the serving delegates and alternates; it works like a mock Conference before the GSC (March 12-14, 2027).

Southwest Regional A.A. Service Assembly: held every two years in October, hosted in turn by the region's 11 areas (2024 Area 65; 2026 Area 67; October 13-15, 2028 Area 66). The Southwest alternate delegates carry its business meeting.

A quarterly General Service Board weekend in New York, when trustees' committees and the corporate boards meet. The 1st, 3rd and 4th quarterly board meetings fall on the fifth Monday after a calendar quarter ends; the 2nd is the Saturday the Conference closes (p. 140). Conference committee chairs attend one each year (the October/November weekend from 2026; 2026 Final Report, p. 49).

The papers on each agenda item that Conference committee members study before the Conference, in English, French and Spanish (p. 45). It now goes out in all three languages at once in mid/late February (February 17-20, 2026; 2026 Final Report, p. 83).

The traditional A.A. symbol. AAWS stopped official use of its circle/triangle trademarks in 1993, but any group or district may use the symbol on newsletters, meeting schedules or other A.A. material without AAWS permission.

A special type of A.A. meeting, usually a weekend of speakers, panels, presentations and workshops, often set up by the area committee or a special committee the area chair appoints. Assemblies are usually not held during a convention, though sometimes just before or after.

The acknowledgement printed under reprinted A.A. material. For AAWS literature: 'Reprinted from (name of publication, page number), with permission of Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc.' For the Preamble and Grapevine/La Viña material: 'Copyright © (Month, Year) AA Grapevine, Inc./La Viña. Reprinted with permission.'

The whole Fellowship, beyond any one group, district or area. The service structure brings the groups' collective conscience to bear on matters affecting A.A. as a whole (p. 2), and the GSR is the group's link to it (p. 7).

A packet of service material from GSO. Newly listed GSRs and DCMs get a complimentary kit; the GSR kit holds a welcome letter, the Service Manual/Twelve Concepts, pamphlets and leaflets, an AAWS literature order form and Grapevine materials. Staff desks also offer committee service kits. All service kits can be downloaded from aa.org, and Group Services coordinates the yearly kit list update.

The Conference-week session that selects one regional trustee nominee by the Third Legacy Procedure. It is co-chaired by the chairs of the trustees' Nominating Committee and the Conference Committee on Trustees. Its voters are the region's delegates plus an equal number drawn half from each of those committees, and it meets in a roped-off section that all Conference members may watch.

The written material given to Conference members in which many of the Conference's proceedings are set out. Delegates also take their own notes to help them report back, and the Final Conference Report later gives the complete record.
A forum for A.A. members who would not normally be able to attend a Regional Forum or a Local Forum, or held where there is an expressed need based on culture, language or geography.

Tradition Eight's phrase for paid workers at A.A.'s service centers. In the board chapter it means the paid AAWS and AA Grapevine employees who also sit on the corporate boards. They are the one exception to the rule that trustees, directors and appointed committee members serve without pay; the GSB covers those volunteers' travel and lodging.

A GSO leadership title (the GSO Staff page lists who has held it). In the manual's agenda process, the A.A. staff member on the Conference assignment sends a suggested disposition of each submitted agenda item to the Director of Staff Services and the chair of the trustees' Conference Committee so they can reach consensus.

GSO service pieces that gather the shared experience of members and groups across the U.S. and Canada on particular topics, such as archives, in light of the Traditions and Conference guidance. They help groups reach an informed conscience.

glossary.term: General Fund (of the General Service Board)
glossary.definition: The General Service Board's fund that receives Seventh Tradition contributions from groups and members (p. 87). It pays the balance of delegates' Conference expenses after the areas' contributions (p. 36) and covers any La Viña shortfall (p. 68). The Reserve Fund is capped at one year of the combined operating expenses of AAWS, Grapevine and the General Fund (p. 65).

An online collection of almost every Grapevine article and letter since June 1944, including all of Bill W.'s Grapevine articles. It can be browsed by department, topic or date, and the Grapevine and La Viña apps carry the digital archives.

AAWS's app that makes it easy for anyone to find a meeting. It began as a project for members in Santa Clara County, California, launched in November 2015, and now gathers listings from area, district and intergroup/central office websites and from general service office websites around the world (those listed on A.A. Near You), which keep control of their own information (p. 168). Communication Services runs it alongside aa.org (p. 74), the AAWS Services and Technology Committee oversees it (p. 66), and the 2026-2028 edition added it as a source for GSR reports (p. 11).

A.A.'s twelve principles for group life and for relations with the outside world. The long form is the original wording, first published in the Grapevine in May 1946. The short form is the familiar version. Appendix B prints both.

GSO lists groups, not meetings. Holding meetings is one function of a group. An A.A. group takes part in the general service structure and provides Twelfth Step services beyond its regular meeting times. Long-form Tradition Three: any two or three alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call themselves a group, provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation.

The 30 days that follow once GSO or the area registrar logs a new group's complete information, under a 1990 Conference Advisory Action, so the delegate and DCM can welcome the group. A digital Group Handbook is then emailed (print copy on request).

F-30 New Group Form (Appendix H), to list a group. F-28 Group Information Change Form (Appendix I), for changes such as a new GSR or alternate. F-43 DCM & DCMC Information Change Form (Appendix J). Each can be returned by GSO mail or email, or locally through the area registrar.

The member GSO uses as its contact for a group. Often the GSR, but any member with a current email address can serve. If a group names no preferred district and area, or a virtual group has no city or state of its own, the primary contact's location is used.

In the long form of Tradition Eight, 'the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire'. A.A. stays nonprofessional, but service centers may employ special workers, and Twelfth Step work is never paid.

A group's emergency fund, often a few months' rent and expenses (p. 69). Long-form Tradition Seven views with concern treasuries that keep accumulating funds 'beyond prudent reserves' for no stated A.A. purpose (p. 107). The manual's FAQ compares the GSB Reserve Fund, capped at one year of expenses, to a group's prudent reserve (pp. 65, 69).
A copyrighted AAWS design and registered trademark. Its use is reserved for the AAWS board, the AA Grapevine board, the General Service Board and GSO.

How the Charter's footnotes describe AAWS and AA Grapevine: separate not-for-profit corporations, not subsidiaries of the General Service Board. Their own boards run day-to-day business, and the trustees, as members, elect their directors.

The resolution Bill W. offered at the Twentieth Anniversary Convention in St. Louis on July 3, 1955. It made the General Service Conference guardian of the Traditions, voice of the Fellowship's group conscience and sole successor to the co-founders. It also requires three-quarters of the responding groups to consent in writing to any change in the Traditions or the Article 12 Warranties.

Bill W.'s term in the 1955 Resolution for groups known to the general service offices. Such groups are asked to consent to any change in the Traditions or Warranties. Being listed with GSO does not mean AAWS monitors or oversees the group.

In the GSB bylaws, the defined name for all members of the General Service Conference, not only the area delegates. A majority of them can disapprove a proposed trustee, a bylaw amendment or a new affiliate corporation, and in a mail vote they can turn down a board decision of principle.

The yearly legal meeting at which a corporation's members act. For the GSB, the board breaks off its 2nd quarterly meeting (the Saturday right after the Conference closes) to hold it: the trustees, as members, elect or re-elect trustees and receive the certified annual report. For AAWS and AA Grapevine, the trustees meet as Members on the day after the Conference's scheduled close to elect the directors and receive each corporation's annual report.

The New York State law under which the General Service Board, AAWS and AA Grapevine operate. The bylaws cite it for the certified annual report given to members, the matters no committee may decide and, at AAWS, the conflict-of-interest and whistleblower policies.

glossary.term: Committee of the Board / committee of the corporation
glossary.definition: A Committee of the Board is formed from among the board's own members by a majority of the entire board and holds whatever board powers its resolution gives it (at AAWS and Grapevine, at least three directors). Every other committee is a committee of the corporation, whose members are appointed or elected like officers; at AAWS such committees may include non-directors and cannot bind the corporation.

A corporation's founding legal document under New York law. The GSB's can be amended by 75% of all trustees, acting as members. The board is expected to put any change to Conference delegates and to hold back if a majority disapproves, unless the law requires the change; if they do not disapprove, a majority of members present can adopt it.

Tradition Two's name for A.A. leaders, who serve and do not govern (p. 112): anyone in a service role, such as a GSR, DCM, area officer, delegate or trustee, each helping make the groups' conscience known (p. 4). Concept III says they should be trusted to decide, within their duties, how to use their authority; Concept V says they must do for the groups what the groups cannot or should not do for themselves, even when that means disagreeing with uninformed group opinion.

A delegate told by the groups exactly how to vote. The groups have that right, but Concept III warns that a delegate who cannot vote their own conscience on a final Conference vote is not a trusted servant but just a messenger.

A written statement of a minority's view. Concept V encourages minorities in staffs, committees, corporate boards or among the trustees to file one when they think the majority is badly wrong, and makes bringing one to the Conference a duty when the issue is grave for A.A. as a whole.

The democratic alternative to an authoritarian setup: no person or group holds unqualified authority over another. Bill W. based the Concepts on it because, as he wrote, we tend to enlarge our own authority when in charge and resist someone else's when we are not.

The board's legal right to decline a Conference action, seldom used. Concept VII names three cases: an action that clearly violates the Conference's or the board's charter, or is reckless enough to seriously harm A.A. (only after the Conference refuses to reconsider); reducing the budget during a fiscal year; and cancelling a plan made unworkable by unforeseen conditions.

Bill W.'s comparison in Concepts VI and VIII: the groups are stockholders, the delegates their proxies at the annual meeting, and the trustees the directors of a holding company that controls the operating services. A footnote clarifies that AAWS and AA Grapevine are legally affiliates, not subsidiaries.

Each Concept exists in two versions. The long form is Bill W.'s original 1962 wording, which opens each essay. The short form was approved by the 1971 Conference, added to the manual in 1974, and also appears in the General Service Board Bylaws.

A name many A.A.s give to Article 12 of the Conference Charter, the General Warranties (Concept XII), because it protects members' spiritual liberties, above all against anyone holding unqualified authority over others.

The 'senior' trustees' committee in Bill W.'s 1962 Concept XI essay. It met town-meeting style before each quarterly board meeting to sift business and send recommendations, with minority views, to the trustees. In October 1977 it became the General Sharing Session.

Ultimate (final) authority for world services rests with the groups (Concept I); immediate, active authority is delegated to the Conference and through it to the trustees and service corporations (Concepts II, VI). Concept X traces the chain: the groups over the Conference, delegates over trustees, trustees over AAWS and Grapevine, directors over their officers, and officers over staff. Ultimate authority is used in full only in emergencies; delegated authority is the clearly defined power each trusted servant needs for daily work. Tradition Two pairs them as group conscience and trusted servant.

Bill W.'s term for splitting authority over one job between two bosses or bodies, which Concept X says must be avoided at all costs. Concept XI uses it to explain why AAWS should not run the Grapevine's business side.
When two committees or bodies share a matter, the one with the main responsibility. The junior body must be heard, and there must always be a clear point where the final decision is made.

The Conference's role as 'guardian' of the A.A. Traditions. Concept XII says this does not mean publicly punishing or suing violators. The Conference informs them privately, keeps up persuasion, and relies on A.A. opinion, public opinion and education.

A table at the front of the 2026-2028 Service Manual, added at the 76th Conference's direction. It lists each change from the previous edition, the page it is on and its source: a Conference action (such as the 75th or 76th) or an editorial update by the Publishing Department, GSO staff, AA Grapevine, the AAWS Board or the General Service Board.

A.A.'s worldwide celebration of sobriety, held every five years and open to all members; it draws about 50,000 members from about 80 countries. It is not the General Service Conference, which is the annual service meeting on the 'business of A.A.'.

glossary.term: Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need
glossary.definition: Bill W.'s April 1959 Grapevine article on good service leadership: lead by example, consult widely, never pass the buck, compromise cheerfully but stand firm when needed, and take criticism well. Excerpts are in the delegate chapter; the full text is in the Concept IX essay.
A local meeting or process before the annual Conference, such as an area or district session, where members study the Conference agenda and give their delegate their group conscience on it.
A vote cast for an absent voting member by someone they designate. At area assemblies the alternate GSR normally votes when the GSR is absent; proxies are used in some areas but are not common.
A regular get-together, which an intergroup/central office may host, where group program chairs meet to exchange meetings with other groups (p. 166).

The Intergroup/Central Office/AAWS Seminar. The first, in 1986, discussed literature distribution, pricing and discounts and how to work together. It is now held every year; its history is at icoaa.org (p. 167).

The committee most communities set up to run an intergroup/central office's administration. It meets regularly, deals with general policy and plans, and reports periodically to the group representatives so information flows both ways (pp. 168-169).

The member each group names, with an alternate, to serve a set term as the group's link to its intergroup/central office. Not to be confused with the GSR, who links the group to the general service structure. In large communities a zone representative may serve several groups (p. 169).

A.A.'s short statement of what the Fellowship is. A Grapevine editor wrote it, basing it on the foreword to the first edition of the Big Book, and it first appeared in the June 1947 Grapevine. AA Grapevine holds the copyright, and its credit line should appear beneath any reprint.
An active district shares its experience and suggestions with an inactive neighboring district to 'jump start' activity among that district's groups.

The standard parliamentary rulebook. The Conference generally follows it, as informally as the rights of all concerned allow, and has adopted some exceptions to stay closer to the spirit of A.A. Tradition. Appendix W summarizes how each kind of motion works.

A common name for an amendment that the maker of a motion simply accepts without a vote. The manual says there are no 'friendly' amendments under Robert's Rules: at the Conference members are asked not to amend a committee's work spontaneously, and any amendment needs a second, is debatable and needs two-thirds.

The motion the chair asks for once a floor action's maker has had two minutes to explain it. It is made without comment, needs a second, is not debatable and needs two-thirds. If it passes, the floor action is not taken up.
