rules.topic: One member, one vote in the group
rules.summary: In group conscience matters, each member of the home group has one vote. The home group is where members take part in business meetings and vote.

quotes.text: As with all group conscience matters, each member has one vote.

rules.topic: Who votes for the group at district and area
rules.summary: Any A.A. member may attend district meetings and area assemblies. In most areas only the elected GSR votes, and the alternate GSR votes only when the GSR is absent.

quotes.text: In most areas, only elected GSRs and alternates (when the GSR is absent) may vote.
although an alternate may vote only when the GSR is not present

rules.summary: Each GSR has one vote on district matters and in district elections. Whether the DCM and alternate DCM vote depends on the district. A GSR who also holds another district position (such as treasurer) still has only one vote.

quotes.text: Each GSR has a vote on district matters and in district elections.
This GSR would still have one vote.

rules.topic: DCM voting and quorum at the area
rules.summary: Only the elected DCM, or the elected alternate DCM when the DCM is absent, may vote at an area meeting, so a DCM cannot send someone else to vote in their place. Generally, only elected DCMs (and alternates whose DCMs are absent) count toward an area quorum.

quotes.text: Only the elected DCM or alternate DCM (when the DCM is absent) may vote in an area meeting.
only elected DCMs (and elected alternate DCMs if their principals aren’t present) count toward the requirements of the quorum.

rules.summary: GSRs, DCMs and alternate DCMs serve two-year terms, and alternate GSRs are usually elected to the same two-year term as the GSR. In many areas GSR and DCM terms line up with the area delegate's panel.

quotes.text: GSRs serve two-year terms.
DCMs serve a term of two years. Alternate DCMs also serve two years.

rules.topic: Rotation when no successor is found
rules.summary: The Traditions and Concepts encourage rotation even when it looks like the position will go unfilled. GSRs and DCMs should step aside at the end of their term and consider another service role.

quotes.text: The Traditions and Concepts encourage rotation of service, even when it appears the position will be left unfilled.
When our terms are up, we step aside.

rules.topic: Notifying GSO of a new GSR
rules.summary: When a GSR is elected, the group sends the district and area committees, the local intergroup/central office and GSO three things: the group name and service number; the new GSR's name, address, email and phone; and the previous GSR's name. GSO then sends a GSR kit and adds the GSR to the Box 4-5-9 email list.

quotes.text: the group should provide the district and area committees, the local intergroup/central office, and GSO with the following information

rules.summary: The alternate DCM backs up the DCM. When the DCM is absent, the alternate can chair the district meeting and vote at the area. If the DCM resigns, the alternate often steps in, but the district's GSRs decide how the vacancy is handled.

quotes.text: If the DCM resigns or is unable to serve for any reason, the alternate often steps in. How this is handled is up to the GSRs in the district.

rules.summary: Each group decides whether to reimburse its GSR, and each district decides whether to reimburse its DCM. The DCM should discuss a budget with the district at the start of the term, before spending anything. In both cases, a person's finances should not be a barrier to service.

quotes.text: an individual’s finances should not be a barrier to service.
Budgeting for expenses is a discussion a DCM ought to have with the district at the beginning of the term and certainly before incurring any expense.

rules.summary: Items approved by a two-thirds majority of Conference members become Conference Advisory Actions. They go to the General Service Board's trustees, who refer them to trustees' committees, GSO or AA Grapevine to carry out, and who report back through quarterly reports.

quotes.text: Items approved by a two-thirds majority of Conference members become Conference Advisory Actions

rules.summary: If a group decides not to hear a GSR report during a meeting, the GSR can share it as a printed written report, by email or group messaging, in a shared online document or on a noticeboard. The GSR must respect Tradition Eleven so that members' names are not made public.

quotes.text: it is important to respect Tradition Eleven and protect anonymity so that members’ names are not publicly available.

rules.summary: Each part of general service is supported by voluntary contributions plus literature sales. The exception is AA Grapevine: under its charter it cannot accept group contributions and gets no share of contributions made to the General Service Board.

quotes.text: According to its charter, the AA Grapevine cannot accept group contributions

rules.summary: Candidates' names are posted and each voter casts a written ballot with one choice. The first candidate to reach two-thirds of the total vote is elected. Withdrawals start after ballot 2, when anyone under one-fifth of the total is dropped. After ballot 3, anyone under one-third is dropped. The top two always remain, as do all candidates tied for second.

quotes.text: Withdrawals start after the second ballot.
After the third ballot, candidates with less than one-third of the total vote will be withdrawn automatically, except the two top candidates remain.

rules.topic: Third Legacy Procedure: ballot 4, ballot 5 and the hat
rules.summary: If no one has two-thirds after ballot 4, the lowest candidate is dropped (top two remain). The chair asks for a motion, second, and simple majority of hands to hold a fifth and final ballot. If the motion fails, the choice goes to the hat immediately. If ballot 5 elects no one, the top two (or all tied for first, or the top candidate plus any tied for second) go into the hat, and the teller draws the winner.

quotes.text: At this point, the chairperson asks for a motion, second, and a simple majority of hands on conducting a fifth and final ballot.
If this motion is defeated, balloting is over and the choice is made by lot — “going to the hat” — immediately.

rules.topic: Who votes when alternates are present
rules.summary: Generally, area officers (including the delegate), GSRs and DCMs vote, and some areas also let committee chairs vote. Alternate GSRs and DCMs typically vote only when the regular GSR or DCM is absent. Proxy voting is used in some areas but is not a common practice.

quotes.text: Alternates for GSRs and DCMs typically vote only if the regular DCM or GSR is not present.

rules.summary: Each group should preferably have its own GSR. A GSR serving two groups still casts only one vote, so one group's voice may not be included.

quotes.text: a single individual is allowed only one vote in any decision

rules.summary: Each area decides its own quorum; some require a specific number of DCMs to be present. Alternate DCMs typically count toward quorum only when their DCM is absent.

quotes.text: Alternate DCMs are typically counted toward a quorum only when the DCM is not present.

rules.summary: Substantial unanimity, typically two-thirds or more and in some situations three-fourths or more, is used for controversial or complex issues and some elections. A simple majority, typically one-half of votes cast plus one, is used for simple or routine matters.

quotes.text: Substantial unanimity typically means a two-thirds (or more) majority.
Simple majority is typically defined as one-half of votes cast plus one.

rules.summary: An assembly makes its own rules, and the chair should make sure members know the manual's current suggested procedures. Any rule change should be made before a vote is taken or before an election is conducted.

quotes.text: If members want to make a change in the rules, it should be done before a vote is taken, or before an election is conducted.

rules.summary: Whenever practicable, committee members are elected by written ballot without personal nomination. Delegates are chosen from among those committee members by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot.

quotes.text: delegates are selected from among such committee members by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot

rules.summary: Unless the Conference directs otherwise, GSR, area committee member and delegate terms are concurrent and two years long. About half the areas hold assembly elections in even years and the rest in odd years, which creates the Conference's rotating panels.

quotes.text: Unless otherwise directed by the Conference, these terms of office shall all be concurrent and of two years’ duration each.
In approximately half the areas, assembly elections will be held in the even years; the remaining assemblies will elect in the odd years, thus creating rotating panels of the Conference

rules.summary: A delegate serves one term of two consecutive years, and a single term is strongly recommended. Rotation prevents delegates from succeeding themselves or returning later as delegate. An alternate who filled in at one Conference may still be elected to a full term.

quotes.text: It is strongly recommended that a delegate serve a single term.
the A.A. practice of rotation prevents delegates from succeeding themselves or from returning later as delegates

rules.topic: How a delegate votes at the Conference (Concept III)
rules.summary: Delegates are primarily world servants of A.A. as a whole, so on final decisions they may vote by their own best judgment and conscience. When they depart from what they know their area's conscience to be, they are asked to tell the area and explain why.

quotes.text: When delegates veer from what they know their area’s conscience to be, they are asked to report this to their area and the reasons why they voted as they did.

rules.summary: Some areas rotate the delegate between rural and urban sections or between parts of the area, to avoid domination by heavily populated places. Even so, a well-qualified member should not be passed over just for geographic rotation.

quotes.text: However, no well-qualified A.A. should be passed over in the interest of geographical rotation.

rules.summary: Every matter of policy (Advisory Action) needs a two-thirds majority, meaning two-thirds of members voting as long as the total vote is a quorum. Any actions, including amendments, that affect an Advisory Action also need two-thirds.

quotes.text: All matters of policy (Conference Advisory Actions) require substantial unanimity, that is, a two-thirds majority.

rules.summary: A quorum is two-thirds of registered members. By tradition, a two-thirds vote of members voting, provided the total vote is at least a quorum, binds the General Service Board and its related corporate services, but it ought not impair their legal right to conduct routine business and make ordinary contracts.

quotes.text: A quorum shall consist of two-thirds of all the Conference members registered.

rules.summary: By tradition, a three-quarters vote of all members participating in the vote can reorganize the General Service Board and the directors and staff members of its corporate services. The Conference may then request resignations, nominate new trustees, and make other necessary arrangements.

quotes.text: a three-quarters vote of all Conference members participating in the vote may bring about a reorganization of the General Service Board

rules.topic: Changing the Steps, Traditions or Article 12
rules.summary: No change to Charter Article 12, the Twelve Traditions or the Twelve Steps without the written consent of three-quarters of the A.A. groups. This applies to the original English version only.

quotes.text: no change in Article 12 of the Charter or in the Twelve Traditions of A.A. or in the Twelve Steps of A.A. may be made with less than the written consent of three-quarters of the A.A. groups

rules.topic: Approving the board's Charter and Bylaws
rules.summary: The General Service Board's Charter and Bylaws, and any amendments, are subject to approval by a two-thirds vote of all Conference members. Conference approval of the Bylaws is a matter of tradition, not a legal requirement.

quotes.text: The approval of the Bylaws by the Conference is a matter of tradition, rather than a legal requirement.

rules.summary: Each Conference member has one vote, even if they attend in more than one capacity.

quotes.text: Each Conference member has one vote, even if they attend in more than one capacity

rules.summary: After each policy vote, the side that did not prevail may speak. If the motion passed with two-thirds, the minority speaks; if it got a majority but fell short of two-thirds, the majority speaks. A member who voted with the prevailing side may then move to reconsider.

quotes.text: If the motion receives a majority vote but fails to pass for lack of a two-thirds vote, the majority may speak.

rules.summary: Any matter within a committee's scope ought first to go through that committee. The maker submits the floor action in writing to the Conference secretary and gets two minutes to state the rationale. The chair then asks for a motion to decline to consider it, which is made without comment, is not debatable, and needs two-thirds. If it is considered, it is debatable and needs two-thirds to pass. Floor actions on committee business not yet concluded are out of order.

quotes.text: Any floor action regarding a piece of committee business that has not yet been concluded will be considered out of order.

rules.summary: Committee assignments are determined by lot, typically each December, by the Conference coordinator and the chair of the trustees' Committee on the General Service Conference, to replace outgoing delegates. A delegate keeps the same committee for both years. Since December 2020 the draw uses a custom app; for Panel 73 the best of five rounds was kept (2023 Final Report, p. 64), and since 2025 it follows four prioritized criteria (2025 Final Report, p. 47).

quotes.text: This selection is typically held in December of each year

rules.summary: Chairs and alternate chairs are elected by plurality at the committee's last meeting of Conference week. They take office as soon as the Conference ends and serve through the end of the next year's Conference. In practice they are always first-year members, so they chair in their second year. The manual has them attend the January board weekend (p. 45); from 2026 they attend the October/November weekend instead (2026 Final Report, p. 49).

quotes.text: Committee chairs and alternate chairs are elected by plurality at the committee’s last meeting during Conference week.

rules.summary: Agreed to at the beginning of each Conference: speakers line up at the microphones and address the chair, each gets two minutes, and no one speaks a second time on a topic until all who wish to have spoken once.

quotes.text: No one may speak for a second time on a topic until all who wish to have spoken for the first time.

rules.summary: Committee recommendations arrive as motions already made and seconded; they are debatable and need two-thirds. Members are asked to refrain from spontaneously amending them (any amendment needs a second and two-thirds). Once on the floor, a motion is owned by the entire Conference, no longer by the committee.

quotes.text: Recommendations of Conference committees are automatically motions that have been made and seconded.

rules.summary: Considerations are not actionable. After the Conference deliberates on a committee's recommendations, members may ask questions about the considerations, without comment or debate.

quotes.text: Committee considerations are not actionable and, therefore, not subject to debate.

rules.summary: Only a member who voted with the prevailing side may move to reconsider; it may be seconded by anyone. It is not debatable and passes by simple majority, after which full debate resumes. No action may be reconsidered twice.

quotes.text: A motion to reconsider a vote may be made only by a member who voted with the prevailing side

rules.summary: No one becomes a trustee until all Conference delegates have been polled, by mail or at the Conference. The proposed slate becomes final unless a majority of Conference members disapproves any or all trustees on it. If delegates disapprove, the person cannot be elected unless the member trustees present vote for them 100%; otherwise a majority of member trustees elects at the meeting of members.

quotes.text: this becomes the final slate unless a majority of the Conference members votes to disapprove
unless there is a 100% vote of member trustees present at a meeting of members to the contrary

rules.summary: The Board can remove a trustee for cause by a vote of at least 3/4 of the total board. The trustees acting as members can remove one with or without cause by 3/4 of the entire membership, if removal is in A.A.'s best interests as a whole. Trustees are expected to resign if the Conference asks, even mid-term.

quotes.text: by a vote of at least 3⁄4 of the total Board of Trustees, may remove a member trustee for cause

rules.summary: Except for regional trustee seats, the board may fill a vacancy at any regular or special meeting, or leave it open until the next annual meeting. A board-elected replacement serves until the next annual meeting. For Class A trustees, time served this way between annual meetings does not count toward total service.

quotes.text: shall not count in determining a Class A trustee’s total term of service

rules.summary: If the vacancy occurs before September 1 of the first year, the region nominates at the next Conference and the replacement may serve at most three consecutive one-year terms. If it occurs between September 1 of year one and August 31 of year three, the region's delegates may nominate a replacement (who may serve no more than 'five or six one-year terms, as the case may be') or leave the seat vacant. If it stays unfilled for the rest of the term, the trustee-at-large or the regional trustee from an adjacent region may cover the region. A replacement who is elected is expected to serve two years on an affiliate corporate board.

quotes.text: if a vacancy for a Regional Trustee occurs prior to September 1 in the first year

rules.summary: A trustee who reaches the term limit while serving as, or newly elected as, chair stays a trustee for the chair's term. This can raise Class A to 8, Class B to 15 and the board to 22. Their trusteeship ends the day the chair term ends.

quotes.text: even if such service during his or her term as chair will expand the number of Class B member trustees then serving to fifteen (15)

rules.summary: An area's delegate sends the candidate's name and contact information to GSO's Nominating desk, and the résumé must be in by January 1. Late résumés are returned and not considered, and an area whose nominee withdraws after the deadline may not substitute another. Prior Conferences have recommended that no area submit the same person for both regional trustee and trustee-at-large at the same Conference.

quotes.text: If an area’s nominee withdraws after the deadline, the area may not submit another.

rules.summary: A past delegate may stand for trustee one year after their last Conference (p. 63), and may become an ACM one year after rotation (p. 61). The same one-year wait applies to applying as a nontrustee director of AAWS or Grapevine (2021 Final Report, p. 49).

quotes.text: An area delegate may stand for a trustee position one year after their last Conference.

rules.summary: The 2nd quarterly meeting is held the Saturday right after the Conference closes; it pauses for the annual meeting of members, which elects trustees. The 1st, 3rd and 4th quarterly meetings fall on the fifth Monday after a calendar quarter ends. One-third of the Board or the chair may call special meetings. The chair may postpone a regular meeting (but not later than one month before the next scheduled one), and a majority of the Board may eliminate regular meetings. Meetings are held in New York City unless the board decides otherwise.

quotes.text: shall take place on the fifth Monday following the close of a calendar quarter

rules.summary: Meetings need 10 to 50 days' notice. Quorum is two-fifths of member trustees, and a majority of those present decides.

quotes.text: two-fifths of the member trustees shall be sufficient to constitute a quorum

rules.topic: Mail vote of Conference members on matters of principle
rules.summary: If one-third of the trustees present judge a decision to involve principle or basic policy, and at least one-third of the trustees judge that a delay will not harm the Fellowship, the matter goes to a mail vote of all Conference members (the bylaws call them “Conference delegates”, p. 135) with at least two weeks' notice. If a majority votes against, the board is expected to refrain.

quotes.text: the matter shall be submitted to a mail vote of Conference delegates

rules.summary: By law no committee may: submit to members any action that needs members' approval; fill vacancies on the board or any committee; fix directors' compensation for board or committee service; amend or repeal the bylaws or adopt new ones; or amend or repeal a board resolution that says it cannot be.

quotes.text: The law provides that no committee shall be empowered to act on the following

rules.summary: Amendments need a 75% vote of all trustees. The board is expected, though not legally required, to submit amendments to Conference delegates and to hold back if a majority disapproves, unless the law requires the change. If delegates do not disapprove a bylaw amendment, a majority of trustees present is enough.

quotes.text: may be amended by the affirmative vote of 75% of all the members of the Board of Trustees

rules.summary: The GSB may create new corporations only if it owns all their capital stock, and it is expected not to form one if a majority of Conference delegates disapproves.

quotes.text: the General Service Board is expected to refrain from forming any new corporate body if a majority of the Conference delegates shall disapprove

rules.topic: Custodial oversight of the operating corporations
rules.summary: The GSB does not interfere with the daily operation of AAWS or Grapevine. It oversees them by electing their directors, approving their budgets and holding authority over their bylaws. The trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee reviews both corporations' budgets before recommending them to the GSB.

quotes.text: The General Service Board has custodial oversight over both of these corporations, which it exercises by electing the directors of each.

rules.summary: Directors serve one-year terms and are elected by majority ballot of the Members (the GSB trustees) at the Annual Meeting. That meeting is held the day after the scheduled close of the Conference.

quotes.text: The Directors shall be elected for a term of one year, at the Annual Meeting of the Members

rules.summary: At least four directors on each corporate board must be trustees, and at least two of those must be Class B. The AAWS board has nine directors. Grapevine's may have 7 to 10, currently nine.

quotes.text: At least four Directors shall be Members of the Corporation, at least two of whom shall be Class B Trustees of the General Service Board

rules.summary: Anyone who is not a trustee (other than the AAWS President or the Grapevine Publisher) may be elected to at most four consecutive full one-year terms as a director, then becomes ineligible for further service as a director.

quotes.text: No person who is not a Member of the Corporation … shall be elected to more than four consecutive full terms as a Director

rules.summary: Vacancies are announced through Box 4-5-9 and mailings. The corporate nominating committee, working with the trustees' Nominating Committee, reviews résumés and interviews candidates. The full corporate board gives the nominee a final interview. The name then goes to the trustees' Nominating Committee for approval by the GSB and is placed on the corporate slate presented to the Conference.

quotes.text: Qualified candidates are interviewed by the corporate board’s nominating committee.

rules.summary: The board can remove a director for cause by a 3/4 vote of the entire board. The Members can remove a director with or without cause by a 3/4 vote of the entire Membership.

quotes.text: the Members of the Corporation, by similar 3/4 vote of the entire Membership, may remove a Director with or without cause.

rules.topic: Chair must not be an employee
rules.summary: The board elects its Chair and President each year from among its own directors. No employee of the corporation may serve as Chair.

quotes.text: No employee of the Corporation may serve as the Chair.

rules.summary: A quorum is a majority of the entire board, with at least one trustee-member present. The Chair must call a special meeting when at least one-fifth of the entire board demands it in writing.

quotes.text: a majority of the entire Board of Directors (provided that at least one of the directors present is a Member of the Corporation)

rules.summary: Only the Members (trustees) can amend the bylaws, by a two-thirds vote, and the meeting notice must include the proposed amendment. The board of directors has no authority to change the bylaws.

quotes.text: The Board of Directors shall not have the authority to alter, amend or repeal the Bylaws.

rules.summary: Each corporation prepares a budget before its fiscal year (January 1 to December 31) begins. The budget goes to the first GSB trustees' meeting after January 1 for approval.

quotes.text: submit such budget for approval at the first meeting of the Trustees of the General Service Board held after January 1

rules.summary: The Reserve Fund is capped at one year of combined operating expenses. Withdrawals need GSB approval on the recommendation of the Finance and Budgetary Committee. If the fund exceeds 12 months, there is one year to review the level and a second year to formulate actions to bring it back under the limit.

quotes.text: The board of trustees, on recommendation of the trustees’ Finance and Budgetary Committee, is responsible for authorizing withdrawals from the Reserve Fund.

rules.summary: The GSB accepts money only from A.A. members, groups and A.A. entities. Individuals may give up to $7,500 a year, not earmarked. A member's estate may leave one bequest of up to $12,500. Groups have no limit.

quotes.text: The General Service Conference limits contributions by an individual member to $7,500 USD per year, which cannot be earmarked for any specific purpose

rules.summary: A manuscript must first be recommended by the appropriate Conference committee. It then needs a two-thirds vote of Conference members to be called Conference-approved.

quotes.text: If two-thirds of Conference members agree to the manuscript as presented or with specific edits approved by the body

rules.summary: The Conference reviews proposed Grapevine and La Viña book topics and Grapevine policies, but not magazine content before publication. The Conference Charter preserves the editor's right to accept or reject material. So individual Grapevine and La Viña issues are not Conference-approved: a 1986 Advisory Action instead recognized AA Grapevine as A.A.'s international journal, and the recognition extends to La Viña (p. 86).

quotes.text: The Conference does not review material in advance of publication in the Grapevine or La Viña magazines
Since each issue of the Grapevine cannot go through the Conference-approval process, the Conference recognizes AA Grapevine as the international journal of Alcoholics Anonymous.
nothing herein shall compromise the Grapevine editor’s right to accept or reject material for publication

rules.summary: Most GSO staff members change desk assignments every two years. The rotation period was one year until an AAWS board discussion in March 1965. All staff are paid on the same basis, with raises based only on time served.

quotes.text: GSO Staff assignment changed from a one-year term to a two-year term per discussion by the AAWS Board in March 1965.

rules.summary: First the area committee informs GSRs of the pros and cons. A simple majority of GSRs (one-half plus one) must be present or answer a mail poll, and two-thirds of them must agree. The delegate notifies GSO, which provides a form for the delegate to confirm the conditions were met. On behalf of the assembly, the delegate writes to the secretary of the trustees' Nominating Committee with the form and copies the trustees in both regions. GSO then writes to every area delegate in the two regions, who get their areas' group conscience and return an approval/disapproval card. Two-thirds of the delegates from each region must approve before the Conference acts, and the change takes effect at the end of that Conference.

quotes.text: A simple majority (one-half plus one) of GSRs should be present (or respond to a mail poll).
Two-thirds of the majority present or responding should agree before an area petitions for a change of region.
A change of region will become effective at the end of the Conference, at which it may be approved.

rules.summary: The area committee(s) ask GSO for the four-page application for an additional delegate area. It asks about assemblies, the alternate delegate, district meetings, active DCMs and GSRs, and five years of yearly growth figures. Proposals accepted for the agenda go to the appropriate Conference committee; the Policy/Admissions Committee reviews requests for additional delegate areas before the full Conference considers them.

quotes.text: the area committee or Committees involved may write to GSO and request an application for an additional delegate area.
Review proposals for changes to, and expansions of, the Conference including requests for the creation of additional delegate areas

rules.summary: A district that has grown too large for one DCM can (1) split into new districts, each with its own DCM; (2) form subdistricts, each electing a local committee member; or (3) become a large district led by a DCMC, with subdistricts or zones each served by a DCM. A DCM's qualifications and election methods serve as the guideline for any new committee members.

quotes.text: New Districts: Divide the district into two or more districts, each with its own DCM.
When additional committee members are elected to respond to expansion, qualifications and election methods listed for a DCM can serve as guidelines.

rules.summary: Each service entity decides what makes a GSR, DCM or other servant 'inactive'. An alternate may be able to help. If the servant clearly can't carry out the position, experience suggests asking them to resign, and the entity then elects someone new.

quotes.text: Experience in the Fellowship suggests that the trusted servant be asked to resign if it appears they are unable to carry out the responsibilities of the position.

rules.topic: Stepping aside when a term ends
rules.summary: GSRs and DCMs are encouraged not to stay on, or take another two-year term, just because no successor has come forward. The Traditions and Concepts encourage rotation even if the position goes unfilled for a while; the outgoing servant can look for a different service role.

quotes.text: The Traditions and Concepts encourage rotation of service, even when it appears the position will be left unfilled.
the Traditions and the Concepts encourage rotation of service. When our terms are up, we step aside.

rules.summary: Delegates serve once: they cannot succeed themselves or come back later as delegates. Past delegates are usually asked not to serve as GSRs or DCMs. They may stand for trustee one year after their last Conference and are eligible as ACMs one year after rotation. The wait also applies to nontrustee director applications (2021 Final Report, p. 49).

quotes.text: the A.A. practice of rotation prevents delegates from succeeding themselves or from returning later as delegates
An area delegate may stand for a trustee position one year after their last Conference.

rules.topic: Changing the Traditions or the Article 12 Warranties
rules.summary: The Conference can amend the first eleven Articles of its Charter itself. The Twelve Traditions and the Warranties of Article 12 (Concept XII) are different: under the 1955 Resolution, the registered groups must be notified and given at least six months, and at least three-quarters of the groups that respond must consent in writing. The Concept XII essay describes this as three-quarters of the directory-listed groups that vote.

quotes.text: would require the written consent of three-quarters of all the directory-listed A.A. groups who would actually vote on any such proposals
shall be allowed no less than six months for consideration thereof.

rules.summary: Substantial unanimity usually means two-thirds or more (sometimes three-fourths) and is used for controversial or complex matters and some elections. A simple majority is one-half of the votes cast plus one and is used for routine matters.

quotes.text: Substantial unanimity typically means a two-thirds (or more) majority.
Simple majority is typically defined as one-half of votes cast plus one.

rules.summary: The more responsible the job, the longer the term needs to be. A group secretary can change every six months and an intergroup committeeman every year, but a delegate needs two years and a trustee four.

quotes.text: a Delegate has to serve two years, and a Trustee must serve four.

rules.topic: Paid staff cannot be trustees (Concept IV)
rules.summary: Concept IV makes one exception to participation: paid staff cannot become trustees, because it would interfere with the trustees' four-year rotation and could create a vested interest. Staff are still invited to the board's quarterly meetings, where they can take part in debate but cannot vote.

quotes.text: Members holding paid staff positions cannot become Trustees. This cannot be permitted because such a practice would interfere with the four-year rotation of the A.A. Trustees.

rules.summary: GSO staff members rotate among assignments and are paid on the same basis; Bill W. gives the security and continuity of the office as the main reason. Assignments first changed every year. AAWS, with the board's approval, moved most staff to two-year rotations; the change came from an AAWS Board discussion in March 1965.

quotes.text: AAWS, Inc., with the approval of the General Service Board, has implemented a two-year rotation of assignments for most Staff members.

rules.summary: In Bill W.'s original plan, a two-thirds Conference vote could give the trustees flat directions, and a simple majority was a strong suggestion. Today Advisory Actions are, by tradition, treated as binding on the General Service Board.

quotes.text: the delegates could issue flat directions to the trustees on a two-thirds vote.
Advisory Actions are, by tradition, considered binding on the General Service Board.

rules.summary: An A.A. website is a public medium, so members' anonymity is protected there just as in press, radio and film. Some areas add password-protected, members-only sections where full names may be used. Where an intergroup/central office already lists meetings, area sites may link to it instead of duplicating it, and a committee rather than one or two people should run the site.

quotes.text: An A.A. website is a public medium, which has the potential for reaching the broadest possible audience
requires the same safeguards that we use at the level of press, radio and film.

rules.summary: A delegate has three kinds of expense: attending the Conference, reporting back, and serving the area for the rest of the term. For the Conference, the area contributes and the GSB General Fund pays the balance. Each delegate gets a cash advance on arrival in New York, and areas typically add some money for extras. Each area is also asked to send at least $3,000 USD to the GSB toward the annual Conference meeting, but no delegate is kept away because the area cannot afford the full amount. Areas are asked to pay report-back travel, and many set an annual travel budget so the delegate can accept invitations without waiting for assembly approval.

quotes.text: Many areas establish annual travel budgets that allow the delegate some flexibility to decide on which invitations and events to accept
no delegate will be denied attendance at the Conference if their area cannot afford the full amount.

rules.topic: The board's freedom of action and its duty to consult the Conference (Charter Art. 10)
rules.summary: The Conference has final authority, but it is not incorporated and does not run A.A.'s business. Under the Charter the General Service Board has entire freedom of action in the routine conduct of the policy and business affairs of the service corporations, except for decisions on policy, finance or A.A. Tradition that could seriously affect A.A. as a whole. Except in a great emergency, neither the board nor its service corporations should take an action likely to greatly affect A.A. as a whole without first consulting the Conference, though the board decides which of its actions need Conference approval. AAWS and AA Grapevine are separate not-for-profit corporations whose own boards handle their routine affairs. Concept VII says the arrangement gives the Conference final authority while legally protecting the trustees' right to act freely.

quotes.text: the General Service Board has entire freedom of action in the routine conduct of the policy and business affairs of the A.A. service corporations
ought ever take any action liable to greatly affect A.A. as a whole, without first consulting the Conference.
the board shall at all times reserve the right to decide which of its actions or decisions may require the approval of the Conference.

rules.topic: Reprinting Grapevine and La Viña material (Appendix N)
rules.summary: Permission to reproduce Grapevine or La Viña articles or other material, in print or online (such as web pages), must come from AA Grapevine, Inc.; requests go by email to its licensing desk. Each article or item is reprinted whole, with the credit line 'Copyright © (Month, Year) AA Grapevine, Inc. Reprinted with permission.' Publications, organizations or websites outside A.A. must also state that the permission does not imply affiliation with or endorsement by A.A. or AA Grapevine, Inc. AA Grapevine does not give permission to reproduce its logo, registered trademarks, artwork or cartoons on any other website or publication.

quotes.text: Each article or item must be reprinted in its entirety

rules.summary: As a general rule, no one may reproduce Conference-approved literature without AAWS's prior written permission. Experience says that A.A. groups and entities, and only they, may reproduce limited amounts of it, and the material may never be amended or modified. After a quotation from a book or pamphlet, the credit line reads: Reprinted from (name of publication, page number), with permission of Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc. (What local newsletters may quote without asking first is on p. 23.)

quotes.text: A.A. groups and entities, and only A.A. groups and entities, should have the authority to reproduce limited amounts of A.A. Conference-approved material.
In no case should this material be amended or modified.

rules.summary: Local A.A. newsletters, bulletins and websites may reprint the Steps, Traditions and Concepts and quote a phrase, sentence or brief paragraph from A.A. literature without asking first, but they should include the proper credit line so A.A.'s copyrights stay protected. The Preamble is copyrighted by AA Grapevine and takes the Grapevine credit line, as do reprinted Grapevine and La Viña articles. Groups and districts may use the circle and triangle symbol without AAWS permission.

quotes.text: Reprinted from (name of publication, page number), with permission of Alcoholics Anonymous World Services, Inc.
The A.A. Preamble is copyrighted by AA Grapevine.
no permission from AAWS is needed to use this symbol.

rules.topic: The board, the Steps and the Traditions
rules.summary: The General Service Board claims no ownership of the Twelve Steps, but claims the right to stop any change to them unless the Fellowship asks for it under the Conference Charter. The Fellowship regards the board as custodian of the Twelve Traditions, so it may not change them, or let others change them, except as the Charter provides. The board is also guided by the spirit of the Twelve Concepts.

quotes.text: claims no proprietary right in the recovery program
it is regarded by the Fellowship of Alcoholics Anonymous as the custodian of these Traditions

rules.topic: Annual audit of AAWS and Grapevine
rules.summary: Each year the AAWS board (or one of its committees) retains or renews an independent auditor and reviews the audit plan before work starts. Afterwards it goes over any internal-control weaknesses, limits on the auditor's access, disagreements with management and the soundness of financial reporting, and it weighs the auditor's performance and independence. The Grapevine board appoints an auditor each year, who reports to it in writing.

quotes.text: shall annually retain or renew the retention of an independent auditor to conduct the audit
The Board of Directors shall annually appoint an auditor

rules.topic: Who can bind AAWS or Grapevine
rules.summary: Only the board can authorize an officer or agent to sign contracts or pledge the corporation's credit, either in general or case by case; without that, no officer, agent or employee can bind the corporation. Even the President needs the board's specific authority for any bond, mortgage or contract. At AAWS, committees of the corporation cannot bind it either.

quotes.text: no bond, mortgage or contract shall be executed without the specific authority of the Board of Directors

rules.topic: The trustees' veto and the budget (Concept VII)
rules.summary: The board legally reserves a veto over any Conference action but seldom uses it. Concept VII names three cases: an action that clearly violates the Conference's or the board's charter, or is reckless enough to seriously harm A.A., when the Conference refuses to reconsider (the trustees may then appeal to the groups); reducing the Conference budget during a fiscal year; and cancelling a plan that unforeseen conditions have made unworkable. The trustees should never substantially exceed an approved budget without consulting the Conference.

quotes.text: our Board of Trustees does reserve a veto power over any Conference action
they should feel entirely free to reduce the Conference budget figure during any fiscal year

rules.topic: Voting on one's own performance (Concept IV)
rules.summary: Trustees, corporate directors and staff are voting Conference members, but by tradition they do not vote on reports of their own past activities. Bill W. also lists job qualifications, pay, and a sweeping reorganization of the board caused by its own misfunction as cases where their vote may be withheld. None of this ever bars the trustees from voting on structural changes.

quotes.text: Trustees and service workers alike should refrain from voting on reports on their own past activities.

rules.topic: Who decides what goes up (Concept III)
rules.summary: The Conference decides which matters it settles itself and which it refers to the groups (usually through committee members or GSRs). The trustees decide when to act on their own and when to ask the Conference. The corporations, committees, staff and executives decide when to act and when to refer to the next higher authority. The right never excuses missing reports, exceeding defined authority, or failing to consult those entitled to be consulted.

quotes.text: the Conference always should be able to decide which matters it will fully dispose of on its own responsibility
This “Right of Decision” should never be made an excuse for failure to render proper reports of all significant actions taken

rules.topic: Minority reports and personal grievances (Concept V)
rules.summary: Any minority in a staff, committee, corporate board or among the trustees is encouraged to file a minority report when it thinks the majority is badly wrong, and should bring one to the Conference when the issue is grave for A.A. as a whole. Any worker, paid or unpaid, may take a personal grievance directly to the General Service Board without fear of reprisal.

quotes.text: it should then charge itself with the actual duty of presenting a minority report to the Conference.
He or she should be able to do this without prejudice or fear of reprisal.

rules.summary: Final authority runs down the structure: groups, Conference delegates, trustees, corporate directors, executives, staff. It is held in reserve and used in full only in an emergency, when delegated authority has gone wrong or keeps overstepping. Proper uses: groups elect better delegates or withhold funds; delegates censure or reorganize the trustees; trustees do the same with the corporations; a corporation replaces executives or staff. Otherwise, people with delegated authority are left to do their jobs.

quotes.text: Indeed ultimate authority should practically never be used in full, except in an emergency.
If the Delegates must, they can censure or reorganize the Trustees.

rules.topic: Agreeing in advance on the majority needed (Warranty Four)
rules.summary: Important decisions are debated, time permitting, until a heavy majority supports them. By simple majority, the Conference may agree in advance whether a particular question needs two-thirds, three-quarters or an even greater majority. In a real emergency a majority (even a bare one) may decide to end debate and act, and it must override a small minority that obstinately misuses substantial unanimity to block clearly needed action. (This is Bill W.'s principle in the Concept XII essay; under today's rules of debate, calling the question needs two-thirds, p. 175.)

quotes.text: whether a two-thirds, three-quarters, or even a greater majority, will be required to settle a particular question.
Such an advance agreement can, of course, be had on a simple majority vote.

rules.topic: No punishment, no public controversy (Warranty Five)
rules.summary: The Conference never punishes anyone and never enters public controversy, even in self-defense. Public attacks: usually silence at the public level; if critics are misinformed, a private, temperate, purely informative note, often through friends; if criticism is justified, private thanks. Tradition violations: tell the violator privately, persist with persuasion, and rely on A.A. opinion, public opinion and education, never lawsuits. Internal disputes: offer mediation and keep them out of public view; purely local gray areas are left to local members.

quotes.text: our best defense in these situations would be no defense whatever — namely, complete silence at the public level.
Privately, however, we can inform Tradition-violators that they are out of order.

rules.summary: A.A. shares its principles with anyone but asks that its name not be used publicly by others. If the name is misused, the Conference presses for the practice to stop, without public quarreling. Early Conferences decided not to incorporate the name or seek the power to sue, since a lawsuit is a public controversy; the name and the abbreviation A.A. were legally registered in 1972.

quotes.text: always short, however, of public quarreling about the matter.
Those early Conferences believed that the power to sue would be a dangerous thing for us to possess.

rules.topic: Paid workers: pay, tenure and participation (Concept XI)
rules.summary: Paid executives, staff and consultants are paid in reasonable relation to similar work in the commercial world. GSO staff are paid on the same basis, with raises for time served only, and rotate among assignments. There is no fixed term of employment. Key paid workers vote on committees and corporate boards and are treated as friends and teammates; their need for the paycheck must never be used as a lever, though those who cannot or will not do the job may be let go.

quotes.text: recompensed in reasonable relation to the value of his or her similar services or abilities in the commercial world.
In the World Service Office we have found it impractical and unfair to set any fixed term of employment.

rules.summary: An active service needs one executive with ample freedom and authority, supported by assistants; boards and committees advise but do not manage. Under the Right of Decision the executive judges when to act alone and when to consult, and can be censured after acting but seldom before. None of the board's committees is executive: they recommend to the corporations or the trustees.

quotes.text: A board or a committee can never actively manage anything, in the continuous executive sense.
He can always be censured after his acts, but seldom before.

rules.topic: Listing a new group with GSO
rules.summary: GSO lists groups, not meetings. A group sends the New Group Form (F-30) to GSO or through its area registrar, usually after meeting for a month or two. Once its information is logged, a 30-day pending period (1990 Advisory Action) gives the delegate and DCM time to welcome it. A listing is not an endorsement, and GSO neither monitors nor oversees any group. The Traditions suggest a group not be named after a facility or a person, and that its name imply no outside affiliation.

quotes.text: Each new group is subject to a 30-day pending period according to a 1990 Conference advisory action.
The GSO neither monitors nor oversees the activities or practice of any A.A. group.

rules.summary: The GSR works with the group treasurer on Seventh Tradition support for the General Service Board, the area, the district and the local intergroup/central office. The pamphlet F-3 suggests how to share contributions among them, but groups may vary the suggestions or not contribute at all, and each group decides by group conscience how much goes to each entity; many areas also suggest a formula, and many groups use the Regular Contribution Plan and the Birthday Plan. Members often say they are 'contributing to GSO', but what GSO receives is treated as meant for the General Service Board, which is responsible for all Seventh Tradition contributions. Because each service entity is autonomous, GSO does not pass shares on to areas, districts or intergroups, and a contribution sent with a request to distribute it is returned, so the group sends each entity its own contribution. Memorial gifts follow the same rules: they come only from A.A. members or groups, and a gift from an individual member is subject to the $7,500 limit.

quotes.text: Groups may veer from these suggestions as they see fit, or not contribute at all.
contributions that come to GSO are assumed to be for the GSB
Groups will want to decide through group conscience how much and to what entities contributions are to be made individually.

rules.topic: Using A.A. trademarks, logos and copyrighted material
rules.summary: AAWS and AA Grapevine have registered A.A.'s trademarks, logos and copyrights, which are held for the benefit of A.A. as a whole. Using the marks on goods or services that do not come from A.A. and were not approved by A.A. infringes and dilutes them. Before using A.A. logos, photographs or copyrighted material, even for an A.A. event flyer or website, ask GSO and the AAWS intellectual property administrator first. GSO usually asks for a copy of the planned item and answers within a few days. AAWS does not grant permission for novelty items, and any Internet posting of any Big Book edition needs AAWS permission (p. 69). AA Grapevine does not grant permission to reproduce its logo, trademarks, artwork or cartoons on other websites or publications (p. 85).

quotes.text: both infringes upon and dilutes A.A. marks, in legal terms
AAWS holds the copyrights of A.A. material in trust for A.A. as a whole.
You’ll typically have your answer in a few days.

rules.topic: Actions affecting A.A. as a whole (Tradition Four, long form)
rules.summary: A group answers only to its own conscience in its own affairs. It should consult neighbouring groups when its plans affect them. No group, regional committee or individual should take action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without first conferring with the General Service Board trustees.

quotes.text: no group, regional committee, or individual should ever take any action that might greatly affect A.A. as a whole without conferring with the trustees

rules.topic: Paid service workers vs. professionalism (Tradition Eight)
rules.summary: A.A. stays nonprofessional, but its service centers may employ special workers. The long form defines professionalism as counseling alcoholics for fees or hire. Alcoholics may be well paid for services A.A. would otherwise hire nonalcoholics to do, but Twelfth Step work is never paid.

quotes.text: We define professionalism as the occupation of counseling alcoholics for fees or hire.
But our usual A.A. Twelfth Step work is never to be paid for.

rules.summary: Most areas welcome any A.A. member to attend assemblies, in the spirit of Concept IV's right of participation, but only voting members vote. Whether a visitor may speak at the microphone is up to each area. The member's home-group GSR already gives them a voice, and some areas have guidelines, mindful of Concept V and minority opinion, that let the request be heard while the meeting gets through its agenda.

quotes.text: We wish to be just as inclusive as we can, never exclusive.
Each area is autonomous in how they handle such situations.

rules.topic: Linking aa.org material on local websites
rules.summary: When a local A.A. website, such as an intergroup's, offers material from aa.org, it should link to the item on aa.org instead of downloading and reposting the PDF, so visitors always get the latest version. Many intergroup sites also offer online chat, material in local languages and an ADA-accessible format.

quotes.text: When adding materials from aa.org to local websites be sure to use the weblinks instead of downloading PDFs.

cycle.what: The General Service Conference meets in New York. The Conference meets for only six days a year, but its members are active in Conference affairs all year.
A GSR may make an impassioned plea about an agenda item to the delegate on the eve of the annual General Service Conference meeting.

Each delegate reports back to the area on the proceedings, the Advisory Actions and the committee considerations. GSRs, after hearing the delegate and asking questions, inform their groups. DCMs may organize or deliver report-backs to their districts (p. 16).
The trustees review the Conference Advisory Actions, refer them to trustees' committees, GSO or AA Grapevine to carry out, and report progress in their quarterly reports.
GSO publishes the Box 4-5-9 newsletter and the General Service Board publishes its Quarterly Report. Both are good sources for GSR reports.
GSR and DCM terms (and usually alternate terms) turn over. In many areas they line up with the area delegate's panel.

cycle.when: Between election and start of term
cycle.what: There are often weeks between a GSR's election and the start of the term, a good time to study the manual. The outgoing DCM typically briefs the incoming DCM before the new term begins (p. 17).
The new DCM prepares the first district meeting and discusses a travel-expense budget with the district before spending anything.
Conference committee assignments drawn by lot to replace outgoing delegates

Each Conference committee is encouraged to hold a conference call with its staff secretary and the chair of its trustees' committee to give delegates a further voice in agenda selection and review housekeeping details
Conference committee chairs attend a General Service Board weekend in New York: the end of January per the manual (p. 45); from 2026 the October/November (Q4) weekend (2026 Final Report, p. 49)
Background material on all agenda items is sent to committee members in English, French and Spanish at once (p. 45; February 17-20, 2026: 2026 Final Report, p. 83)
A delegates-only meeting is often held (outside the Conference itself)
The annual General Service Conference meeting, lasting a full week
Conference committees hold information-only joint meetings with their trustees' committees and meet twice early in the week

cycle.when: Committee's last meeting of Conference week
cycle.what: Committee chairs and alternate chairs elected by plurality; they take office when the Conference ends

cycle.when: Last two days (or more) of Conference week
cycle.what: Full Conference discusses and votes on committee recommendations

cycle.when: Saturday after the last business day
cycle.what: Closing breakfast; rotating trustees say farewell
The General Service Board votes to affirm the Advisory Actions, which then go to trustees' committees, GSO or the corporate boards for implementation
Final Conference Report provided through area delegates in print (English, French, Spanish); also online as an anonymity-protected file
Area assemblies elect delegates; about half the areas elect in even years and the rest in odd years (rotating panels)
World Service Meeting of delegates from the various Conferences
Deadline for regional trustee candidate résumés (electronic or postmarked).
Conference committee chairs attend the GSB weekend and their trustees' committee meeting (p. 63); October/November from 2026 (2026 Final Report, p. 49).

The week-long General Service Conference in New York. Nominating sessions select regional trustee and trustee-at-large nominees, and the trustee and officer slates are presented for disapproval, if any.
Most Conference committees meet jointly with their corresponding trustees' committees.
2nd quarterly board meeting: it pauses for the annual meeting of members, which elects trustees and receives the annual report. The Board also elects its officers here.
GSO mailing tells delegates and area officers in regions due to select a regional trustee candidate. An issue of Box 4-5-9 also tells the region's groups (the manual does not say which issue).

cycle.when: 3rd quarterly board meeting (fifth Monday after June 30, so late July or early August)
cycle.what: The Board approves the chair's appointments of trustees' committee members.
Cutoff date that decides how a regional trustee vacancy is filled.
Trustees' committees meet, and the board holds a General Sharing Session (p. 61; the Concepts footnote says three times a year, C-36).
The Audit Committee meets the independent auditor and recommends one; the Compensation Committee meets with consultants.
The GSB fiscal year; the annual report for it is presented at the annual meeting of members.
World Service Meeting every two years; REDELA (Meeting of the Americas) in the other years.
2026: Eastern Canada and Pacific; 2027: Northeast and Southwest; 2028: Western Canada and West Central; 2029: Southeast and East Central; then repeating every four years.

cycle.when: Day after the General Service Conference closes (the Conference is usually in April)
cycle.what: Annual Meeting of the Members (trustees) of AAWS and AA Grapevine: directors are elected for one-year terms

cycle.when: Immediately after the annual election of directors
cycle.what: Newly elected corporate boards organize and elect officers (Chair, President, etc.)

cycle.when: Week before each quarterly GSB meeting
cycle.what: Regular meeting of the AAWS board and of the Grapevine board

cycle.when: First GSB trustees' meeting after January 1
cycle.what: AAWS and Grapevine budgets submitted for approval
Fiscal year of AAWS and AA Grapevine, Inc.

cycle.when: At least four times a year
cycle.what: AAWS board meets

cycle.when: Quarterly, plus four planning meetings a year
cycle.what: Grapevine board meets as a board and as a planning committee of the whole
AAWS Finance committee recommends an independent auditor to the GSB
Most GSO staff rotate to a new desk assignment

cycle.when: Generally four per year (each region every two years)
cycle.what: Regional Forums
World Service Meeting (coordinated by the International desk)
International Convention (about 50,000 members from about 80 countries)
Updates to The A.A. Service Manual/Twelve Concepts for World Service, per Conference approval
Public Information desk sends the Anonymity Letter to the media
Operations supervises group record updates; Group Services coordinates the service kit list update
Grapevine and La Viña Workbooks updated

cycle.when: Up to five times a year
cycle.what: Grapevine and La Viña Editorial Advisory Boards meet virtually
Box 4-5-9 newsletter published
About A.A. bulletin for professionals published
LIM bulletin and La Viña magazine published
Sharing from Behind the Walls published
Birthday Plan contribution to the GSB
Open A.A. meeting at GSO in New York
The General Service Conference meets in New York for six days. The first was held in April 1951.
The area assembly elects a delegate and area committee officers.
In approximately half the areas, assembly elections are held in even years and in the rest in odd years. This creates the rotating panels, originally called Panels One and Two.
One panel of delegates is elected and one retires, so the Conference rotates but keeps continuity.

cycle.when: Every two years, in each region
cycle.what: A Regional Forum (a weekend of sharing and information) is held.
Most GSO staff members move to a new assignment.
An approved change of region takes effect.

cycle.when: Saturday after the last day of Conference business
cycle.what: Closing breakfast, where rotating trustees say their farewells.

cycle.when: One year after a delegate's last Conference
cycle.what: A past delegate can stand for trustee; past delegates are also eligible as appointed committee members one year after rotation.
GSO publishes the Box 4-5-9 newsletter.
AA Grapevine publishes La Viña, and the Loners-Internationalists Meeting (LIM) bulletin goes out.
Deadline for proposed agenda items for next year's Conference; later items go to the following year (2025 Final Report, p. 85).
October feedback call before the November board weekend (2025 Final Report, p. 84).

cycle.when: After a new area committee is elected
cycle.what: The outgoing delegate sends GSO contact information for all incoming area officers and committee chairs. It goes into GSO's database, which the area registrar can also use.

Regional meetings of past and current delegates and their alternates, some lasting a full weekend, mainly to help new delegates prepare for the Conference. (In this app's calendar, the Southwest's is SWRDA in March.)

cycle.when: Before the Conference (advance information, then background material in mid/late February)
cycle.what: Reporting to the Fellowship starts here: the advance information sent to delegates includes significant questions to take to their areas for input. Assemblies and district meetings take a good look at the Conference agenda, and areas and groups hold pre-Conference sessions to give the delegate their group conscience. The delegate may also set report-back dates and places with the area committee.

cycle.when: 30 days after a new group's information is logged
cycle.what: The new-group pending period (1990 Advisory Action) ends; it gives the delegate and DCM time to welcome the group. GSO then emails the digital Group Handbook. Many groups meet for a month or two before sending the New Group Form (F-30).

cycle.when: Whenever a group or district changes trusted servants
cycle.what: The group reports a new GSR or alternate (or a new name, location or format) on the Group Information Change Form (F-28), and new GSRs automatically get a digital GSR Kit. A new DCM or DCMC goes on the DCM & DCMC Information Change Form (F-43), after which the DCM gets instructions for read-only Fellowship Connection access. Each form goes to GSO by mail or email, or locally to the area registrar.

cycle.when: Three days ending on each 1st, 3rd and 4th quarterly board meeting
cycle.what: Regional trustees are expected at the board; they also attend Conference week and the 2nd quarterly meeting the Saturday after it. General service trustees serve at these times and between them.
The trustees' Finance and Budgetary Committee asks AAWS and Grapevine for budget revisions if earlier estimates have gone too far wrong (Concept XI, kept in the revised essay).
AA Grapevine publishes the Grapevine magazine (La Viña comes out every two months). At GSO, the Staff Coordinator facilitates the monthly in-house Steps, Traditions and Concepts ('1728') meeting.

cycle.when: Late in year two of a delegate's term
cycle.what: The outgoing delegate works with the newly elected delegate to pass along a basic knowledge of Conference proceedings.

Each trustees' committee chair calls the chair of the matching Conference committee to review the weekend's discussions and actions. The trustees' chair also leads a call with the Conference committee's members to hear their views on proposed agenda items.

cycle.when: Between the January 1 résumé deadline and the Conference
cycle.what: The trustees' Nominating Committee reviews every regional trustee and trustee-at-large nominee for eligibility before the Conference. (In trustee-at-large years the regional caucuses that narrow the list come later, during Conference week.)

cycle.when: Most areas: quarterly or every other month
cycle.what: Regular (non-election) area assemblies. A few areas meet monthly; where distances are great, assemblies may meet only twice a year or once a year, with more emphasis placed on district meetings.

cycle.when: On election (fall of an election year)
cycle.what: The new delegate is put on GSO's mailing list for Conference materials and gets a password to the Conference dashboard, where the Conference coordinator and other GSO staff post materials and messages.
